items.title: CUDA spill tier: GLM-5.3-Flash kept prompt states on local disk (--spill-gib)
items.body:
## Summary

Addresses #373 for GLM-5.3-Flash at TP=2 and `--parallel 1` (the `--parallel` pool hook follows #243). On CUDA a kept prompt state that leaves memory costs a full prefill on its next turn, and nothing survives a restart: with GLM-5.3-Flash on two GB10s that is about 340 s for a 200k-token prompt, every time a conversation comes back after another one pushed it out. The Mac server has had a disk tier for this since #68 (`--spill-gib`). This brings it to CUDA for GLM-5.3-Flash (`glm5_next`): a kept state that leaves memory is written to local disk on every rank, and a later request that extends the same tokens reads it back instead of prefilling, also after a restart. Off unless `--spill-gib` is given.

## Related work

- **#300** proposes a generic CUDA `TieredCache`/`DiskTier` (per-segment SHA-256, atomic renames, O_DIRECT, compat hash, reconcile) for families built on its new lane decoder; nothing in the tree uses it yet, and GLM's engine doesn't use `PrefixCache`. Its review lists asynchronous disk writes as not done: this PR's writer threads (pinned staging, their own streams, copies waited for only before the rows they read change) are that piece, and I'd be glad to offer them as a tier there, or move GLM's hooks onto `DiskTier` if GLM moves to lanes. The two can share one `--snapshot-dir`: this writes only under `spill-<hash>/` and prunes only `spill-*` folders.
- **MiaAI-Lab's patch 0132** (`pcache.DiskCache`, `TF_GLM_DISK_CACHE`, in their full GLM-5.3 recipe, on at `--parallel 1`), which #402 lists as a follow-up to propose here. Same engine hooks, so I'd rather converge than compete: whichever lands first, the other can adopt its settings and file format.
- **#342** keeps DeepSeek-V4.1's prompt states on disk (`TF_DSV41_DISK`), and **#106** (closed) was a host-RAM tier for Qwen3.8-27B that you said you want back for 24-32 GB cards.
- **#386** keeps prefix snapshots on disk across a Qwen/Nemotron sleep. Different families and lifecycle; the same offer applies.
- **#243** brings GLM `--parallel` to CUDA. This PR hooks the one-stream engine only and refuses `--spill-gib` with `--parallel` > 1, so the flag can never be silently ignored whichever lands first. The `--parallel` pool hook is written and tested (as a patch for the MiaAI-Lab recipe, whose multi-stream engine #243 upstreams) and would follow #243 here, adding the reads beside decoding and the caller-placed rows that pool needs.
- Open PRs touching the same files, by trial merges against this branch on 2026-10-05: #301, #343, #354, #357, #378, #396, #397, #398, #400 and #404 merge cleanly, and so do those updated later that day (#303, #304, #315, #328, #338, #389, #408, #409, #410, #411, #415, #416). #399, #194, #386, #407, #243 and #320 conflict only where both add lines at the same spot (an argument, a keyword, a call, a changelog entry, the lines before `class GlmEngine`); keeping both resolves each. #399 (`prompt_logprobs`) and #194 (image prompts) gate resuming, and the disk lookup here reads the same `resume` condition, so their gates cover it too. #343's `_drop(why)` would let the tier write only real evictions, and its "a turn reusing it re-prefills it" log line would want the stored case.
- The recipe-side request for the same thing is MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold#57, and the recipe-side PR is MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold#78.

## Change

`--spill-gib N` now works on CUDA for families that set `CUDA_SPILL = True` (`glm5_next` today), with `--parallel 1`. Other CUDA families, and `--parallel` 2 or more, refuse the flag with an error instead of ignoring it. Without the flag the tier's modules (and torch) aren't imported, and the only new work is one 5-int all-gather at GLM's start, checking that every rank was given the same `--spill-*` settings.

| Flag | Default | |
|---|---:|---|
| `--spill-gib N` | 0 (off) | reused from #68; on CUDA the cap is per rank |
| `--snapshot-dir DIR` | `~/.cache/tensorfold/prefix-snapshots` | reused from #68; where the tier writes (see *Spill directory*) |
| `--spill-highwater F` | 0.70 | new: past F of the kept-prompt memory, the states eviction takes next are written early, in the background (1.0: only at eviction) |
| `--spill-min-tokens N` | 8192 | new: shorter states are not written |
| `--spill-min-free-gib N` | 50 | new: no write leaves less disk free than this, on any rank |
| `--spill-keep-builds N` | 1 | new: other builds' spill folders kept at start |

Environment only: `TF_SPILL_WRITERS` (2 writer threads), `TF_SPILL_DIRECT` (1: O_DIRECT where the file system takes it) and `TF_SPILL_FLUSH_S` (60, the shutdown flush budget).

Code: `cuda/spill.py` (524 lines: config, index, rank agreement, pruning, save, load, the shutdown flush), `cuda/spill_format.py` (216: file layout, keys, encode/decode, CRCs), `cuda/spill_io.py` (385: writer threads and reads), `families/glm5_next/cuda/spill_hooks.py` (257: GLM's hooks, a mixin of `GlmEngine`). `engine.py` grows from 590 to 601 lines: the mixin base and short call sites.

## Design

- **Generic serializer, family hook.** `tensorfold.cuda.spill` knows no model. A family hands it the snapshot object it already keeps; `encode` walks its fields into the safetensors-plus-JSON layout `engine/prefix_snapshots.py` uses on MLX (tensors in the file, plain values in the metadata, the class by name). `decode` rebuilds only the classes the family gives the store (GLM's `Snapshot`) and imports nothing. A `materialize` hook attaches rows that still live in the engine's caches (GLM's is `_spill_rows`). A restore decodes the object and hands it to the family's existing resume path.
- **Key inputs as MLX names them.** Files live under `spill-<compat>/rank<N>/`. `compat` covers the weights' resolved path, the TensorFold version and a digest of the family's and `tensorfold.cuda`'s sources and kernels (`build_id`, hashed with `families.hash_sources`, factored out of `kernel_source_version`; every family's MLX key is unchanged, checked for all 10), the runtime whose kernels make the bits (torch, CUDA, GPU and driver), the drafter's path, each rank's own copy of the weights and drafter (every `*.safetensors`/`*.json` file's name, size, mtime and inode: weights rewritten in place start a new folder), the settings `GlmEngine` already makes both ranks agree on at start (draft model, long context, `--no-drafts`, `TF_GLM_LATENT`, prefill rows, `TF_GLM_MTP`, `TF_GLM_DRAFT_RING`; a setting added to that list later joins the key by itself), KV row shapes and dtypes and the rank count. Ranks compare the shared part at start and log any rank that differs; ranks started with different `--spill-*` settings are refused at start instead of waiting on each other. Other builds' folders are pruned at start.
- **Integrity.** Every 8 MiB of a file carries a CRC-32 in its header and every read checks all of them. The CRCs come from `zlib` (the CPU's CRC instructions, where zlib is built with them) and are computed beside the I/O: a writer hashes each staging buffer while the same buffer goes to disk, and the reader hashes a chunk's blocks on four threads while the next chunk is read. A file that fails is forgotten on every rank (`crc_failed`, `load_failed`) and the request prefills. Measured with the same store on the MiaAI-Lab recipe (200k-token states): restore p50 306-312 ms with the CRCs against 285-288 ms without, about +20 ms.
- **Writes off the engine thread, queued writes capped** (both asked on #155). Writer threads have their own CUDA stream and pinned staging buffers, and at most 4 GiB of writes wait on a rank; a write past that first waits for the oldest. A state written from rows `_take_over` saved never waits for its copy (only the queue cap can make a save wait). One written from the live caches holds the next prefill until its last bytes are off the device, about the time it takes to write (`copy_wait_s`; see *Exactness*).
- **DFlash2 window.** A state resumes a drafting request only with its drafter's ring window, and the copy `_take_over` keeps in memory drops that window (`save_rows`), so that copy could never be resumed with drafts, nor written usefully. The tier writes the state at that moment, from the saved rows, with the window it had. Rank 0 reads only entries whose stored drafter fields fit the request. Without the ring (`TF_GLM_DRAFT_RING=0`) no state is written.
- **Crash safety.** Each write goes to its own `.partial`, then `fsync`, a rename only while its entry is still indexed, and a directory `fsync` (at most once a second, and always when the writes drain); the header is padded to 4 KiB so the data can use O_DIRECT. At start a `.partial` is deleted, and so is a file whose size doesn't match its header; at load the same size check, then the CRCs. Files are 0600 and folders 0700, owned by `--snapshot-dir`'s owner: they hold prompts' token ids.
- **Ranks agree.** Every rank takes the same decisions in the same order from the same index. Rank 0 picks the saves, early writes, loads and the shutdown flush; rank 1 follows through the request header it already receives (a load is `-n`: resume from n stored tokens). Eviction under the cap reads only the index, never how far a rank's own writes got: an entry still being written can go, and its writer then removes the file. An entry about to be read is made the newest first, so the saves made while making room for it evict older entries before it. One all-gather per save agrees on the file size and the free-disk floor. A read is used only if it worked *and* its draft caches fit the request on every rank (one 2-int all-gather); otherwise every rank prefills and forgets the entry. At start only entries every rank holds are kept, in rank 0's order, and a rank that cannot create or scan its folder stops every rank.
- **What is written.** A kept state as it leaves memory or when `_take_over` copies its rows, and, past `--spill-highwater`, the ones eviction takes next, early. Not written: states under `--spill-min-tokens`; a state that a longer kept state of the same conversation extends, while that one is stored or can be (`checkpoints.extends`, the Mac tier's rule); with a drafter, a state without its ring window.
- **Bounded disk.** LRU under `--spill-gib`; the free-space floor is checked before every write. Early writes never evict a stored copy of a snapshot still kept: under a cap smaller than what they would write, those copies would evict each other in turn (a write storm seen on the recipe's pool with a 4 GiB cap). The shutdown flush keeps only its own newer picks, and a save that cannot fit beside the entries it must keep evicts nothing.
- **Shutdown flush.** On SIGTERM or Ctrl-C, between requests, kept snapshots not yet on disk are written newest first within `TF_SPILL_FLUSH_S` (the engine is looked up when the signal comes, so a server that swaps engines flushes the one serving). Best effort: a SIGKILL skips it. Stop rank 0 first: a rank stopped before it leaves the flush waiting.
- **Observability.** `/health` reports `"spill"`; `/metrics` adds `tensorfold:spill_*`: gauges (`entries`, `pending`, `stored_bytes`, `disk_free_bytes`, `restore_p50_seconds`, `restore_p95_seconds`) and counters ending in `_total` (written, loaded, `load_failed`, `crc_failed`, `load_unfit`, early writes, unwritten evictions, bytes, seconds, copy waits and more).

### Spill directory

The Mac tier writes conversations to a sibling of `--snapshot-dir` (`<parent>/session-snapshots`). This writes inside `--snapshot-dir`, under `spill-<compat>/rank<N>/`, on purpose: on CUDA `--snapshot-dir` is usually a mount (`-v /nvme:/spill --snapshot-dir /spill`), and a sibling of it lands outside the mount. The subfolders can't collide with the Mac's files, whose readers glob only top-level `*.safetensors`. Matching the Mac layout is a one-line change in `SpillConfig.from_args` if you prefer it.

## Receipt

**Environment.** This branch at `31a3d4e` on 0.6.5 (`609ca41`; the receipt and the restart run below used an earlier commit of this branch, `c6fbbba` (*On the final commit* covers the cap on the GPU); the final commit adds two fixes that act only when the disk cap is reached (a save that cannot fit beside the entries it must keep evicts nothing; the flush keeps only its own newer picks), covered by the CPU tests below, and makes one docstring a single line. The first fix is in `SpillStore._make_room`, the same code as in MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold#78, which ran it on these Sparks under a 4 GiB disk cap in the `--parallel` pool: 8 writes, no copy waits, replies after a restart equal to `"draft": false`); PyTorch 2.13.0 (NGC 26.07), CUDA 13.3; two ASUS GX10 (GB10, driver 580.173.02) at TP=2; `Mia-AiLab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-4bpw-TensorFold` at `078455ff`, DFlash2 drafter `incoai/GLM-5.3-Flash-DFlash2` at `bf582e4e`. "Before" is 0.6.5 as released; "after" is this branch with `--spill-gib 64 --spill-highwater 0.70`; one run each, page caches dropped before each start.

**Exactness.**
`tools/bench_concurrent.py --levels 1 --alone --serial` on this branch with the tier on: 12 of 12 replies equal their alone runs and 4 of 4 equal the serial reference, over code and chat prompts at temperature 1.0 and 0.0, no failures.

**Through the spill tier**, 3 conversations of 100k tokens, each small enough to stay in memory (so each takes the DFlash2 path above). Storing them (`suite.py core`: 3 cold prompts, then each resent), the cold prompts took 165.9-167.1 s each, and each state was written as the next prompt took over (`written 3`; the copies kept in memory had dropped their DFlash2 windows). Resent, the live one resumed from the caches in 0.18 s and the other two were read from disk in 0.92 s and 0.48 s (`loaded 2`, `load_failed 0`, restore p50 320 ms); without the tier those two are full prefills. After a clean restart the new start reported `3 stored prompts from before this start, 5.2 GiB`; two conversations were left as stored and the third had one data bit flipped on rank 1 while the server ran; then each conversation's 256 greedy tokens were compared with a fresh `"draft": false` prefill:

- `conv 0 live none ranks [] PASS equal True loads 1 load_failed 0 cached 100192 files r0 ['valid'] r1 ['valid'] (control: restored from disk and exact)`
- `conv 1 live none ranks [] PASS equal True loads 1 load_failed 0 cached 100161 files r0 ['valid'] r1 ['valid'] (control: restored from disk and exact)`
- `conv 2 live flip ranks [1] PASS equal True loads 1 load_failed 1 cached 0 files r0 ['rewritten'] r1 ['rewritten'] (CRC-32 mismatch at load, forgotten on both ranks, prefilled, exact)`

Rank 0's `/health` shows `load_failed 1`; the CRC failure is counted (`crc_failed`) on rank 1, which read the damaged file. Files were 0600 and the rank folders 0700 on both Sparks.

**On the final commit** (`31a3d4e`), under a disk cap. With 4 conversations of 100k tokens and `--spill-gib 6` (three fit), the cap evicted the least recently used state (5 writes, 3 kept, 2 resends read from disk, copy waits 1.42 s in all), and the restart reported `3 stored prompts from before this start, 5.2 GiB`. With 4 conversations of 30k tokens and `--spill-gib 1.9`, the conversation read from disk after a restart (30,170 tokens) answered in 6.3 s against 64.1 s for a fresh `"draft": false` prefill, with an equal reply. The other three were prefilled, because the test's own newer states had pushed their files out under the cap, and their replies were equal too.

**Decode speed** (`tools/bench_openai.py`):

| Prompt | Temperature | 0.6.5 tok/s | this branch tok/s |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| `fibonacci-raw` | 1 | 35.5 | 35.6 |
| `fibonacci-raw` | 0 | 41.9 | 41.8 |
| `gpu-chat-no-think` | 1 | 26.7 | 26.5 |
| `gpu-chat-no-think` | 0 | 24.2 | 24.1 |

Medians of five runs each (`tools/bench_openai.py` defaults).

**Prompt speed** (`tools/prefill_cold.py`, cold 2k-64k):

| Prompt | 0.6.5 first token | this branch first token |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 2,041 tokens | 3.94 s (518 tok/s) | 3.94 s (518 tok/s) |
| 8,186 tokens | 16.43 s (498 tok/s) | 16.45 s (498 tok/s) |
| 16,378 tokens | 32.96 s (497 tok/s) | 33.00 s (496 tok/s) |
| 32,762 tokens | 65.75 s (498 tok/s) | 65.98 s (497 tok/s) |
| 65,530 tokens | 127.65 s (513 tok/s) | 128.45 s (510 tok/s) |

Medians of three cold prompts per length (`tools/prefill_cold.py`).

**Tests.** CPU, in a container without a GPU: `tests/test_cuda_spill.py` (26, the metrics test among them) and `tests/test_glm_cuda_spill.py` (17), the new cases in `test_cuda_cli.py` (`--parallel` refused), with every `tests/test_glm*.py`, `test_cuda_cli`, `test_cuda_server_health`, `test_health_memory`, `test_metrics*`, `test_cli_plan`, `test_checkpoint_spill` and `test_issue155_spill`: **231 passed, 16 skipped, 1 failed**. The failure, `test_health_memory.py::test_health_reports_the_budget_and_the_process_footprint`, fails the same way on 0.6.5; the skips need `mlx`. The full suite in the same container, 8 workers, 180 s a test: 0.6.5 has 4,073 passed, 128 failed, 11 errors and 175 skipped; this branch has 4,120 passed: its own 46 more, and `test_cuda_memory_plan.py::test_the_drafter_loads_after_the_target`, which failed on an earlier run of this branch as on 0.6.5 and so passes or fails from run to run here. No test fails only on this branch; the others fail on both, most for want of `mlx` or a GPU in the container. Each was checked to fail without the change it covers: the slow-writer test of `_take_over` with the wait removed (the stored rows are the next prompt's), the flipped-bit test without the CRC check, two ranks dropping the same entry under the cap while one still writes it, a rank that cannot use its folder stopping both, the cap on queued writes, `_take_over` writing a state with the window its saved copy drops, an older turn written when the longer one cannot be, an entry whose stored drafter fields don't fit not being read, a stored prompt not evicted by the room made for its own read, early writes leaving copies of kept snapshots alone, a save that cannot fit beside the copies it must keep evicting nothing, the flush writing the newest snapshot under a full cap, and a state larger than the cap evicting nothing.

**What I did not run.** Metal: nothing here runs on a Mac. The changes in shared code are `families.hash_sources`, factored out of `kernel_source_version` and checked to give every one of the 10 families the same key as before by resolving their sources as files (MLX doesn't import on CUDA), not on an Apple Silicon machine; and `server/metrics.py`, `cli_args.py` and `cuda/http.py`, which the CPU tests above cover. TP=3 or 4, one GPU, and families other than GLM (they refuse `--spill-gib`). The full fault matrix on the GPU: the same store, as a patch on the MiaAI-Lab recipe, passed truncated, header-damaged, bit-flipped and deleted files on one rank or both, at rest and while serving (every request prefilled, every reply exact); on this branch the GPU run covers a flipped bit (above) and the CPU tests cover each other case.

### Exactness

Validating this branch found one bug, fixed here: kept prompts that `_take_over` dropped for the next conversation were written from views of the live caches, and the next prefill overwrote those rows before the copy finished, so a restored state could differ (2 of 3 replies did, one from its first token). `_take_over` now waits for such copies before the caller's prefill or restored rows touch the caches; `tests/test_glm_cuda_spill.py` reproduces it with a slow writer and fails without the fix. Upstream's own in-memory resume, checked the same way without this branch, is exact.

A review before submitting found two more, also fixed here with tests that fail without the fix: the ranks could disagree on which entry the cap dropped while one rank's write of it was still running (a later save or read would then pair unrelated all-gathers), and with a DFlash2 drafter a state that fit in memory was never written (its saved copy had lost the window).

### Earlier measurements

Before the race fix, the CRCs and the review fixes, on the same machines, 15 conversations of 200k tokens (states larger than the kept-prompt memory, so each was written from the live caches as it left), 0.6.5 against this branch:

| Scenario | 0.6.5 | this branch |
|---|---|---|
| 15 evicted 200k prompts resent | 0/15 resumed, 340.5 s | **15/15, 1.2 s** |
| The same 15 after a clean restart | 0/15, 339.7 s | **15/15, 1.3 s** |
| 4 evicted 200k prompts returning at once (+4 new) | 0/4, mean 1294.6 s | **4/4, mean 192.3 s** |
| An evicted 200k prompt returning behind 3 queued requests (GLM on CUDA serves one at a time, so this includes the wait) | 518.1 s | **81.5 s** |
| Cold 200k prompts (the cost of writing) | 340.2 s, 589 tok/s | 340.2 s, 589 tok/s |

## Limits

- The CRCs catch flipped bits and torn, cut or misplaced blocks; they are not signatures against someone who can write the files on purpose.
- GLM-5.3-Flash, `--parallel 1` (the pool hook follows #243). The store is family- and rank-agnostic (`SpillStore(world=1)` needs no communication); other families need their own `materialize`/`save`/`load` wiring (`docs/cuda-spill.md`, *Adding a family*) and refuse `--spill-gib` until they have it.
- One file per stored state, resumed exactly where it was taken (the recurrent KDA state can't be cut shorter). An earlier turn superseded by a later kept one isn't written, so regenerating an old turn after newer ones prefills it, as it would from memory.
- If a stored read fails, the request prefills from the start even when a shorter state was kept in memory (both ranks must agree on one resume point, and rank 1 learns only the stored one).
- With a DFlash2 drafter the tier needs the drafter's ring (`TF_GLM_DRAFT_RING`, on by default).
- A write that fails on one rank leaves its entry indexed on every rank (they must stay alike) until a read of it fails, which forgets it everywhere, or it ages out under the cap; until then that state is not written again.
- The shutdown flush is best effort.

## Checklist

- [x] Every token still goes through the lane rounds. No serial path, and nothing that needs drafts off. (A restored state replaces only the prefill it covers; the request then runs as before.)
- [x] Drafted output equals `"draft": false`, a resumed prompt equals a fresh one, and concurrent equals solo (*Exactness* above, the three restored conversations included).
- [x] No precision traded for speed. No bits change: a restored state is the bytes that were stored, CRC-checked.
- [x] Prompt processing is no slower than the last release (*Prompt speed* above).
- [x] The description says which platforms I ran (CUDA on two GB10s) and which I could not (Metal; see *What I did not run*).
- [x] New tests fail before the change, pass after it, and skip cleanly without their dependency (`pytest.importorskip("torch")`).
- [x] Comments and docstrings are one line. No measurements or history in the source.
- [x] No personal data, machine names, internal hosts or local paths. No AI attribution lines.

## Credits

- Persisting session state on NVMe per rank: MiaAI-Lab's GLM-5.3-Flash vLLM kit, MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks#232 (@gabewillen); the idea only, no code from that AGPL-3.0 project.
- The multi-rank design (rank 0 decides, per-rank files, agreement on reads, reconcile at start): patch 0250 of jayleaton/glm53-tensorfold-spark (Apache-2.0); the code here is new.
- The spill-on-evict hook, file conventions and flag names: the Mac spill, #68 (@gilby), and #155 (@raymondkpwong), whose discussion asked for spill writes off the engine thread.
- Checking every file on read, private file modes, a per-rank weights fingerprint and naming a rank whose settings differ: the session tier of JSpark3 v2.0.1 (jakejharris/jspark3), which keeps a SHA-256 for every saved tensor; this uses CRC-32 per 8 MiB block to keep restores fast.

items.title: [Draft] EXL3 Flash Next on CUDA: TP=2, BF16 paging, cache reuse, graphs
items.body:
**Draft for upstream review; not merge-ready.** This is the working line for serving the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next EXL3 pack on two RTX 5060 Ti 16 GiB cards, based on current upstream `main`. The immediate goal is a working, optimized implementation; this deliberately broad draft will be split into focused PRs before merge.

## What it adds

- EXL3 loading and CUDA execution in TensorFold's Flash Next path.
- Routed-expert offload with per-layer GPU pools, pinned host banks, and asynchronous H2D staging.
- Expert-parallel TP=2 with split routed experts, shared-expert execution, vocabulary-sharded `lm_head`, and NCCL collectives.
- BF16 KV paging to host RAM, snapshot/restore, and prefix/cache reuse.
- MTP drafting, plus CUDA graph capture/replay for decode and prefill paths.

## Proposed PR segmentation

The PRs should be split and reviewed in dependency order; each PR owns one coherent layer, includes focused tests, and records correctness and performance evidence. Until then, this mega PR remains a tracking draft and should not be merged as one piece.

1. **EXL3 foundation and resident forward:** format/config parsing, real weight loading, upstream CUDA adapter, and layer/model oracle gates. This establishes a correct non-offloaded path.
2. **Expert pool and offload:** host-bank layout, device line pools, replacement policy, asynchronous copies, and pool lifecycle tests. Gate: pooled output matches resident execution; document copy/compute overlap.
3. **TP=2 execution and serving:** expert partitioning, shared-expert placement, vocabulary head split, collectives, and rank lifecycle. Gate: TP=2 logits/outputs match the defined numerical tolerance and server works on both GPUs.
4. **BF16 KV paging and state reuse:** device/host page tables, paging/eviction, snapshots that preserve paged state, restore, and prefix branching. Gate: paged equals resident; snapshot/restore and cache reuse preserve exact state/logits, including long-context tests.
5. **MTP drafting:** draft head fed from real logits, TP=2 draft/verify path, and prompt-cache interaction. Gate: drafted committed tokens equal serial decoding with drafting disabled.
6. **CUDA graph decode:** stable graph inputs/outputs, TP=2 collectives, expert-offload boundaries, capture/replay lifecycle, and snapshot restore. Gate: graph and eager outputs match across replay and recovery.
7. **CUDA graph prefill and scheduling:** chunked prefill capture, expert-major scheduling, staging overlap, and profiling-driven tuning. Gate: graph-on improves controlled prefill/decode measurements without correctness or memory regressions.
8. **Final capacity and product integration:** repeated 200k-context × 2-concurrency TP=2 runs with BF16 paging/cache reuse, resource margin, failure cleanup, then family/recipe registration. Registration stays out until all preceding gates pass.

Dependencies: PR 1 precedes the rest; PRs 2 and 3 build on it; PR 4 needs stable TP=2 allocation/lifecycle; PR 5 needs TP=2 and cache semantics; graph PRs depend on stable paging/offload and eager behavior. The graph decode and prefill PRs may be developed in parallel after those interfaces are fixed, then merged in that order. Do not create eight duplicate implementations: use stacked branches or cherry-pick cleanly after each preceding PR lands, and keep the umbrella draft as an index until the sequence is complete.

## Evidence and remaining gates

- TP=2 serving, draft-on/off parity, BF16 paging, snapshots/cache reuse, and graph/eager correctness have been exercised on development hardware on earlier source-tree revisions.
- CUDA graphs currently match eager in tested paths, but controlled profiling has not established a graph-on speedup. That is a hard performance gate, not a claimed win.
- The strict golden-prompt near-tie and remaining TP numerical-parity questions still require closure.
- Re-run the full TP=2, snapshot/restore, cache-reuse, graph-prefill/decode, and 200k × 2 gates on the current branch before merge or model registration.
- `tools/zig/lean_check.py` reports 1,317 findings beyond upstream `main`; this remains a CONTRIBUTING blocker.
- CPU expert execution is out of scope. BF16 remains the required KV-cache format; int8 KV is not part of the serving path.

Upstream base: `d1018b318fb51981c4a18f12e40269a4d3ee9713`

items.title: Flash Next on CUDA: the qwen4_exp family on the native CUDA host, every stream through the lane rounds
items.body:
## What this changes

Adds a CUDA engine for Qwen3.8 Flash Next (`qwen4_exp`) to `tensorfold-native`: an MLX affine 4-bit, group-32
checkpoint with its MTP head, served through the core's lane rounds, lane host and prompt cache, with drafted windows,
shared rounds, kept prompt states and prompt chunks between other streams' rounds. Every kernel it launches is built
from this repository, so it boots with no capture. `TENSORFOLD_CUDA_KERNELS` can name a captured set of the Python
0.6.1 engine's Triton kernels, which then stands in for our glue so its tokens can be compared with that engine's
teacher path; `TF_FLASHNEXT_OWNED` swaps single entry points back to ours beside a set. It builds on @AdrianBinDC's
#476 and answers #472. His commits are here with his authorship and messages, rebased onto `main` with #835's cache
guard (027ddea9): five needed their `zig/build/cuda.zig` or `zig/tests/cuda/copies.py` hunks fitted to what `main` has
now, and his formatting commit is left out, since `main` has the same line from his 7bbe2208.

Following `docs/recipes/adding-a-zig-family.md` and CONTRIBUTING.md:30-31, the family supplies its config check, weight
map, layer graph and kernels for what is its own; shared pieces are the core's:

- the round loop, verify/accept and the lane host schedule every token; the family adds no scheduler;
- the prompt cache's store and rules keep and resume states; the family copies a stream's state (with the MTP head's
  rows for a drafting stream, lookahead 1 as Nemotron);
- prompts run a chunk a call through the core's `prefill_step`;
- shared row kernels: token rows (`embed_rows.cu`, now in groups of 32 with a copy a stream), RMS rows with their group
  sums (`norms.cu`, the MTP head's norms), a new `route_rows.cu` for router logits and softmax top-k with a shared
  gate, and the routed experts over a window's rows on the core's plan (`cuda/grouped.zig`) and a new core lane kernel,
  `experts_rows.cu` (`cuda.experts.RowsExperts`), which gives every row the decode kernel's sums;
- the family's own kernels: the hyper-connections and the n-gram gate and conv (`flashnext_hc.cu`), attention with its
  output gate and the sparse indexer's pooling and scores (`flashnext_attn.cu`), the indexer's block selection and the
  Gated DeltaNet chain (`flashnext_batch.cu`), and the MTP head;
- shards are read with `core.safetensors.File`; a captured set is packed with `tools/zig/triton_aot_pack.py` and
  launched through `cuda.aot.Set`.

Every kernel keeps a row's own sums in a fixed order, so a row's bits are the same at any row count: drafted windows
equal serial decoding, rounds equal lone streams, resumed prompts equal fresh ones. Our glue rounds to bf16 where the
Python engine's kernels do, with IEEE division and square root and the core's within-one-ulp exp (`glue_math.cuh`);
the router and the hyper-connections' 4-bit dots run on mma tiles with K in ascending order.

Commits:
- @AdrianBinDC's 22 commits from #476: the embedding, every layer type and the final mix matched to the Python engine's
  host checks one by one, then a drafts-off prompt token for token.
- The token-id and position uploads go on the compute stream, and attention runs over every 512-key chunk a prompt has.
- `native/cuda.zig` reads a family's prompt-cache copies, cache rules and device weight bytes from what it declares
  (Nemotron's paths unchanged); Flash Next registers.
- Core: `experts_rows.cu` and `tf-cuda-test experts-rows`.
- Core: `triton_aot_pack.py` leaves out constexprs Triton folded from `None` and takes a `--jit` per capture.
- The engine on one batched pass (prompts and decode rounds), the sparse indexer and the 262,144-token window.
- The MTP head, its chains, verify windows and the DeltaNet rollback.
- The lane backend: drafted windows, shared rounds, kept prompt states (drafting streams too), prompt steps.
- A sequence's buffers are zeroed on the compute stream (a fill with no stream raced the first pass).
- The config check refuses semantic settings the kernels fix (RMS epsilon, RoPE, gate and activation types, layer
  roles, the n-gram layer), by field name.
- A failed zero fill frees the buffer it was filling.
- A pass's uploads read pinned staging the scratch owns until the copies land.
- Core: `route_rows.cu` (router logits on mma tiles, softmax top-k with a shared gate) with `core/route_ref.zig` and
  `tf-cuda-test route-rows`.
- Core: token rows in groups of 32 with copies, and RMS rows with their group sums; `norm-rows` covers both.
- Our glue, `flashnext_hc.cu` and `flashnext_attn.cu`, with `tf-cuda-test flashnext-hc` and `flashnext-attn`.
- The engine boots on our glue; a captured set that holds every entry point is used for comparison; `flashnext-compare`.
- `TF_FLASHNEXT_OWNED`, our glue for the named entry points beside a captured set.
- Docs: `docs/recipes/flash-next-cuda.md`, the Flash Next, CUDA and recipe-index pages, RUNBOOK, CHANGELOG.

## Receipt

- Environment: TensorFold `flashnext-cuda` 7746bb9d on 027ddea9 (`main` c7137bb3, v1.0.11 + 19, with #835's cache guard),
  Zig 0.17.0; NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark, sm_121), driver 580.178.04, CUDA 13.0.88, Ubuntu 24.04.5; checkpoint
  `leimroth-lab/Unbound-LR7` revision 2ae3a2ff (Qwen3.8 Flash Next, MLX affine 4-bit group 32, MTP head). "Captured"
  is the same build with `TENSORFOLD_CUDA_KERNELS` naming the 76-kernel set packed from 4 captures of the Python 0.6.1
  engine; `main` has no Flash Next on CUDA to compare against.
- Our kernels, each against float64 at the model's shapes (`tf-cuda-test`): `route-rows` (logits within the fp32
  dot's bound, picks equal to the reference rule's, weights and the shared gate within half a bf16 ulp plus 2^-18),
  `norm-rows` (the group-32 token rows with copies, RMS rows with group sums), `flashnext-hc` and `flashnext-attn`
  (each bf16 output within one bf16 ulp of a float64 chain that rounds where the kernel rounds, fp32 sums within their
  sum-of-|terms| bound, attention within 2^-8 of sum p|v|/l plus half an ulp, copies and stream adds exact). Every case
  also checks that 1, 3 and 17 rows (attention: 1, 3 and 20, both of its forms) give each row the same bits.
- Exactness on our kernels (the default):
  - `TF_FLASHNEXT_DRAFTS=6`: drafted equals serial token for token on 6 prompts greedy and 5 seeded.
  - `tools/bench_concurrent.py --alone --serial`, 1/2/4 streams, code and chat, greedy and T=1, drafts on and off:
    every cell equal to its solo run (112 of 112) and drafted cells equal to `"draft": false` (30 of 30), 0 failed.
  - Resumed equals fresh: a 1,160-token prompt resumes 1,153 tokens and two more resume a 1,139-token system cut, with
    drafts and without, alone and with 4 at once; every `token_sha` equal to the fresh run.
  - 45,030 tokens at `--context 65536`: the same `token_sha` drafted, `"draft": false` and both resumed (45,025 cached).
  - `flashnext-select` equals Triton's block lists.
- Against the Python engine's teacher path, `flashnext-prompt` (32 greedy tokens): captured 32/32 on all five prompts
  (19, 52, 600, 3,001 and 12,001 tokens). Ours: 32/32 on the 19-, 52-, 600- and 12,001-token prompts; on the
  3,001-token prompt ours parts at token 15, where the captured path's best two scores are 0.375 apart.
- Ours against the captured set, every prompt row teacher-forced on one loaded engine (`flashnext-compare`):

  | prompt | rows | top-1 agree | KL mean / median / max | perplexity captured / ours |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | 19 tokens | 19 | 19 | 1.7e-3 / 2.4e-5 / 0.027 | 5.786 / 5.791 |
  | 52 tokens | 52 | 52 | 7.1e-4 / 2.9e-5 / 0.0096 | 440.3 / 420.4 |
  | 600 tokens (code) | 600 | 577 | 0.027 / 3.8e-3 / 3.32 | 15.38 / 18.40 |
  | 3,001 tokens (Python reference) | 3,001 | 2,873 | 0.028 / 3.3e-3 / 4.27 | 134.3 / 186.0 |
  | 12,001 tokens (Python reference) | 12,001 | 11,651 | 0.019 / 1.2e-3 / 8.68 | 368.7 / 411.6 |
  | 4,096 tokens of this repo's docs | 4,096 | 3,890 | 0.012 / 5.1e-3 / 0.95 | 6.168 / 6.178 |

  On natural documentation the two agree to 0.15% in perplexity, with a median per-token NLL difference of 1e-6 nats.
  The Python-reference prompts are hypersensitive: with everything else captured, swapping in any single one of our
  kernels that is not bit-identical moves the 3,001-token prompt's perplexity as far as the whole set does (from
  134.3 to between 119 and 183; past 2,048 tokens, from 262 to between 209 and 654, where all of ours gives 483), and
  on the 600-token prompt from 15.38 to between 12.9 and 16.2. Four of our entry points give the captured cubins'
  bits exactly, so swapping them alone changes nothing (KL 0): `_embed`, `_router`, `_pool` and `_scores`.
- Decode and prompt speed, the same build and session (`tools/bench_openai.py` 256 tokens median of 3;
  `bench_concurrent.py` aggregate tok/s; `bench_cache.py --require-cold`):

  | | captured | ours |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | 1 stream drafted, code / chat | 82.5 / 62.1 | 84.2 / 62.6 |
  | 1 stream `--no-drafts`, code / chat | 35.2 / 35.2 | 35.1 / 35.1 |
  | `--no-drafts` 1 / 2 / 4 streams, code T=1 | 35.2 / 53.0 / 77.1 | 35.0 / 53.1 / 77.9 |
  | `--no-drafts` 1 / 2 / 4 streams, code greedy | 35.1 / 55.8 / 82.2 | 35.0 / 55.5 / 81.9 |
  | drafted 1 / 2 / 4 streams, code greedy | 82.3 / 81.1 / 80.7 | 83.8 / 82.7 / 82.2 |
  | drafted 1 / 2 / 4 streams, code T=1 | 76.6 / 65.7 / 70.2 | 77.0 / 65.6 / 67.9 |
  | cold first token, 3,001 / 12,001 tokens (s) | 2.67 / 10.30 | 2.67 / 10.40 |
  | 45,030-token prompt, no cache, `"draft": false` (s) | 35.8 | 36.5 |
  | another stream's longest wait during a 12,001-token prompt (s) | 1.29 | 1.31 |

  `flashnext-prompt` on the five prompts: prompt 92.5 / 150.1 / 662.6 / 2,483 / 9,574 ms ours against 90.8 / 154.5 /
  690.3 / 2,504 / 9,533 captured; decode 29.9 / 31.6 / 30.5 / 33.2 / 31.9 ms a token against 30.3 / 31.9 / 32.6 /
  32.0 / 30.7 (the replies differ on the 3,001-token prompt). With the prompt cache on, the 45,030-token prompt comes
  back resumed at 45,025 tokens in 0.11 s without drafts and 0.17 s drafted.
- Memory: the model takes 75.8 GiB with the head (74.2 without); a stream at a 16,384-token window 0.74 GiB with drafts
  and 0.54 without; at 65,536, 2.15 GiB.
- Tests: `zig build test-cuda-host` from a fresh cache: 29/29 steps, 503/503 tests pass, 0 skipped, and each commit after #476's builds (`zig build`) and passes them; `zig build native` builds from 8391cac7 on (#476's tip 0d04c434 and the commit after it stop at `native/cuda.zig`'s `F.max_segments`, which the registry commit supplies); `tf-cuda-test` smoke 7, symbols 1, experts-rows 7, norms 1, norm-rows 1, sample 1, glue 1, pocket
  3, quant-ref 4, modelopt 4, exlr8 7, route-rows 1, flashnext-hc 1, flashnext-attn 1: all pass, 0 fail, 0 skip;
  `lean_check.py` 0 new problems against 027ddea9; `zig fmt --check` clean; all 42 fatbins build for sm_86, sm_120 and sm_121. A captured set without Flash
  Next's entry points is passed over at load and the server answers on its own glue.
- Not run: Metal (no change there; the Mac Flash Next host is untouched), sm_86 and sm_120 cards (none here), CUDA
  graphs (none in this engine).

## Checklist

- [x] Every token still goes through the lane rounds. No serial path, and nothing that needs drafts off.
- [x] Drafted output equals `"draft": false`, a resumed prompt equals a fresh one, and concurrent equals solo.
- [x] No precision traded for speed. If the bits change, the description says which sums change and why. Ours against
  the captured kernels: `_embed`, `_router`, `_pool` and `_scores` give the same bits; the others change at the ulp
  level, from IEEE division and square root and a within-one-ulp exp where Triton uses its approximate forms (the
  norms' 1/sqrt, sigmoid, SiLU and softmax exps, the output gate), from fixed-order block and warp sums where Triton
  reduces in its own tree (the write-back's and n-gram gate's squared sums, the group sums the 4-bit dots take, the
  attention rows' p sums), from attention tiles of 32 keys where Triton's are 64 (the online softmax rescales at other
  points), from explicit fused multiply-adds in the dots' epilogues and the merge, and from sincosf with full range
  reduction for RoPE. Which tokens that moves is in the receipt.
- [ ] Prompt processing is no slower than the last release. (No release has this engine; against the captured set a
  cold 12,001-token prompt is 1% slower, 10.40 s against 10.30 s.)
- [x] The description says which platforms I ran, Metal M1 to M5 and CUDA, and which I could not. (GB10 only.)
- [x] New tests fail before the change, pass after it, and skip cleanly without their dependency.
- [x] Comments and docstrings are one line. No measurements or history in the source.
- [x] No personal data, machine names, internal hosts or local paths. No AI attribution lines.

## Not in this PR, said plainly

- Our glue's tokens are not the Python engine's teacher path's on every prompt: on the 3,001-token prompt they part at
  token 15. The captured set, given by `TENSORFOLD_CUDA_KERNELS`, still gives that path's tokens (32/32 on all five).
- Dense projections run #476's copy of the Python engine's group-32 lane matmul (`qmm.cu`); the core's `qmm_group` and
  `lane_gemv` are built for groups of 64. I have not checked whether a group-32 `qmm_group` instance gives the same bits.
- No CUDA graphs and no GPU-side rounds. Drafted streams verify their windows one batched pass each, so drafted
  throughput does not grow with streams, and the MTP head drafts one stream at a time (Nemotron batches them, #768).
- Prompts are slower than the Python engine's: a cold 12,001-token prompt takes 10.4 s here against 6.7 s there.
- Draws are made on the host from each row's scores (a 248,320-wide bf16 row a token).
- int8 KV is not in this PR; bf16 only.
- Checked on a GB10 only; the kernels build for the release SMs but have not run on sm_86 or sm_120.
- The core's `DeviceBuffer.fill8(..., null)` returns before the memset lands on device memory and is not ordered with a
  non-blocking stream. This PR stops Flash Next using it; a doc line on `fill8` may save the next family the same hunt.

items.title: KV pages: one core owner with reservation leases, Nemotron CUDA pilot (#781)
items.body:
The first slice of #781, as agreed there: a model-free core layout and reservation owner, then Nemotron on CUDA. Rebased on main 46a08c18 (1.0.12).

**Core (`zig/src/core/kv_pool.zig`)**

- `Layout`: fixed bytes, token bytes, page rows, snapshot slot bytes; `need(prompt, max_tokens, window)` = pages of prompt + max_tokens + 16.
- `plan`: room, less the engine's own sequence (counted once), the other streams' fixed parts, the snapshot slots and the copied-KV budget, then pages. Never more pages than every other stream could hold at once.
- `Pool`: page ids, holders, free list and promised count. Leases beside it: `promise` / `unpromise` / `take` / `cover` (rolls back if the table write fails) / `adopt` / `share` / `finish`. A promise that doesn't fit asks the store to reclaim first, then fails with `LaneMemory`. `prompt_radix.pagesOf` hands a Pool to the paged store as its `Pages`.
- `test-kv-pool`: Nemotron's arithmetic (2,048 + 4,096 + 16 rows = 13 pages, 45.5 MiB). Every table write and every allocation fails in turn, and nothing leaks. 300 random admit/keep/resume/finish/cancel/failure runs through `prompt_radix`, with every page's holders checked after each step and everything free at the end. A lane host where a second request waits for the first stream's pages and runs when it ends; a `LaneMemory` requeue; past the whole pool alone, it fails in words.

**Nemotron CUDA**

- The engine's own full-window sequence, its graphs and the lone fast path are unchanged.
- The other `--parallel` streams get paged sequences made at load (64 MiB fixed each). Their K and V rows (6 attention layers + the MTP head, 7 KiB a token) come from one arena of 512-row pages.
- Admission: the engine's own sequence is free, or the pool holds the request's pages.
- `kv_write`, `attn_chunk` (and its prefetch and shared-window copies) and the prompt chunk's `pattn` read a page table at a fixed device address. A null table keeps the contiguous rows.
- The copy store stays, with the MTP lookahead. It copies a paged sequence's rows page by page.
- Snapshot Mamba states live in slots made at load. These replace the spares and the per-save `cuMemAlloc`. `--prompt-cache-gib` is split into slots and the copied rows' budget, and `Store.most` caps the number of states at the slot count.
- The startup line shows the pool. An idle pool logs `promised 0, free + store == total; slots free + held == count`.
- `TF_KV_PAGES=0`: a window per stream, as before. `TF_KV_PAGES=all`: every stream on pages (for checks; with `--parallel 1` the one stream keeps the engine's own). `TF_KV_POISON=1`: NaN in pages a stream takes.
- The captured Triton set and `--slide` keep a window per stream.

**What 1.0.12 changed that touches this**

- `prefill_attention.cu` now shares one row body (`prefill_attention_rows.cuh`) between `pattn_kernel`, the tree kernel and the full kernel. The page table goes into that body; the tree and full kernels pass a null table, so LFM2 and the vision towers read contiguous rows as before (`lfm2-attention` and `lfm2-vision` output identical to main's).
- Super VL (`nemotron_h_omni`) opens the same Nemotron engine, so its other streams take pages too. Its vision tower and image rows are engine-wide, not per stream, and ranks past 0 of a latent MoE hold no KV. Not run here (no checkpoint on this box).
- GLM and the other CUDA families have no layout and keep a window per stream. The paging and slot code in `native/cuda.zig` (moved to `native/cuda_kv_pool.zig`) only applies to a family that declares it.
- `--learn-conversations` reads disk states into a kept state, which takes a snapshot slot. The disk recall now frees a slot first, as the in-memory paths do (new test in `rows_test.zig`). Its probe at startup takes a slot after the slots are made.
- `--record` with paged streams: the recorder reads the per-stream hidden rows, which every paged sequence has.

**Checks** (GB10, NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit, main 46a08c18 as reference)

- `zig build test`, `test-kv-pool`, `zig fmt --check` pass. Lean check: 516 problems against main's 517.
- `tf-cuda-test glue`: 1,365 of 1,365 comparisons equal, including the paged kernels against contiguous ones, alone and in shared windows, at page edges.
- `tf-cuda-test paged`, pages shuffled and NaN-filled: the paged prompt pass and 24 decoded tokens equal the own sequence's. States at 511/512/513, 1023/1024/1025, 2047/2048/2049 and len-5 resume equal to fresh in both directions. `tf-cuda-test resume` passes.
- Resumed == fresh:
  - `reuse_served.py record` on `TF_KV_PAGES=all TF_KV_POISON=1 --parallel 4`, replayed on `TF_KV_PAGES=0 --prompt-cache-gib 0`: 43 of 43 token SHAs equal.
  - The same record on main: identical SHAs and cached counts for all 44 rows. The 6 "not cached as planned" rows fail the same way on main (the tool's expectations: the lookahead's one row, and `--min-prompt`).
- Seeded and greedy drafted == plain, and concurrent (4 at once) == solo: 24 of 24 with every stream paged, with the default split, and at `--parallel 1`. All three give main's SHAs.
- Admission: with a 54-page pool, three 15,000-token requests ran one after another, each starting after the previous one ended. Idle log even.
- `reuse_served.py evict` (1 GiB): same rows and SHAs as main. Its 3 expectation failures fail the same way on main.
- `--record` with paging on: 24 of 24 token SHAs equal to the run without it. The recorded rows equal main's recording byte for byte (36 of 36 streams). Whether a stream's last row is recorded depends on how its verify windows fell, on main too.
- `--learn-conversations`: after a restart, turn 2 read 5,255 tokens from disk, and its SHA equals a fresh pass.
- Decode, alternated against main (`--parallel 4`, two rounds): fibonacci 77.8/78.1 tok/s on main, 78.0/78.1 on this branch; chat 55.1/55.3 vs 55.0/55.2. 4 streams, code: 193.6/225.3 vs 229.4/224.6.
- 23 guard mutations (pool, lane host, store slot caps, disk recall, paged kernels, page copies, page release), each caught by a test.
- Not run: Super VL and multi-rank tensor-parallel paging (no checkpoint, one Spark), and `structured_served.py`.

items.title: Gemma 4 31B served natively on Metal: the dense family, DFlash drafts, tensor-unit prompts past mlx-lm, and core affine_mm without its epilogue
items.body:
## Gemma 4 31B served natively on Metal

The dense 31B (`mlx-community/gemma-4-31B-it-4bit`, groups of 64) as the native family `zig/src/families/gemma4`, registered as `gemma4`, with the recipe in `docs/recipes/gemma-4-native.md`:

- The loader admits the dense 31B's geometry only (60 layers, five sliding layers to each global one, GeGLU, the tied 262,144-token head with its soft-cap) and refuses the MoE, the 12B, per-layer inputs, shared KV layers and per-module widths, each by name. The vision tower is not loaded.
- Decode: every linear on the core lane projection (M5 tensor units), the rest of a layer in `zig/kernels/metal/gemma4/glue.metal`, ported from gilby's `gemma4-dense` Python engine (#360) with its rounding points. Each kernel equals the reference bit for bit at 1, 2 and 16 rows (`tf-gemma4-kernels`, `tf-gemma4-glue`), and greedy decode matches the oracle token for token and logit for logit. Global layers' decode attention runs a key head's query heads as one tensor-unit tile.
- Lane core: shared rounds, copy drafts, and z-lab's DFlash block drafter (`--drafter`, 150-190 tok/s for one stream, the same tokens); every stream equal to its plain reply (`tf-gemma4-lanes`). The target hands the drafter each prompt chunk's tapped rows as it makes them.
- Prompts in 512-row chunks on `core/affine_mm` and a tensor-unit attention kernel (32 query rows a threadgroup, a simdgroup scoring 32 keys over the whole head and owning 64 output columns, fp32 probabilities crossing threadgroup memory 128 keys at a time).
- Core `affine_mm` now dequantizes each step's weights to bf16 in its tile (scale times code plus bias in fp32, rounded once, as mlx-lm's quantized matmul does) and accumulates over the whole depth: the per-group epilogue, the row-sums kernel and its host plumbing go, across the GLM callers and tests too. `tf-affine-ref` checks against the rounded weights with the tensor unit's 16-deep chain as its bound and keeps the exact reference for the lane kernel; `tf-glm-rows-check` passes.
- `tools/zig/gemma4_gate.py`: the oracle's receipts, the token gate, the served gate, and the long-context prompts up to 252k; `tf-gemma4-bench` for stage costs.

Measured on an M5 Ultra (macOS 27), 49 decoded tokens after each prompt, against mlx-lm 0.32.0 prefilling in 2048-token chunks:

| Prompt | Native prompt tok/s | mlx-lm | Native decode tok/s | mlx-lm |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 8k | 1385 | 1305 | ~38 | 39 |
| 32k | 1241 | 1139 | ~35 | 32 |
| 64k | 1072 | 944 | ~33 | 32 |
| 128k | 882 | 651 | ~27 | 25 |
| 252k | 570 | 440 | ~20 | 16 |

Decode receipts (arithmetic, code, copy) equal the oracle's tokens; the story prompt parts at token 56 on an exact native tie. The long prompts equal it at 32k, 64k and 252k and part at 8k (token 25) and 128k (30), each where mlx-lm's own top two logits are exactly tied. Served gate (thinking and a tool call) passes; `zig build test`, `zig fmt --check` and `lean_check.py` clean.

Plain one-row decode at short context is 19.7 ms a token, 51 tok/s against mlx-lm's 46 (45 at 8k against 39, 40 at 32k against 32): each shape's lane projection takes the K split it streams fastest at on one row (o and down 4, the gate/up stack and the head 8), another fp32 summation order than the reference's, so `tf-gemma4-kernels` keeps the reference split bit for bit and reports the decode split, where a handful of outputs a linear move by one bf16 step; and the core reg lane kernel takes a family prologue and epilogue (`Fused`), so a one-row layer's dense tail, attention tail and geglu run inside the next projections, and a sliding layer's attention kernel preps its own heads and merges itself at one key chunk (five to seven dispatches a layer, the same bits).

items.title: Qwen3.5/3.8 on CUDA: image input on #836's engine (2B, 27B; on #836 and #853)
items.body:
## Image input on #836's Qwen CUDA engine

Asked for on #726 and #856: the Qwen checkpoints read images, so the family does too. This brings #726's vision tower and M-RoPE onto #836's engine. The prompt cache and the fp8 KV cache are not part of this; they come as their own changes.

**Stacked on #836 and #853.** #853 supplies the native server's image parts: `Request.images`, `vision_inputs.zig` and `qwen_image`. Its decoder refuses images until the shared libjpeg-turbo decoder lands, and this PR does not change that. The first commit after them merges #853 into #836, resolving conflicts in `build.zig`, `zig/build/cuda.zig` and `native/cuda.zig`: #836's drafter wrapper, plus #853's `follow`, `setStreams`/`setRoom`, `vision` and `admit`. Review the last three commits:

1. **`qwen3_5: image rows and M-RoPE positions in the CUDA forward`**
   - A prompt chunk can carry an image prompt's rows (`Part.images`). After the embedding, `tf_q35_splice` replaces the placeholder rows with the tower's features.
   - `tf_q35_rope` turns each row by its t, h and w positions (interleaved sections 11, 11, 10), read from a staged table.
   - Rows after the prompt rotate at their position plus the stream's `rope_delta`, carried in `Seg.delta`. Decode, verify windows and trees therefore keep their captured graphs.
   - Text rows rotate at one position on all three axes, which is the same arithmetic as before.
2. **`qwen3_5: the vision tower on CUDA, and --vision on the Qwen engine`**
   - #726's tower and kernels (`qwen_vision.cu`, Linears on cuBLASLt). Width, heads, depth and MLP size are read from `vision_config`, so the 2B's tower (24 blocks of 1024, heads of 64) runs as well as the 27B's and the 35B-A3B's.
   - The weights and the scratch of one 16,384-patch call are a single allocation made at startup and counted as model memory.
   - Video parts are refused by name.
3. **`tf-qwen35-cuda: vision and mrope checks`**

## Checks (RTX 5090, sm_120, Linux)

**Text keeps its bits.** Qwen3.8-27B, 96 ids after a 300-token prefix with a second stream beside it. `step`, `window` and `tree` logits are byte-identical to the build without this change. `mrope` sends a 300-token prompt through the image table with text positions; its logits equal `prompt`'s byte for byte, from position 0 and from 77. As a control, `TF_Q35_SHIFT=1` (the h axis moved by one) changes 135,331 of 248,320 logits, which shows the table is read.

**Tower against 0.6.6** (`tools/qwen_vision_fixtures.py` from the qwen38-27b-vision recipe, 9 images):

| checkpoint | row cosine, mean | row cosine, min |
|---|---:|---:|
| Qwen3.8-27B | 0.9997–0.99998 | 0.981 |
| Qwen3.6-35B-A3B | 0.9985–0.9999 | 0.942 |
| Qwen3.5-2B | 0.979–0.99998 | 0.378 |

- **27B:** the rows are byte-identical to #726's tower on all 9 images (max error 0).
- **2B:** this tower is fragile in bf16. 0.6.6 against itself (flash against math attention) already drops to 0.45. Against an fp32 run of 0.6.6's tower, this PR is closer than 0.6.6's bf16 tower on 8 of 9 images and within 0.0004 on the ninth (photo.jpg): mean 0.982–0.9999 here, 0.976–0.9998 there.
- **35B-A3B:** the tower only. Its engine is #856, and image input for it follows there.

**Served** (27B + DFlash2, `--parallel 2 --context 32768 --vision`; the native decoder is stb in a local test build only):
- The five image chats from the 5090 recipe: prompt token counts equal 0.6.6's in all five. The replies are correct and read "ORANGE 7351", and the follow-up is word for word. Replies track 0.6.6 about as far as #726's did before parting at a near-tie.
- **25 of 25 exactness cells** with image prompts:
  - drafted = `"draft": false`, 5 of 5. The undrafted runs log `accepted=0/0`, so drafting was really off.
  - repeated = first, which covers resume: the turn is re-read, since this engine has no kept states yet.
  - concurrent = alone, 10 cells: image beside image, image beside text, and the same image twice.
  - seeded sampling at T 0.7: repeat = first, and undrafted = drafted.
  - a second turn after an image reply: again = first.
- **2B, served:** it reads all four images correctly, and 25 of 25 cells pass. It has no drafter, so its drafted cells compare undrafted with undrafted.

Host: `zig build test` 284/289 (5 skipped); `test-cuda-host` passes, including the new placeholder, layout and config tests. `zig fmt` is clean, and the lean check reports 0 new problems.

Not run: Windows, a GB10, the 35B-A3B served.

items.title: Living Weights: facts learned and checked in conversation, not only asked cold
items.body:
## The problem

A fact's lesson fits its pocket neurons on single-turn prompts, and every check asks a single-turn question. In a real
chat the question comes after other turns, and then it reads differently.

I measured this on Qwen3.8 Flash Next (our CUDA port, the Living Weights code of this repo): 8 user facts taught, then
the same held-out questions asked in five contexts, all greedy. The assistant turns of the conversations are the model's
own live replies.

| context | user facts recalled |
|---|---|
| cold | 14/18 (78%) |
| after a "You are a helpful assistant." system prompt | 14/18 |
| after 3 turns of small talk | 13/18 |
| after an unrelated ~4k-token task chat (debugging a CSV script) | **8/18 (44%)** |
| chained (one fact's question after another's) | 6/6 first in a chain, **5/24 after it** |

The untaught model scored 0 everywhere. I read every answer: the misses are "I don't have access to your personal
information" or an invented value.

The gate shows why. I read each learned neuron's `u x` at the decide row of each probe prompt, with the fit's scale.

- When a fact is recalled cold, its reply neurons sit at about +3 (fit level 1, silence margin -0.5).
- After the long chat or mid-chain, the same question puts them at about 0, under the firing level.
- Over all contexts, prompts whose neurons fired were recalled 55/61. Prompts whose neurons were quiet were recalled
  2/27.

So the conversation moves the residual under the gate, and nothing in a lesson ever saw a conversation.

## What this changes

**1. `quiet()` moves to `pocket_quiet.zig`, unchanged** (`6921253a`). `pocket.zig` is at 593 lines. This is the same
patch as the first commit of the refit PR (#876), with the same patch-id, so either can land first.

**2. Facts are learned and checked in conversation** (`cc7c89f0`).

- **The conversations** (`server/slide_context.zig`, `server/slide_talks.zig`). A lesson also asks its questions after
  four conversations:
  - three turns of small talk;
  - a 3-turn JavaScript task;
  - a 6-turn bash and git task (about 2.8k tokens on Nemotron);
  - a chain: an opener ("How many legs does a spider have?", then "What did I eat for breakfast today?"), then the
    latest two learned facts' questions with the answers their lessons wrote.

  The assistant turns are the model's own greedy replies, written once and kept in the graph file (`talks`, and a
  fact's `chain` pair), so every later lesson and a restarted server read the same text. The scripted lines are
  generic, and none of them is a probe below.
- **What a lesson learns there.** Per fact and per conversation:
  - six of its questions, fitted to fire;
  - four of its near misses, and two questions about the user that no fact answers, fitted to stay silent;
  - up to three of its answers, learned there too, when the whole answer fits the trainer's pass.
- **The checks.** Each fact's two held-out questions are also asked after two conversations that no lesson learns in:
  a Docker task, and a chain's opening that ends on a question the model cannot answer. A fact that only comes back
  cold does not pass.
- **Reading long prompts** (`families/nemotron/pocket_read.zig`, `cuda_train_tap.zig`). An example now carries
  `Example.context`: the rows of its conversation, which every question asked after it shares. The pocket reads such an
  example through an optional trainer hook, `tapRows`.
  - Nemotron's CUDA hook runs the prompt through the engine's prompt chunks (`cuda_forward.zig`'s `chunkPre`,
    `chunkMixer` and `chunkPost`, the states carried from chunk to chunk as serving's prefill carries them), with the
    keys pass's MoE (`cuda_train_fwd.experts`, the same pocket kernel). It copies the MoE input at the asked rows as
    the keys pass does, so any length works.
  - It uses a sequence of its own. Each conversation runs once. Its Mamba states are kept, and its KV rows stay in
    place, for the next question after it.
  - Every eighth row of a conversation is read as a row to stay silent on.
  - `TF_SLIDE_TAP_CHECK=1` compares each tapped prompt with a fresh run (nothing kept, cut in 1,024-row pieces instead
    of at the conversation's end), and with the trainer's own keys pass when one holds it.
- **Learners without the hook.** A learner without `tapRows` keeps the conversation prompts its passes hold and leaves
  out the rest (`lesson_examples.readable`), logging how many. That is Metal today: the chains fit in its 256 rows, the
  task conversations do not. Answers in a conversation are always read by passes, so a learner leaves out the ones
  longer than its passes, on CUDA too.
- **The pocket's log line** (`layer N at the reply fires on ...`) adds the fact's own questions in a conversation and
  the most the neuron reads on other prompts there.

**3. An earlier fact's refit holds the conversation rows it fires on** (`4a63c4bb`). A fact learned after another is
also asked after a chain that holds the earlier fact's own question and answer, and the earlier fact's neurons fire
there.

- `quiet()` read those rows as rows to push below zero. It could not, and so it undid the refit.
- On Flash Next, that was 7 of 7 refits in the first run: the new fact was learned with the earlier neurons still firing
  on its questions.
- Now a conversation's rows where the earlier neuron fires are held as they read (`.none`), beside the rows its own
  lesson stored.
- A test builds the case. Before the change the refit is undone (`expected 1, found 0`). After it, the neuron is silent
  on the new fact's questions and reads its own question in the chain as before.
- `cuda.zig` and `tensorfold.zig` import `pocket_quiet.zig` in their tests, as #876 does. So this test and the pocket's
  earlier tests run in the Linux `zig build test`.

## Receipt (Nemotron)

- Environment: `lw-ctx-main` on `main` c7137bb3 (v1.0.11 + 19), Zig 0.17.0; NVIDIA GB10 (DGX Spark, sm_121), driver
  580.178.04, CUDA 13.0.88, Ubuntu 24.04.5; checkpoint `TensorFold/NVIDIA-Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B-MLX-4bit`
  revision d9d758fb. Each run used a fresh `cp -RL` copy:
  `tensorfold-native serve <copy> --no-thinking --temperature 0 --slide --slide-graph <graph.json>`.
- The runs:
  - `main` and this branch each taught the ten facts of 1.0.8's receipt ("I like blue." to "I am allergic to
    peanuts."), one learn request each.
  - After every lesson, I asked the two fixed wordings per fact and every learned fact's stored held-out questions.
  - Before the first lesson and after the last, I ran a context matrix over the 20 fixed wordings, greedy, 120 tokens:
    - cold;
    - after a system prompt;
    - after 3 small-talk turns;
    - after an 8-turn unrelated task chat (4,171-4,232 prompt tokens with the question);
    - 4 chains of 5 questions.
  - The small talk and the task chat are fixed user lines (not the lesson's). The assistant turns are generated live
    and greedy by each build's model.
  - A reply counts when it names the fact's value and does not open with a refusal. I read every reply; the counts are
    the same as plain keyword hits, except for one `main` reply that names sushi as an example after "I don't know".
  - Before teaching, both builds gave the same 100 matrix replies and 12 unrelated replies byte for byte, and 0 hits.
    `main` was built at c7137bb3. The branch binary was built at a586a277, which differs from the head 4a63c4bb by one
    comment's wording.

| context | `main`, 10 facts taught | this branch | `main`, the 6 facts both kept | branch, the same 6 |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| cold | 13/20 | 11/20 | 11/12 | 11/12 |
| system prompt | 14/20 | 12/20 | 12/12 | 12/12 |
| 3 turns of small talk | 14/20 | 12/20 | 12/12 | 12/12 |
| ~4k-token task chat | **6/20** | **10/20** | **6/12** | **10/12** |
| chained | 14/20 | 12/20 | 12/12 | 12/12 |

- **Of the wordings recalled cold, after the task chat:** `main` 6/13, this branch 9/11.
- **Per fact, after the task chat:**
  - sushi 0/2 → 2/2;
  - Leo 1/2 → 2/2 (`main` says "Your son is called **Hadi**");
  - 14 March 0/2 → 1/2.
  - On `main`, "When is my birthday?" and "Where do I live?" after the chat answer "My name is Nemotron. I am created
    by NVIDIA researchers."
- **Facts kept.** `main` kept 7 of 10, this branch 6.
  - Both took out Ginger ("it kept answering questions about something else"), and both missed nurse and Volvo.
  - The branch also missed Bristol. Its lesson failed the same check for 5 rounds: the held-out "Do you know which city
    is my home?" asked cold with thinking on ("I remember you mentioned that you know which city is your home, but I
    don't have that information stored"). No conversation check failed it.
  - That costs the branch Bristol's 2 wordings in every context. The fixed questions after lesson 10 are 11/20 on the
    branch against 13/20 on `main`, and 13/20 is also the A2 receipt's `main`.
- **Chains.** On Nemotron chains were already fine on `main`. Every chained miss on both builds is a fact that was not
  kept.
- **In-conversation checks.** Over the 10 lessons they failed 14 times. 10 were Volvo's yes/no held-outs ("Is my car a
  Volvo?" → "Yes, you do.", which names no value). 3 were nurse ("your work is **running a small Go web server in
  Docker**"). 1 was Ana in round 1, recalled in round 2.
- **Unrelated prompts** (11 general ones and "What is my cat called?"): the branch 12/12 identical to before teaching;
  `main` 11/12 (a reworded haiku).
- **Restarts:** plain and `--slide`, on both builds, gave the 20 cold replies and 12 unrelated replies identical to
  after lesson 10. The base checkpoint's sha256 is unchanged.
- **Lesson time:** 1,628 s for the 10 lessons against 1,502 s on `main` (+8%).
  - The first lesson writes the conversations once: +26.5 s.
  - A round-1 read takes 9.9 s against 5.9 s (the taps: about 110 reads of up to 2.9k tokens, against 37 passes).
  - A round's checks take 8.3 s against 7.3 s.
- **Taps equal the trainer's pass, bit for bit.** A 2-lesson run with `TF_SLIDE_TAP_CHECK=1` read 102 prompts in a
  conversation (2,180 tapped rows, prompts up to 2,855 tokens).
  - Every tapped value at every pocket layer equalled a fresh run's.
  - The 30 prompts a keys pass holds (the chains, up to 205 tokens, conversation cut at 146-271) equalled the pass's
    own values: 0 values differ, most 0.0000.
  - So kept conversation states, cuts at any row, and the engine's chunks against the trainer's pass give the same
    bits.
- **The refit fix (commit 3) was not exercised here.** In the branch run, 13 refits were kept and 2 undone, and none
  met a conversation row its neuron fires on (`0 conversation rows held`). Its test covers it, and Flash Next below
  needed it.
- Tests: `zig build test` on Linux:
  - `main` 743/748 (5 skipped); commit 1 743/748; commit 2 746/751; commit 3 750/755. Commit 3's four more are its own
    test and the pocket's three that now run on Linux.
  - `zig build test-server-cpu`: 209/209 (`main` 207; +2: the conversations persist across a reopen of the graph, and
    the learned and checked conversations differ).
  - Every commit builds and passes. `zig fmt --check build.zig zig` is clean. `python3 tools/zig/lean_check.py` gives
    527 problems against 527 on `main` (0 new).
- Metal: not run on a Mac (I have none). `zig build native` and `zig build test-native` with `-Dtarget=aarch64-macos`
  and a stub `xcrun` compile every Zig module and stop only at linking Apple's frameworks, as on `main`. Metal's
  trainer has no `tapRows`, so it learns the chains, leaves out the task conversations, and logs how many it left out.
  It runs the same checks, so it checks in conversation. A Mac lesson is still needed.

## Supporting evidence: the same fix on two other models

The fix was developed on Qwen3.8 Flash Next and carried to Qwen3.8-27B in our CUDA ports. Neither is in this repo yet,
so these numbers support the design and are not this PR's receipt. Each port has its own `tapRows`, through its own
engine's batched pass. On both, `TF_SLIDE_TAP_CHECK` found 0 values different from the trainer's pass: Flash Next on 48
prompts, and the 27B on a 128-row conversation, run and found kept.

- **Flash Next, the same 7 facts before and after:**

  | context | before | after |
  |---|---|---|
  | task chat ~4k | 7/16 | 11/16 |
  | chained | 7/14 | 10/14 |
  | small talk | 12/16 | 15/16 |
  | thinking on, after the task chat | 4/7 | 7/7 |

  - Of the wordings recalled cold, after the task chat: 8/14 → 11/13.
  - Gate after the 4k chat, recalled probes: median `u x` +2.44 → +3.68 (cold +3.77).
  - Lesson time for 8 facts: 5,351 → 5,410 s.
  - Before the refit fix, the first run's earlier-fact refits all failed (7 of 7). With it, 72 succeeded and 56 failed,
    against 116 and 199 in the study before this work.
- **Qwen3.8-27B, with the fix:** cold 15/18, task chat ~4k 15/18, chained 14/16. Of the wordings recalled cold:
  - after the task chat 14/15;
  - chained 14/14.

## Checklist

- [x] Every token still goes through the lane rounds. No serial path, and nothing that needs drafts off. (Serving is
  untouched. The taps run inside a lesson, on the trainer's own sequence, as its passes do.)
- [x] Drafted output equals `"draft": false`, a resumed prompt equals a fresh one, and concurrent equals solo. (Not
  touched. Both builds gave identical replies before teaching.)
- [x] No precision traded for speed. If the bits change, the description says which sums change and why. (The tapped
  rows equal the trainer's pass's bits.)
- [x] Prompt processing is no slower than the last release. (Not touched.)
- [x] The description says which platforms I ran, Metal M1 to M5 and CUDA, and which I could not. (GB10; Metal
  type-checked only.)
- [x] New tests fail before the change, pass after it, and skip cleanly without their dependency.
- [x] Comments and docstrings are one line. No measurements or history in the source.
- [x] No personal data, machine names, internal hosts or local paths. No AI attribution lines.

## Not in this PR

- **Asking earlier facts again in conversation.** `main` has no re-check of earlier facts after a lesson. When the #870
  fix adds one, it should ask each fact's conversation wordings too. In our build that was one line in the re-check
  (`Asking.before` from the wording's conversation). The graph would also need to keep each wording's conversation
  name, which this PR leaves out (`questions` keeps the cold wordings only).
- **The take-out restore and checks on the rounded pocket** (our 0ffc5167, in #877). This PR does not need it, and I
  expect your #870 fix to cover that ground.
- **A Metal `tapRows`.** Metal reads the chains and leaves the long conversations out, as above.
- **Gate readings on Nemotron after teaching.** The `u x` table above is from Flash Next's diagnostic tool, which I did
  not port. Nemotron's lessons log only the fit-time reading. On the branch, in all 60 of those lines (every lesson,
  every reply neuron), the fact's neurons fire on all 27 of its questions in a conversation, and other prompts there
  read at most -0.20.
- **Thinking on in a conversation, and document facts in a conversation.** Neither is learned or checked.

## How it relates to #878 and your #870 work

- **#878 (draft)** moves the learner and pocket from `families/nemotron` to `zig/src/living`. This PR changes
  `learner.zig`, `lesson_examples.zig`, `pocket.zig`, `pocket_read.zig` and `pocket_quiet.zig` where they are on

  `cuda_train_tap.zig` stays Nemotron's.
- **#870 / #876.** The first commit here is #876's first commit, the same patch. Commit 3 holds conversation rows in

  hold sits beside that in the same place: one more condition on which rows are held.

items.title: ling: Ling-3.1-flash on CUDA at TP=1 on #804's kernels (draft, stacked on #804)
Flash Next keeps its buffers wired between requests: a residency set, and a keepalive tick the GPU runs
items.body:
_Posted by Claude (Anthropic's AI assistant) on behalf of @sethforprivacy, as part of our local-inference tuning work on a Mac Studio M5 Ultra._ On 1.0.8 (`0efbd44`), Flash Next's first token after an idle gap of 2 s or more takes about 2 s; back to back it takes 0.095 s. With this change it stays at 0.095 s after any gap we tried, up to 10 s. **Cause.** macOS unwires an idle process's GPU memory within a second or two. The next request's first command buffer then waits in the queue while that memory comes back. On our shared-sessions build we timed that buffer at 0.5 ms to encode, 1.2-2.3 s queued and 90 ms on the GPU. The idle keepalive doesn't prevent this on Flash Next, for two reasons: - The host gives the keepalive no residency set. - Each tick commits an empty command buffer, which need not reach the GPU. **Change:** - `Run.held` lists the buffers that `buffer`, `load` and `group` make. The Flash Next host puts them in one residency set (`resident.zig`), which its keepalive target uses. `FLASHNEXT_NO_RESIDENCY=1` leaves the set out. - `keepalive.Target.tick` copies 16 bytes inside the set (`Target.scratch`), so each tick's command buffer runs on the GPU. `Resident.init` adds the scratch buffer, so the 27B's served host ticks the same way. We have not measured the 27B. - *(A working-set gate was added and then reverted: the slow rounds BobClawblaw measured came with sets under the working set. The all-buffers design that fixes them is proposed [here](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/732#issuecomment-6137106735).)* **Receipt.** - **Machine:** Mac Studio M5 Ultra, 256 GB, macOS 27.0. - **Checkpoint:** `TensorFold/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-6bit-MTP` @ `45032a1`. - **Server:** `serve --context 262144`, the single-reply host. - **Method:** one greedy streaming request at a time, each sent N seconds after the one before it finished, four per gap (`idle_ttft.py` below). Median time to the first token: | Idle gap | 1.0.8 | With this change | |---:|---:|---:| | 0.2 s | 0.095 s | 0.095 s | | 1 s | 0.095 s | 0.095 s | | 2 s | 2.026 s | 0.096 s | | 3 s | 2.022 s | 0.096 s | | 5 s | 2.045 s | 0.096 s | | 10 s | 2.034 s | 0.096 s | Across the 16 requests after gaps of 2 s or more, the slowest took 2.062 s on 1.0.8 and 0.097 s with this change. On our shared-sessions build (#606 plus additions), the residency set alone, with empty ticks, still left about half the bursts after an idle second waiting ~1.3 s. With the copy, none did. The keepalive still stops `--keep-warm` seconds after the last request (900 by default), so a request after a longer idle time still pays the cost. **Independent receipt, M3 Ultra** (@cwschroeder, [comment](https://github.com/ashhart/TensorFold/pull/732#issuecomment-6150068720)): 256 GB, macOS 27.0.1, same checkpoint, single-reply host at `--parallel 1 --context 262144 --prompt-cache-gib 8`, main `0efbd44` plus this PR at `b6543fe`: - **With the set:** first token 0.198 / 0.199 / 0.198 / 0.194 s after gaps of 0.2 / 2 / 10 / 30 s, and a cold 32k prompt after 60 s idle in 24.1 s. - **`FLASHNEXT_NO_RESIDENCY=1`:** 0.26 / 3.03 / 2.79 / 2.60 s, and 25.7 s. - Token hashes match across both arms. `zig fmt --check` passes on the four files. In `zig build test` every test passes, here and on main. One step fails identically on both on this Mac: `core.checkpoint_metal`'s split-checkpoint test logs "checkpoint tensor text.weight stays in its file".
idle_ttft.py ```python #!/usr/bin/env python3 """First token after an idle gap: one greedy streaming request at a time, each sent --gaps seconds after the one before finished (a short prompt with its own nonce, so no cache holds it), --repeats times a gap. A server whose GPU memory goes cold while idle answers the first request after a long gap late. python idle_ttft.py --api http://127.0.0.1:8026 --out idle.json """ from __future__ import annotations import argparse import json import random import statistics import string import time import urllib.request from pathlib import Path def one(api: str, key: str) -> float: nonce = "".join(random.choices(string.ascii_lowercase + string.digits, k=12)) body = {"model": "qwen3.8-flash-next", "max_tokens": 16, "temperature": 0, "stream": True, "messages": [{"role": "user", "content": f"Session {nonce}. Name one prime number."}], "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": False}} headers = {"Content-Type": "application/json"} | ({"Authorization": "Bearer " + key} if key else {}) req = urllib.request.Request(api.rstrip("/") + "/v1/chat/completions", data=json.dumps(body).encode(), headers=headers) t0 = time.perf_counter() first = None with urllib.request.urlopen(req, timeout=300) as r: for raw in r: line = raw.decode().strip() if not line.startswith("data:") or line[5:].strip() == "[DONE]": continue for ch in json.loads(line[5:]).get("choices") or []: if first is None and (ch.get("delta") or {}).get("content"): first = time.perf_counter() - t0 return first if first is not None else float("nan") def main() -> int: ap = argparse.ArgumentParser() ap.add_argument("--api", default="http://127.0.0.1:8026") ap.add_argument("--keys-file", default="") ap.add_argument("--gaps", default="0.2,1,2,3,5,10") ap.add_argument("--repeats", type=int, default=4) ap.add_argument("--label", default="run") ap.add_argument("--out", required=True) args = ap.parse_args() key = open(args.keys_file).readline().strip() if args.keys_file else "" one(args.api, key) # warm: the first request's own costs are not the idle gap's rows = [] for gap in [float(g) for g in args.gaps.split(",")]: firsts = [] for _ in range(args.repeats): time.sleep(gap) firsts.append(round(one(args.api, key), 3)) rows.append({"gap_s": gap, "first_token_s": firsts, "median_s": round(statistics.median(firsts), 3), "max_s": max(firsts)}) print(json.dumps({"label": args.label, **rows[-1]}), flush=True) Path(args.out).write_text(json.dumps({"label": args.label, "rows": rows}, indent=1)) return 0 if __name__ == "__main__": raise SystemExit(main()) ```
