items.title: Support Qwen3.8 Flash Next NVFP4 vision on CUDA
items.body:
## Problem

TensorFold rejects the Mia-AiLab Qwen3.8 Flash Next checkpoint with `--vision`. After accepting its architecture aliases, the CUDA vision loader rejects scalar NVFP4 `weight_scale_2` tensors and would also reject the MXFP8 visual linears. Reported in #234.

## Change

- Accept the Qwen3.8 Flash Next model and Qwen3.5 vision configuration names used by this export.
- Validate ModelOpt visual tensor groups, dtypes, shapes, and scale metadata.
- Dequantize supported MXFP8 and NVFP4 vision linears to BF16 with TensorFold's existing format math.
- Account for expanded BF16 weights in vision capacity estimates and ignore quantization sidecars.
- Reject unexpected tensors and non-finite decoded weights; add focused regression tests.

## Validation

- 19 targeted vision/dequantization tests passed.
- Pinned Mia-AiLab revision `925d7be6c14c6c9442ef83e8f05b5a3c39304f69` passed header checks across all 37 safetensors shards. Real NVFP4 and MXFP8 matrices decoded to finite BF16 tensors.
- On a DGX Spark GB10, the candidate TensorFold image loaded the vision tower and returned a useful answer to a synthetic image through `/v1/chat/completions` (HTTP 200, 4.895 s). A text control remained `READY` before and after. Health stayed 200 and host MemAvailable remained 38.3 GiB, above the 20 GiB floor.
- Candidate settings: context 262144, temperature 0.1, top_p 0.8, top_k 20, min_p 0, int8 KV, drafts disabled, and `--parallel 2`. The previous text-only container remains available for rollback.

The end-to-end image check used a simple synthetic image and is a smoke test, not a broad visual-quality benchmark. Video input was not tested.

Fixes #234

items.title: feat(glm cuda): --parallel N on two ranks: one cache pool, batched verify rounds (each reply its solo bits)
items.body:
> **Status: draft.** CPU tests pass; the GPU tests in `tests/cuda/` and the real-weight checks on two Sparks (drafted == serial, 4 streams against solo serial, resumed == fresh, 1M needle) are running next. Results will be posted here, and the PR marked ready once they pass. A stacked follow-up (prompts that arrive together share one prompt chunk) comes after this one.

**TL;DR:** `--parallel N` (2 to 4) for GLM-5.3-Flash on two ranks. Up to N requests decode together: their caches share one pool, and every round verifies all the streams' windows in one forward. Each reply is the one its request gets alone with `"draft": false`. DFlash2 streams draft in one batched block pass per round; MTP streams draft on the MTP head. Without `--parallel` nothing changes.


## What it adds

Today GLM-5.3-Flash on CUDA serves one request at a time, and the others wait their turn. With `--parallel N`, the same flag and value on both ranks:

- **One cache pool.** Every per-token cache lives in one pool of rows: DSA latents, the indexer's keys, gates and pooled keys, and the MTP layer's. Its size is the window's slots plus whatever `TF_GLM_CACHE_GIB` gives kept prompts. A stream or a kept prompt owns an extent of whole 2,048-token blocks and can grow up to the window. KDA states, conv windows and a decode window's scratch get one slot per stream. A request that doesn't fit waits. If every decoding stream is waiting for room, the youngest goes back to the queue and replays later; the tokens it already sent are checked, not sent again.
- **Batched verify rounds.** A round's windows go through one forward, at most 32 rows in all. Each window is a pending token plus its drafts.
  - Embeddings, hyper-connection glue, projections, MoE (the generic EXL3 expert path or the MLX 4-bit one) and the head run on all rows. These kernels already keep rows independent.
  - KDA layers run each stream's rows from its own slot (new segmented chain, replay and conv-shift kernels).
  - DSA layers run each stream's rows over its own extent (new segmented latent write, indexer update, token selection and attention).
  - Each segmented kernel keeps the single-stream kernel's arithmetic row for row. One CUDA graph per window size covers every mix of positions and lengths.
- **Drafts.**
  - DFlash2 streams draft from one drafter's weights, each from its own context ring. All drafting streams share one block pass and one context update per round (`dflash2_multi.py`).
  - MTP streams draft on the MTP head from their own cache rows, on the head's graphs at home and eagerly elsewhere.
  - `auto` uses DFlash2 when it's loaded. Otherwise it uses the single-stream `auto`'s MTP rule. Explicit MTP and DFlash2 policies fall back to each other's twin when their drafter isn't there.
  - **The MTP head under `--parallel`.** With `TF_GLM_MTP` unset, `--parallel` treats it as `auto`. If DFlash2 is loaded, the head is left out, which saves about 2 GiB a rank. If there's no DFlash2, the head loads as before. `TF_GLM_MTP=1` loads it beside DFlash2 too, for MTP policies. The startup log says which. One-stream serving is unchanged (`TF_GLM_MTP` still defaults to `1` there). Without the head, an MTP policy drafts with its DFlash2 twin and gives the same reply.
- **Prompts between rounds.** A prompt fills in chunks between decode rounds:
  - 1,024 rows while others decode (`TF_GLM_FILL_ROWS`), the engine's prompt chunk otherwise.
  - `TF_GLM_FILL_SHARE` (default 0.5) sets the share of iterations prompt chunks take.
  - A chunk never shares a forward with decode rows.
- **Kept prompts.** A drafted prompt is kept before its last token, as the single-stream engine keeps it (#98). The same prompt sent again, or the conversation's next turn, resumes from there: in place, or copied while another stream still writes in that extent. A DFlash2 stream resumes with its window and an MTP stream with its MTP rows.
- **Two ranks.**
  - Rank 0 decides admission, placement and rounds, and sends rank 1 one message per iteration. Rank 1 derives the drafts itself and checks the depths.
  - An idle rank 1 waits on the existing doorbell, not inside an all-gather.
  - A client that leaves ends its stream at the next round boundary on both ranks.
  - `/health` reports the decoding, filling and paused streams and the pool's free tokens.
  - `/v1/decisions` keeps needing `--parallel 1`, and says so.

Speed settings, none of which changes a reply (both ranks must use the same values):

| Setting | What it does |
| --- | --- |
| `TF_GLM_MULTI_SAMPLER=packed` | All samplers in two all-gathers |
| `TF_GLM_MULTI_DEPTH=joint` or `scale:A` | Draft depths chosen across the round's streams |
| `TF_GLM_MULTI_ASYNC=1` | Rank 0 sends its message without waiting for the GPU |
| `TF_GLM_MULTI_LONE=1` | A lone stream moves onto the one-stream graphs (off by default: kept prompts in those rows make way) |
| `TF_GLM_MULTI_PROFILE=N` | A round's time breakdown every N rounds |

`TF_GLM_MULTI_VERIFY=serial` verifies each window as its own forward instead. It's the reference and gives the same replies.

## Design

```
rank 0  GlmScheduler worker ── MultiDecoder.round() ── one message ──> rank 1 MultiDecoder.follow()/apply()
          admit: slot + extent (pool.Pool), resume a kept prompt     ADMIT EVICT MOVE GROW FILL ROUND SLOT FINISH IDLE
          FILL:  decode.prefill_chunk on the lane's State (forward.State views of its extent and slot)
          ROUND: drafts (MultiDrafter / MTP head) -> verify.BatchedVerify (segmented kernels) -> samplers -> commit
```

- `pool.py`: host-side extents (aligned, lowest-first placement, growth in place, moves) and the arena that views and copies plane rows.
- `forward.py`:
  - `Caches` holds every per-token cache as pool planes. `Slots` holds the per-stream KDA states and window scratch.
  - `State` is now a view of an extent plus a slot. Without a pool it builds its own, as before.
  - `kda_segments` and `dsa_segments` are the window's mixers. `compute` and `layer_forward` take a `mixer`.
- `decode.Engine`: a `streams` / `pool_rows` pair, `use(st)` to run the single-stream paths on a lane's state, and `graphed(st)` so only states at the graphs' home replay them. `prefill_chunk` is one chunk of `prefill`.
- `verify.py`: `SerialVerify` and `BatchedVerify` behind the same two calls (`forward`, `commit`). `segments.py` holds the window's device tables.
- `kda.cu`: `chain_wide_segments`, `replay_layers_segments`. `latent.py`: `seg_latent_write`, `seg_attention`. `sparse.py`: `seg_index_update`, `seg_select_tokens` (a split radix select), and `forward.conv_shift_segments`.
- `dflash2_multi.py`: `MultiDrafter`, `DraftContext` and a segmented block-attention kernel. `dflash2.py` gains `merge_candidates` and a `SEG` flag on `_dconv`. Its solo path is unchanged.
- `multi.py`: `MultiDecoder` and `GlmScheduler`. `multi_tune.py`: the speed settings.

Small hooks in the existing code:

- `GlmEngine(parallel=...)` and the `cuda_engine` option. `mtp_head(..., parallel=)`: under `--parallel`, an unset `TF_GLM_MTP` means `auto`.
- The memory estimate: the extra slots, the batched selection's scores, the multi-stream drafter's rings, and the pool from `TF_GLM_CACHE_GIB`.
- The two-rank settings comparison: `--parallel`, the verify kind and the speed settings.
- `generate(..., background=)` hands requests to the scheduler.
- `follow()` hands rank 1 to the decoder.
- `health.py` merges a decoder's own counts.
- `Drafter.chain(confs=...)` for the joint depth.
- `kda.reserve` keeps the wide chain's scratch at fixed addresses for captured graphs.

## Same bits

The guarantee is per stream: its reply equals the request served alone with `"draft": false` by a `--parallel 1` engine, for every sampling mode (greedy, top-k, nucleus, min_p) and with grammars.

CPU, run here in the NVIDIA PyTorch container, no GPU used:

- `tests/test_glm_multi.py`, 28 tests. Two ranks through recorded messages, on a fake model whose logits hash everything its stream committed, read back from its pool rows and slot.
  - Staggered DFlash2, MTP, mixed and serial requests at 2 and 4 streams.
  - Cancellation, pause and give-back with replay, growth with evictions and compaction moves.
  - Resumes in place and copied, for DFlash2 and MTP. The same prompt sent again.
  - One message per iteration, every speed setting, the threaded scheduler with a follower thread, `/health`.
  - The packed sampler against `decode.sample_rows`.
  - Both ranks' pools, arenas, slots and drafter contexts compared after every iteration. Every MTP stream's head rows are checked against its committed tokens.
  - Every reply compared with the real single-stream `GlmEngine.generate(draft=False)` on the same fake.
- `tests/test_glm_pool.py`: extents, arena views and overlapping copies.
- `tests/test_glm_mtp_setting.py`: the `--parallel` MTP default (left out beside DFlash2, loaded without it or with `TF_GLM_MTP=1`, unchanged for one stream).
- `pytest tests/test_glm*.py tests/test_cuda*.py tests/test_family_streams.py`: 1,148 passed and 14 skipped on this branch, against 1,110 passed and 14 skipped on unmodified `main` (the 38 new tests). The rest of the CPU suite needs `mlx` here, and some of it hangs without it on `main` too (`test_cancellation.py`), so it was not compared.

GPU tests (written; they need a free GPU):

- `tests/cuda/test_glm_kda_segments.py`: segmented chain, replay and conv shift against solo runs, `torch.equal`, at real per-rank shapes. Also the one-kernel chain that a stock decode window runs.
- `tests/cuda/test_glm_attn_segments.py`: segmented DSA windows against each segment alone through the stock decode path, eager and graph. Covers dense rows, rows straddling the dense limit, and sparse rows up to 200k tokens; one graph per window size for any mix; `dsa_segments` against `dsa_block` on the synthetic checkpoint; selection kernels against the stable-sort reference; absorb, expand and matmul rows independent of window size.
- `tests/cuda/test_glm_draft_multi.py`: `MultiDrafter` against one solo `Drafter` per stream, bit for bit. Ring wrapped and flat, eager and graphs, two ranks as threads.
- `tests/cuda/test_glm_multi.py`, end to end on the synthetic checkpoint with DFlash2 and the MTP head (`TF_GLM_MTP=1`; one test checks that the default leaves the head out and an MTP policy still gives the serial reply):
  - Concurrent DFlash2 and MTP requests against a `--parallel 1` engine's `"draft": false` replies.
  - Resumed turns, cancellation, a moved extent.
  - Batched windows against serial ones (logits, taps, hidden rows, states, every plane), graphs and eager, dense and long.
  - Grammars, a mirror decoder following rank 0, the lone-stream graphs, every speed setting.
  - The same startup collectives on both ranks, and two ranks in one process with real rendezvous all-gathers.

Real weights, two DGX Sparks, to run before un-drafting: the recipe's exactness checks on this branch (drafted == serial, concurrency 4 × N against solo serial, resumed == fresh, 1M-token needle with `--parallel 4`).

The design was first measured in the recipe below, with its own kernels: 4 streams at once 108.8 / 227.9 tok/s in all (prose / structured) against 60.4 / 114.7 for one, and 22/22 concurrency exactness checks. Stock-kernel numbers for this branch are TBD.

## Limits

- 2 to 4 streams. The segmented kernels hold 4 segments and a window holds 32 rows.
- Needs the latent cache (`TF_GLM_LATENT=1`, the default) for batched windows. `TF_GLM_MULTI_VERIFY=serial` runs without it.
- Text prompts only. GLM has no image input on CUDA upstream yet.
- Without `--context` the window is GLM's dense 2,051 tokens. The pool then holds only the window plus `TF_GLM_CACHE_GIB`'s kept rows, and every stream needs at least a 2,048-token extent. Give `--context` or more `TF_GLM_CACHE_GIB` for several long streams.
- MTP streams draft eagerly outside the graphs' home, so MTP drafting is slower per stream than DFlash2's batched pass. With DFlash2 loaded, `auto` uses DFlash2, and the MTP head isn't loaded unless `TF_GLM_MTP=1`.
- Prompts fill one stream's chunk at a time. Waiting prompts sharing one prompt chunk is a separate follow-up PR (`feat/glm-multi-prefill`).
- `/v1/decisions` needs `--parallel 1`.

## Credit

This engine comes from [MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold](https://github.com/MiaAI-Lab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-2x-DGX-Sparks-TensorFold), the GLM-5.3-Flash EXL3 2x DGX Sparks recipe by Mia's AI Lab (patches 0026-0048, Apache-2.0). It is ported here onto stock 0.6.1 by its author, without the recipe's speed-only changes (copy drafts, prompt grid, noise policies, hyper-connection split, FP8 KV, 4-bit dense weights, the RoCE transport, tuned defaults). `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` has a line for it.

This PR supersedes #200, which carries an earlier copy of the same engine. The MTP concurrency that #200 aimed for is included here: MTP streams verify in the same batched rounds.

## Rank message checks

Added in 8845cd4:

- **Sealed messages.** Rank 0's per-iteration message now ends with a sequence number and a checksum (`multi.seal`), on both transports (`_share`, and `TF_GLM_MULTI_ASYNC`'s `_send`).
- **Checked on rank 1.** `MultiDecoder.follow` checks both before it applies anything (`multi.unseal`). A lost, repeated or altered message is a `RuntimeError` that names it, instead of the two ranks running different ops and waiting on each other's collectives with no output.
- **`TF_GLM_MULTI_WATCHDOG_EXIT=1`.** The stack-dump watchdog ends the process after its first dump, so a supervisor can restart a stalled server. The default (`0`) keeps dumping every `TF_GLM_MULTI_WATCHDOG_S` as before. The setting is read at startup, so a typo fails there.
- **`/health` reports `iteration_s`.** That's how long rank 0's current iteration has run (0 between iterations). It keeps growing on a stalled server.

Replies are unchanged: the two values are added by rank 0 and removed by rank 1 before `apply`.

Tests (CPU):

- `tests/test_glm_multi_seal.py`, 12 tests:
  - A round trip through seal and unseal.
  - A lost, changed, swapped, skipped or repeated message is named.
  - A long prompt's checksum stays in int32.
  - Both transports number their messages in order.
  - Rank 1's `follow` applies unsealed messages and names a gap.
  - The watchdog setting, and `iteration_s`.
- `tests/test_glm_multi.py` now parses the messages it logs without the seal.
- `pytest tests/test_glm*.py tests/test_cuda*.py tests/test_family_streams.py`: 1,160 passed and 14 skipped, against 1,148 passed and 14 skipped before this commit.
- The GPU tests pass rank 0's messages straight to rank 1's `follow`, so they need no change. They have not been run with this commit.

items.title: Qwen3.8-27B CUDA: serve compressed-tensors checkpoints with channel FP8 scales
items.body:
## Summary

This PR lets the Qwen3.8-27B CUDA engine serve compressed-tensors NVFP4 checkpoints whose FP8 layers use channel scales, as many community fine-tunes do. It fixes three problems that stop such a checkpoint today. Tested with `orcarouter/Qwen3.8-27B-Uncensored-NVFP4` on one RTX 5090 (sm_120).

## Changes

1. **Channel and group FP8 scales** (`nvfp4_load.py`, `linear.py`, `format.py`)
   - The loader refused any FP8 projection with more than one scale: `FP8 with 10240 scales; the CUDA engine reads one scale a tensor`.
   - New `Fp8ChannelLinear`: runs the stored bytes on the existing per-tensor FP8 kernels with a unit scale, then multiplies each output column by its fp32 channel scale. Both steps act on one row at a time, so drafted, serial and concurrent rows keep equal bits. Trade-off: the output takes two bf16 roundings where a fused scale takes one. A kernel that takes a column-scale vector would remove this. I kept the change small instead.
   - Group scales `[N, K/G]` with `G` a multiple of 64 go to the existing `Fp8BlockLinear.from_rows`.
   - The 27B loader now also takes `fp8block` (`weight_scale_inv`) projections through `Fp8BlockLinear.from_checkpoint`.
   - `format.dequant("fp8", ...)` reads channel and group scales.
2. **Banded fragment order** (`linear.py`, `_fragment_order`)
   - An FP8 `lm_head` (248,320 x 5,120) needed two int64 index tensors of the full size and ran out of memory on a 32 GB card (`Tried to allocate 9.47 GiB`).
   - The gather now runs over bands of 64-output tiles. The output bytes are the same. A test compares it with the one-gather result.
3. **FP8 KV calibration scales** (`nvfp4_load.py`, `skipped`)
   - `self_attn.k_scale` / `v_scale` / `q_scale` made the load fail as unused tensors. The cache here is bf16, so the loader now skips them.
4. **Saved tokenizer truncation** (new `cuda/tokenizer_file.py`, used by `cuda/server.py` and `cuda/markers.py`)
   - This checkpoint ships a `tokenizer.json` with `truncation: {max_length: 2048}` left by its training run. `tokenizers` applies it on every `encode`, so the server cut every prompt to 2,048 tokens without an error.
   - The CUDA server now turns off saved truncation and padding. Prompts past the window are still refused by the server's own check.

## Tests

- `tests/test_nvfp4_format.py`: channel and group FP8 dequantization against torch float8.
- `tests/cuda/test_fp8_channel_linear.py`: decode and prompt paths against a dequantized reference, row independence (one row alone equals the same row in a 12-row call), `tiles()` and `out=`, banded fragment order equals one gather.
- `tests/test_tokenizer_file.py`: a saved truncation and padding block no longer cuts or pads.
- All pass on an RTX 5090, CUDA 12.8, torch 2.11.

## Served results (one RTX 5090, `--parallel 4`, `TENSORFOLD_MEMORY_RESERVE_GIB=2`)

- Loads in about 90 s. Window 34,815 tokens. 23.0 GiB at idle.
- Decode (512 tokens, greedy): code 189 tok/s, chat 81 tok/s.
- Needle at 10 / 50 / 90 % depth of a 29,754-token prompt: all correct.
- Tool calls with an array parameter: correct, thinking on and off.
- Four concurrent ~6.7k-token prompts with 2,048-token replies, then one 28.8k-token prompt: no errors, peak 29.5 GiB.

## Not in this PR

- The window on a 32 GB card is limited by the bf16 KV cache. `--kv-dtype int8` would help the 27B as it helps Flash Next.
- A follow-up turn on a ~29k-token conversation re-read the full prompt (9.6 s) where an identical resend took 0.23 s. I did not look into the cause.
- `--vision` on this checkpoint was not tried.
- The startup weight estimate does not count the expanded scales of the group-scale path (`Fp8BlockLinear`, 1/16 of the FP8 bytes). The channel path adds only one fp32 value per output.

items.title: feat(glm5_next cuda): dense projections from an EXL3 pack (TF_GLM_DENSE_EXL3)
items.body:
GLM-5.3-Flash's EXL3 checkpoint (`Mia-AiLab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-TR3-4bpw`) quantizes the routed experts only. Attention,
the shared experts, the three dense MLPs and the head stay BF16: ~9.7 GiB a rank that every decode round reads.
`TF_GLM_DENSE_EXL3` names one or more safetensors files (`:`-separated) of EXL3 groups for some of those matrices,
under the checkpoint's own module names (`<module>.trellis`, `suh`, `svh`, `mul1` or `mcg`), for instance the
non-expert groups of `turboderp/GLM-5.3-Flash-exl3`. Each matrix a pack holds runs on `tensorfold.cuda.exl3`'s
row-invariant `Exl3Linear` (decode kernel up to 128 rows, the prompt GEMM above). The others keep the BF16 path.
Without the variable nothing changes.

- **Cuts.** A rank takes the tiles that `split.py`'s rule gives its BF16 twin: output columns and svh for a "row"
  matrix (q/k/v, q_b, gate, up), input rows and suh for a "col" matrix (o, down), the whole group for "rep" (q_a,
  kv_a), its vocabulary columns for the head. Hadamard blocks are 128 wide and every cut lands on a multiple of 128,
  so a "col" shard's output is had(z_r) * svh and the all-reduce sums the ranks into the full layer's output.
- **Fused projections.** KDA's q/k/v/f_a/g_a/b, DSA's q_a/kv_a and gate/up become a `Dense3` stack. Each part is an
  `Exl3Linear` or the BF16 matrix and writes its own output columns, so the forward code is untouched; `qmm.matmul`
  dispatches on the type.
- **Head.** A pack that holds `lm_head` replaces the BF16 head for verification too, so replies follow the quantized
  head. The draft head is still quantized from the BF16 rows. Leave `lm_head` out of the pack to keep the BF16 head.
- **Memory.** `Weights` accounting counts the shards. The startup estimate still counts these matrices at BF16, so it
  is conservative.

## Measured

Two DGX Sparks (GB10), served with MiaAI-Lab's GLM-5.3-Flash TensorFold recipe v1.3 (TensorFold 0.6.0 + its patches;
its FP8 dense weights serve the matrices the pack lacks), DFlash2, 4 streams, 1M window, GPU clocks not capped.
Pack: attention and shared experts at 4 bpw (turboderp 2.05bpw branch), dense MLPs at 5 and the head at 6 (4.05bpw).
sparkDash through the OpenAI API, the same prompts for every row:

Single stream, T=0, thinking off, time to first token excluded (structured = count 1-200; prose = the hash-map
explanation; code = a commented binary search tree asked in French):

| Dense weights | Structured | Prose | Code | 68k-token prefill |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| FP8 (recipe) | 102.5 | 51.7 | 69.6 | 42.5 s |
| EXL3 pack (this PR) | 109.4 | 59.9 | 77.6 | 39.9 s |
| 4-bit round-to-nearest (recipe `q4`, for reference) | 115.6 | 57.2 | 76.6 | — |

With 4 streams (sparkDash, whose code prompt repeats one function 50 times): 257 tok/s of code in all against 248
with FP8.

The prefill row uses `TF_GLM_PREFILL_ROWS=4096`: the prompt GEMM unpacks each matrix once per chunk, so bigger chunks
amortize the unpack. At 2,048 rows prefill is ~9% slower than FP8.

Quality, same setup: HumanEval (164 problems × 5 samples, T=0.7, thinking off) 96.3% (FP8 96.2%). On 8 short
French coding prompts × 5 samples, 1 of 40 replies never ended its turn (FP8 0/40). P(end of turn) right after the
closing code fence on those prompts (40 draws, T=1) was 0.88 (FP8 0.82, BF16 0.76).

## Tests

- `tests/test_glm5_dense_exl3.py` (CPU, no GPU): every cut (row / col for K4, K5 and K6; rep; head columns) is the
  matching block of `format.dequantize`'s float64 weight, column cuts sum to the full output, and off-grid cuts are
  refused.
- `tests/cuda/test_glm5_dense_exl3.py`: row and column shards give the full layer's output on the decode kernel
  (1, 7, 128 rows) and the prompt GEMM (300 rows); a `Dense3` stack with a BF16 part goes through `qmm.matmul`.
- On a GB10 (NVIDIA's 26.07 container): the new tests plus `test_qmm`, `test_glm_split_and_policy` and
  `test_glm_exl3`: 57 passed. The GLM CPU tests that need `mlx` were skipped there.
- End to end, the two-rank engine was served with this change applied to the recipe's tree (the same diff, as a
  recipe patch). Pristine 0.6.0 (BF16 fallback) is covered by the unit tests only.

Written with AI assistance (Claude Code); the author reviewed every change.

items.title: prompt cache: a finished reply becomes a resume point under a plan
items.body:
## Summary

`retain_finished_caches` keeps a finished stream's KV so the next prompt can resume from the end of the reply — but only when no `PrefillPlan` is set, and `_family_start` only accepts a stored cache at a plan chunk start (`cached_tokens in chunks`). On a planned engine — every serve — a finished reply's state is therefore never kept, and could not be used anyway.

Agentic clients pay for this every turn: they re-render the previous reply inside the next prompt, and each request re-prefills that whole reply. On a 26.5k-token conversation with ~1k-token replies that is ~3.9k tokens re-prefilled per turn.

This patch makes a finished reply's cache a usable resume point:

- `_keeps_decoded` keeps a finished stream's state under a plan, gated to prefixes of at least `--finished-prefix-tokens` (default 4096, `0`: any length) — below that, re-prefilling the prefix is cheaper than copying its cache into a store slot.
- `CheckpointEntry.any_position` marks finished-reply entries: they still match only as a strict token prefix of the next prompt, but their length need not be a plan start (the entry's own length is where its state is valid — the grid constraint is about where checkpoints may be *placed*, not where a stored state may resume from).
- Only a store hit flagged `any_position` gets the splice: `_family_prefill_steps` adds that one position to the prompt's chunk starts so the fill tiles from it. Caller-provided caches keep the existing plan-start rule.

Note: `save_conversations` sorts "prompt-side entries before reply ends (a re-rendered reply never matches one)". Measured on Qwen/GLM chat templates the re-rendered reply is token-identical — zero divergence through the reply region; the blocker was positional, not textual.

## Measured (Apple Silicon Mac Studio, agentic multi-turn workload, ~26–31k-token prompts, cached-resume turns)

| Model | Turn TTFT before | Turn TTFT after | Uncached/turn |
|---|---:|---:|---:|
| GLM-5.3-Flash 4-bit g64 | 7.22 s | **5.49 s** (−24%) | 3,865 → 2,840 |
| Flash-Next 4-bit g32 | 3.55 s | **2.80 s** (−21%) | 4,165 → 3,142 |

Decode throughput unchanged. Exactness bench: **ALL EQUAL** (drafted vs serial, code/agentic-long/prose × seed99/seed1234/greedy) on both models. Short-prompt throughput unchanged in an interleaved stock/patch A/B (GLM: 61.1–61.4 vs 61.3–61.5 median tok/s) — short finished states are not kept, so nothing is copied.

## Test plan

- [x] `tests/test_checkpoint_memory.py` — two new cases: a finished reply matches at its own position under a plan, and never extends a diverging prompt (strict prefix still rules)
- [x] `tests/test_family_prefill_chunks.py` — the flag lets an off-grid stored state resume; an unmarked off-grid cache is still rejected; short finished states are not kept
- [x] Live verification on GLM-5.3-Flash and Flash-Next 4-bit builds: multi-turn agentic bench, `cached=` advances to the reply-end boundary, subsequent turns resume there
- [ ] CUDA lane untouched — the change is in the shared server/prefill path; happy to gate it further if a reviewer wants

items.title: feat(flash next cuda): --parallel N on two ranks
items.body:
Follows up #123. Flash Next with `--tp 2` served one request at a time and refused `--parallel`. This lets both ranks share each round between several requests. Measured with your `tools/bench_concurrent.py`, 8 users get 2.4-3.4x the total throughput and every reply keeps its solo run's token ids. A single request under `--parallel` gives up 2-4%, which we left as is (details below).

## What changes

- **Rank 0 plans, rank 1 runs that plan.** Only rank 0 schedules. It sends rank 1 each admission, round, completion and drop, in the order it runs them, over one TCP connection. The connection uses `TCP_NODELAY`, and its ephemeral port on the `--master` address is published through the rendezvous store. An admission carries the slot rank 0 chose and the kept prompt end it resumes from, and rank 1 takes exactly those instead of choosing.
- **The ranks can't drift apart unnoticed, and neither is left waiting.** Before each admission and each round, both ranks confirm the plan in one small all-gather. For an admission that's the stream, slot, resume point, prompt and sampling. For a round it's the live streams, their lengths, drafts and slots. If the plans ever differ, both ranks raise `OutOfStep` at the same point, before any of that step's collectives. The requests in that step fail with the error and serving goes on. Checking over the socket alone would have left rank 0 inside NCCL, which has no timeout, if rank 1 stopped. At startup both ranks must also agree on `--parallel`, beside the settings already checked.
- **A request that ends on rank 0 alone** (the client left) is named in the next round message, so rank 1 ends it too before the check. It is then finished on both ranks as usual.
- **Sampling over the split vocabulary per stream.** `choose_gathered_streams` picks every stream's tokens from the step's gathered candidates with one read-back. A rule wider than the gathered candidates goes through `tp_sample_rows`, and drafts do the same (`_picks_tp`).
- **A lone stream replays the one-stream CUDA graphs**, as #84 does for Qwen3.6. The graphs' `State` is one of the slots. A stream left decoding alone moves into it with `State.copy_from`, which copies in place and keeps the captured addresses. This helps one GPU as well.
- **Admission:** `indexed_stream_geometry(world=...)`. The graphs' buffers are counted as one more stream, which is generous.
- **Structured output under `--tp 2 --parallel` is refused with an HTTP 400 before anything is generated.** The message says why and what to do instead, and the startup line says so too. Images were already refused because Flash Next on CUDA is text-only. One GPU, and two ranks without `--parallel`, are unchanged.

## The checks you listed

| Check | Where |
|---|---|
| Rank 0 plans each round and rank 1 runs the same plan | `follow` runs rank 0's ops in order, with rank 0's slot and resume point. `test_tp_rank_1_takes_rank_0s_slot_and_resume_point_or_both_refuse_the_admission` and `test_tp_ranks_planning_a_different_round_both_refuse_it_and_serve_on` put rank 1 out of step on purpose: both ranks refuse that step, the request gets `OutOfStep`, the next request is exact, and every slot on rank 1 is free at the end |
| Every reply equals its `"draft": false` run and its solo run by token ids at 1, 2, 4 and 8 users | `test_tp_every_reply_equals_its_serial_run_and_its_solo_run_at_1_2_4_8_users`, greedy and 7 sampling rules mixed; on two Sparks, below |
| A resumed prompt equals a fresh one | `test_tp_a_resumed_prompt_equals_the_same_prompt_fresh` (same prompt resumed from a kept slot, fresh on a new decoder, and serial); on two Sparks, below |
| A cancel or disconnect during prefill or decode leaves neither rank hanging | `test_tp_a_client_leaving_in_prefill_or_decode_leaves_neither_rank_hanging` through the real `Scheduler`, and `test_tp_a_stream_rank_0_ends_at_its_first_token_...`, which failed with "out of step" before the round-message change above; both assert every slot free on rank 1 at the end |
| Structured output and images refused, not served one at a time | `test_an_engine_refusing_structured_output_says_why_before_generating`; on two Sparks, below |

## Evidence

**Measured with your concurrency bench, `tools/bench_concurrent.py`**, as docs/recipes/README.md describes: `--levels 1,2,4,8 --alone --serial --reps 3` (256 tokens, `ignore_eos`), unchanged from 0.5.0. Setup: two DGX Sparks, Qwen3.8 Flash Next MLX 4-bit, `--tp 2 --context 65536`, int8 KV. We compared 0.5.0 without `--parallel` against this branch with `--parallel 8`. Figures are aggregate tok/s, 0.5.0 → this PR, medians of 3:

| Users | code greedy | code sampled | chat greedy | chat sampled |
|---:|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 107.1 → 104.9 | 105.6 → 101.4 | 86.0 → 83.9 | 84.0 → 80.7 |
| 2 | 104.5 → 173.2 | 97.1 → 126.5 | 85.2 → 139.7 | 85.8 → 113.3 |
| 4 | 103.8 → 258.5 | 101.4 → 171.8 | 84.4 → 209.2 | 82.1 → 146.8 |
| 8 | 103.6 → 345.4 | 101.9 → 223.7 | 84.0 → 283.8 | 78.7 → 185.5 |

The tool's own checks passed in every cell on both versions. Each concurrent reply had the same token ids as its solo run: 45/45 in each of the 4 cells, 180 in all. Each solo run matched `"draft": false`.

**A single request is 2-4% slower than 0.5.0** when the server runs with `--parallel`, going through the lone-stream path: 104.9 against 107.1 tok/s for code greedy, and 80.7 against 84.0 for chat sampled. We did not try to close that gap in this PR. Our own 512-token greedy run agrees, at about 107.5 against 111 tok/s. Serving without `--parallel` is unchanged. Happy to look into it separately if it matters to you. On one Spark, a lone stream ran at 81.4 tok/s against 81.9 before, and two streams ran 19% faster.

Our own end-to-end checks on the two Sparks, beside your bench. Each reply was compared **by token ids**, using the `token_sha` every reply carries in `tensorfold`, with the same request's `"draft": false` reply on the same server. Its text was also compared with the serial replies recorded on unmodified 0.5.0. The script is `exact3.py`; we can add it under `tools/` if that helps your run.

- 1, 2, 4 and 8 users at once, 8 cases (greedy, and `top_k` 20 and 0, mixed): 15/15 equal to serial by token ids, 15/15 equal to the solo run, and 15/15 equal to 0.5.0's text.
- Resumed against fresh: 6 second turns, each sent first with nothing kept (cached 0), then after its first turn, resuming from 21-29 kept tokens. All 12 equal to serial by token ids. All 6 sent at once: 6/6 equal. Three of them resumed; the other three found their kept slots taken by the requests arriving with them and prefilled fresh.
- Hang-ups, twice over: 2 clients closed 0.4 s into a ~20K-token prefill and 2 mid-reply, beside 4 live requests. The live 8/8 equal by token ids, then 8 at once afterwards 8/8 equal. Neither rank logged an error.
- Our wider suite (`exact2.py`), 16 cases: greedy, `top_k` 20/0/50, `min_p`, `ignore_eos`, stop strings, a 2K-token reply and a ~20K-token prompt. They were run alone, all 16 at once (more than the slots), staggered, mixed with hang-ups and invalid requests, and at once again. All 80 replies and the 4 multi-turn conversations were identical.
- `response_format`, streamed or not, and `guided_regex` gave an HTTP 400 with the reason, in under 10 ms. An image gave a 400 too.

## Checks

- `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_tp_multi.py` is new. It runs two ranks in two threads, as `test_flashnext_tp.py` does, with the same fakes.
- The Flash Next CUDA tests, `tests/test_cuda_response_format.py` and `tests/test_cuda_server*.py` give 342 passed, 18 skipped. The skips are the xgrammar cases, which aren't installed in our container.
- `ruff check` adds no findings on the changed files, compared with `main`.
- Not in this PR: grammar under two-rank `--parallel`. One more thing: a failure inside a step on one rank only, such as running out of memory on one Spark mid-prefill, still leaves the other rank waiting in NCCL, as it does on the serial two-rank path today.

We're happy to rework any of it, for example sending the plan through the store or a collective instead of the socket, if you'd rather.

items.title: TensorFold 0.3.2: GLM-5.3-Flash on EXL3 weights (experimental), tensorfold update
items.body:
TensorFold 0.3.2: GLM-5.3-Flash on Mia-AiLab's EXL3 checkpoint (experimental), and `tensorfold update`.

**EXL3 (experimental).** GLM-5.3-Flash's CUDA engine reads `Mia-AiLab/GLM-5.3-Flash-EXL3-TR3-4bpw` on two DGX Sparks: routed experts in ExLlamaV3's EXL3 format, BF16 elsewhere. On those same weights, against vLLM running Mia-AiLab's recipe with MTP=3 through the same client (decode tok/s, 64-token replies, median of seeds 1234-1238):

| | Code, sampled | Chat, sampled | Code, greedy | Chat, greedy |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| vLLM, MTP=3 | 24.5 | 24.3 | 32.2 | 24.7 |
| TensorFold | 36.4 | 29.7 | 43.8 | 32.9 |

`serve` prints a note that EXL3 support is experimental, and the README and the GLM recipe say so. Other EXL3 variants are refused with a pointer to the recipe book.

**`tensorfold update`.** It installs the newest release. `serve` checks GitHub for a newer release once a day in the background and prints a line when there is one (`--no-update-check` or `TENSORFOLD_NO_UPDATE_CHECK=1` turns it off).

**Fix.** `glue.swiglu` and `attention.kv_write` launched no programs at widths under 512 and 1024. So the synthetic engine tests never ran the dense MLP or DSA attention, and their results depended on leftover memory. The real model's launches are unchanged.

**Validation** (26 September, two DGX Sparks, this tree pip-installed in NVIDIA's `pytorch:26.07-py3` container):
- GLM CUDA tests from the installed package: 30 of 30, in file order and reversed. Host tests: 274 passed.
- EXL3 checkpoint through `tensorfold serve`: 12 of 12 default-policy replies equal serial decoding by token-id SHA-256; 9 of 9 drafted replies equal the same requests with `"draft": false`; prompts resumed from a kept reply or prompt equal fresh prefills.
- MLX checkpoint, as a regression check: greedy hashes unchanged (`9c65654e926ec8fb`, `b6d1267266302457`), 12 of 12 equal serial, 9 of 9, prefix reuse passes. Speeds 49.7 / 43.2 / 66.1 / 45.2, against 0.3.0's 49.4 / 43.3 / 66.3 / 45.2.

items.title: perf(flash next cuda): read a prompt pass's n-gram rows before waiting on the previous step's copies
items.body:
**Branch:** `perf/flash-next-stage-ahead` (one commit, da6caed, on `v0.6.0`, c464617)

**TL;DR:** Flash Next's `stage()` waited for the previous step's copies out of the pinned staging buffers, and only then gathered the pass's n-gram (PLE) rows from the memory-mapped table. The GPU idled through that gather after every prompt pass, and longer when table pages had been evicted. The rows are now gathered before the wait and copied into the buffers after it, so the gather overlaps the previous step's GPU work. The same rows reach the same buffers, so prompts, decode and kept states keep their bits.

## The problem

- `stage()` called `b.staged.synchronize()` first. That event is recorded after the previous step's copies out of the pinned buffers. Only then did it gather each layer's n-gram rows (`p.table.gather(ids)`) and copy them in.
- The gather runs on the host and touches pages of the mapped n-gram table, about 27 GiB for the NVFP4 checkpoint. An NVFP4 table is never locked (`NVFP4Table.lock()` returns `False`), and the memory gate counts its pages as reclaimable.
- Once memory fills and the kernel evicts table pages, the gather page-faults, and the GPU waits for all of it after every pass.

## The change

- `stage()` collects the pass's lookups (layer, row ids, first staging row) and gathers the rows for all layers before the wait.
  - After the wait, it writes the token ids and copies the gathered rows into the pinned buffers, as before.
  - `stage_ple_rows` takes the already-gathered rows (`got=`). Without them it gathers them itself, as before.
- EXL3 packs keep their order: `stage_ple` reads into the pinned buffers directly.
- `TF_FLASH_STAGE_AHEAD=0` restores the old order.
- The buffers, copies and rows are the same; only the moment of the gather moves.

## Measurements

Jetson AGX Thor, one container session (`up-u2`). Upstream 0.6.0 plus this commit, `local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` rev `7c4f1bc1`, `--kv-dtype int8 --parallel 4`. The engine reads the switch at each `stage()`, so both orders run in one process on the same prompts. Cold prefill wall time, every request counted:

| Prompt | `TF_FLASH_STAGE_AHEAD=0` (before) | this change | Change | Head logits |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| synthetic 8k | 903 tok/s | 923 tok/s | +2.2% | identical |
| synthetic 32k | 889 tok/s | 890 tok/s | +0.1% | identical |
| natural text 32k | 862 tok/s | 868 tok/s | +0.7% | identical |
| **natural text 32k, n-gram table dropped from the page cache** | **773 tok/s** | **857 tok/s** | **+10.8%** | identical |
| synthetic 128k | 789 tok/s | 792 tok/s | +0.4% | identical |
| one-user greedy decode, 512 tokens (median of 3) | 66.55 tok/s | 66.57 tok/s | 0% | identical ids |

The decode row is in-process greedy decode with MTP drafts, not a served-request metric. The first decode with stage-ahead on was 58.11 tok/s. The median drops it. The other five runs are 66.50-66.59 tok/s with the same ids.

The prefill cells are single runs; a gain under about 1% is within run-to-run noise.

The cold row drops the table's pages before the prompt. The log records `madvise(MADV_DONTNEED)` (`madvise_rc` 0) and resident pages falling to about 0. That is what a long-running server sees once other memory has pushed the table out.

## Tests

- New: `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_nvfp4_loader.py::test_stage_reads_the_ngram_rows_ahead_with_the_same_bits`. With the switch on and off, a prompt in passes of 16 and then 5 rows gives the same first token, staged rows, streams and decoded tokens.
- An earlier session on the same code (`up-u1`): `test_flashnext_nvfp4_loader.py` **26 passed** (including the new test); `test_flashnext_forward.py` plus `test_flashnext_multi.py` **79 passed, 2 failed**. The measurement session (`up-u2`) did not re-run those full files.
  - The 2 failures are `test_flashnext_multi.py::test_packed_passes_keep_each_prompt_one_token_early[bf16]` and `[int8]`. In the measurement session, the same two tests with 0.6.0's `forward.py` failed the same assertion: stream 4's output is `[2033, 2685, 530, 0]` and `serial_decode` continues `[2033, 2685, 530, 0, 979, ...]`.
  - That failure is already present on plain 0.6.0.
- Not run: DGX Spark, CPU tests.

The commit also applies cleanly to the 0.6.1 branch (`pr-141-0.6.1`): `git cherry-pick` merges `forward.py` and the loader test without conflicts. It was not tested there.

AI disclosure: an AI coding agent (Claude Code) wrote this change and ran the measurements on my Jetson AGX Thor. I approved posting it; I have not reviewed the code line by line.

items.title: fix(flash next cuda): build the CUDA extensions before the weights load
items.body:
**Branch:** `fix/flash-next-build-before-load` (one commit, 5c5931b, on `v0.6.0`, c464617)

**TL;DR:** On a first start after an install or an update, `tensorfold.cuda.build.load` compiles each CUDA extension the first time a step needs it. Flash Next met them in its prompt warm-up, after the weights had loaded. On a Jetson AGX Thor (unified memory), that left the server with **1.36-2.00 GiB less MemAvailable** than the next start (two sessions), still missing 20 s after the server came up. The engine now loads every extension it uses right after admission, before the weights load. With the same builds, the difference is **0.01-0.15 GiB**, about the 0.1 GiB by which two starts that build nothing differ.

## The problem

- Upstream 0.6.0 with an empty extension cache (a first start after `pip install -U` or `tensorfold update`) builds six extensions: `tensorfold_nvfp4_prompt_v1`, `tensorfold_qwen4_exp_gdn_io`, `tensorfold_gdn_v2`, `tensorfold_experts_v7`, `tensorfold_nvfp4_v3` and `tensorfold_qmm_v3`. All six are built after the weights load, in the warm-up.
- After such a start, MemAvailable is 1.36-2.00 GiB lower than after the next start, which builds nothing (MemFree moves with it), measured 20 s after the server is up.
- The missing memory is not in the server's resident set (1.88-1.93 GiB on every start). Net `Cached` moved by 0.07 GiB or less, and `AnonHugePages` by 0.14 GiB. In the first stock session, about 1 GiB moved from `Active(file)` to `Inactive(file)` while net `Cached` stayed put. Where the missing GiB is held is not identified.
- Why it matters: on a unified GPU, `MemoryGate.fits` checks the caches' growth against live MemAvailable. So the streams' caches have 1.4-2 GiB less to grow into for as long as the memory stays missing. How long that lasts in a running server was not measured. The printed "free for their caches" does not show it: it reads the same after both starts.

## The change

- New `engine.build_kernels(exl3=, nvfp4=, solo=)`, which loads:
  - for every start: `experts`, `kernels.gdn`, `kernels.qmm` and `qwen4_exp.cuda.gdn_io`;
  - for NVFP4 (ModelOpt) checkpoints: the NVFP4 linears' two extensions;
  - for EXL3 packs: the EXL3 experts' and linears' extensions;
  - for one stream only: `qwen4_exp.cuda.gdn` (concurrent rounds never use it).
- `FlashNextEngine.__init__` calls it right after admission, so a refused start builds nothing, and before `weights.load`.
- On a start with a built cache it only loads the modules.
- Tests:
  - `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_forward.py::test_the_engine_loads_its_extensions_before_the_weights`, at one and two streams. It records every `tensorfold.cuda.build.load` call and the `weights.load` call during a start and a first request on the synthetic checkpoint, and checks that no extension is loaded after the weights. It clears the loaders' `lru_cache` first, so each one goes through `build.load`.
  - `tests/test_cuda_capacity.py::fake_runtime`, which stops a start at its weights load to test admission without a GPU, now stubs `build_kernels`.

## Measurements

Jetson AGX Thor, `local-inference-lab/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-NVFP4` rev `7c4f1bc1`, `--kv-dtype int8 --parallel 4`. Two container sessions (1: `up-m1`, 2: `up-b4`), each with four starts in a row; the server was stopped and given 15 s between starts. MemAvailable was read 20 s after the server answered `/v1/models`:

| Session | Tree | Builds on the first start | MemAvailable after the first start | after the next start (no builds) | Difference |
|---|---|---|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 0.6.0 | 6, after the weights load | 40.99 GiB | 42.99 GiB | **-2.00 GiB** |
| 1 | an earlier revision of this change, which also built the one-stream chain | 7, before the load | 42.87 GiB | 42.88 GiB | -0.01 GiB |
| 2 | 0.6.0 | 6, after the weights load | 41.65 GiB | 43.01 GiB | **-1.36 GiB** |
| 2 | this change | 6, before the load | 42.91 GiB | 43.05 GiB | -0.15 GiB |

- With 0.6.0, MemFree fell with MemAvailable (-1.98 and -1.36 GiB). The server's resident set (1.88-1.93 GiB in every start), anonymous memory, page cache and slab each moved by 0.14 GiB or less.
- Two starts that build nothing differ by up to 0.11 GiB (the two trees' second starts: 42.88 vs 42.99, 43.05 vs 43.01). The -0.15 GiB with this change is close to that.
- The builds take the same time either way: in session 2, the first start was ready after 285 s on 0.6.0 and 290 s with this change, against 86-87 s for a start that builds nothing. These are single runs.
- The printed "free for their caches" reads 32.2-32.3 GiB in all eight starts.
- The measurement is a small shell script around `tensorfold serve` and `/proc/meminfo`.

The same kind of loss showed up earlier on a local Thor branch, on a first start that built its extensions after the weights loaded. Not measured: DGX Spark. It is also unified memory, so it may behave the same way.

## Tests

- **New test:** `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_forward.py::test_the_engine_loads_its_extensions_before_the_weights`, at one and two streams.
  - Both pass with this change.
  - With 0.6.0's `engine.py`, both fail. One stream lists `tensorfold_experts_v7`, `tensorfold_qmm_v3`, `tensorfold_qwen4_exp_gdn`, `tensorfold_qwen4_exp_gdn_io` and `tensorfold_gdn_v2`. Two streams list the same set without `tensorfold_qwen4_exp_gdn`. The synthetic checkpoint does not load the NVFP4 extensions.
- **On the same Thor, with this change (`up-b4`, `up-b5`):**
  - `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_forward.py`: **56 passed**.
  - `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_nvfp4_loader.py`, `test_flashnext_tp.py` and `test_flashnext_multi.py`: **70 passed, 2 skipped, 2 failed**. The 2 failures are `test_flashnext_multi.py::test_packed_passes_keep_each_prompt_one_token_early[bf16]` and `[int8]`. They fail the same way on plain 0.6.0 (details in the stage-ahead PR).
  - With no GPU visible, the CPU tests that construct engines up to the weights load (`tests/test_cuda_capacity.py`, `test_cuda_kv_dtype.py`, `test_cuda_parallel_admission.py`, `test_cuda_admission.py`, `test_exl3_engines.py` and `test_cuda_nemotron_admission.py`): **147 passed**.
- **Not run:**
  - an EXL3 pack on a GPU, so the EXL3 loaders in `build_kernels` are exercised only by the CPU tests, which stub it;
  - DGX Spark.

The commit also applies cleanly to the 0.6.1 branch (`pr-141-0.6.1`). There, the list in `build_kernels` should be checked against the vision and image-row paths it adds. The new test would show any extension loaded after the weights.

AI disclosure: an AI coding agent (Claude Code) wrote this change and ran the measurements on my Jetson AGX Thor. I approved posting it; I have not reviewed the code line by line.
