items.title: fix: the 27B's one-stream CUDA engine keeps K/V buffers within the admitted window
items.body:
## Summary

The one-stream Qwen3.8-27B CUDA engine (one GPU or two ranks, with `--parallel` at its CUDA default of one stream) never sets `State.limit`, so its attention caches grow to `max(need, 2 × rows, 1024)` with no upper bound. Once a buffer holds more than half the window, its next growth passes the window. At `--context 32768`, a fresh 31,015-token prompt leaves 62,024 rows per attention layer, where the startup admission prices each buffer at 32,768.

`prefill` and `prefill_tp` now take `limit=` and set it on a fresh `State`. `Qwen27Engine` passes its `context_window` at all three call sites. With the limit, every buffer stays at or below the admission estimate's row count.

## Why

`Q/` is `src/tensorfold/families/qwen3_5/cuda/`. References are at `main` (34bae79).

- `State.limit` defaults to 0, meaning no bound (`Q/forward.py:94`). Growth in `_grow` (`Q/prefill.py:39-49`) and in `commit` (`Q/forward.py:375-388`) caps a buffer only when it is set. Only the concurrent decoder sets it (`Q/multi.py:107`).
- The one-stream admission prices four K/V buffers per attention layer: two kept prompt ends, the live state and a growth copy. Each is priced at `next_power_of_two(max(1024, window))` rows (`src/tensorfold/cuda/geometry.py:163-165`).
- Prompts prefill in even chunks of up to 4,096 rows (`Q/prefill.py:120-124`). For 31,015 tokens the buffer grows 3,876 → 7,753 → 15,506 → 31,012 → 62,024 rows. The last chunk needs three rows more than 31,012, and the buffer doubles.
- At `--context 32768`, 3,072 of the 32,767 fresh prompt lengths leave a buffer above 32,768 rows, all between 28,673 and 32,767 tokens. The largest is 65,528 rows. Replies and resumes grow the same way: a 16,000-token prompt whose reply passes 32,000 rows reaches 64,000.
- For the 27B, a row across the 16 attention layers is 65,536 B: K and V, 4 KV heads of 256, bf16 (the checkpoint's `config.json`: 64 layers, a full-attention layer every 4). That prompt's buffer set is 3.8 GiB where admission assumes 2.0 GiB. The engine keeps two prompt ends (`Q/engine.py:119-120`), so two or three distinct long prompts in a row hold several such sets.

## Change

- `Q/decode.py` `prefill` and `Q/decode_tp.py` `prefill_tp` take a keyword `limit: int = 0`. A fresh state gets `st.limit = limit`. A resumed state keeps its own limit (`clone_state` copies it, `Q/decode.py:22`). Other callers see no change.
- `Q/engine.py` passes `limit=self.context_window` on one GPU (`generate`, with or without drafts), on rank 0 (`_generate_tp`) and on rank 1 (`follow`). Cached prompt ends come from these prefills, so resumed states carry the limit too.
- The limit is `context_window`, not `cache_slots`. `cache_slots` is `window + 12` (`src/tensorfold/cuda/capacity.py:56`), which is 12 rows above the estimate's power of two when the window is itself a power of two.
- The concurrent decoder is unchanged. It already bounds its states, and its own estimate prices them row for row (`geometry.py:243-260`).

One keyword on two functions and three call sites. No kernel, admission or cache-policy change.

## Exactness

The change alters buffer capacity only, never a key or value row or the order of any sum.

- **Rows.** Growth copies every committed row into the new buffer (`Q/prefill.py:46-47`, `Q/forward.py:386-387`).
- **Decode attention.** It addresses each cache by its data pointer (`src/tensorfold/cuda/kernels/attention.py:223-236`) and splits keys into 512-key chunks by committed count and absolute position (`:171-190`). Capacity is not an input.
- **Prefill attention.** It checks that the cache holds `p0 + W` rows and reads keys up to each row's position (`src/tensorfold/cuda/kernels/prefill_attention.py:41-54`, `:64`). Capacity is not an input.
- **Room.** Growth keeps `max(need, …)`, so a commit always gets every row it needs. The engine refuses prompts of `context_window` tokens or more and caps a reply at `context_window - len(prompt)` tokens (`Q/engine.py:128-131`). The last sampled token is not committed, so no state passes `context_window - 1` rows.
- **Reallocations.** A limited buffer either has the unlimited size or holds `context_window` rows. No commit needs more, so the limit adds no reallocation.
- **Same path as `--parallel`.** The capped growth path is the one the concurrent decoder already runs (`Q/multi.py:107`).

This is argued from the code. The GPU test below checks it.

## Tests

Host: macOS, Python 3.13.5, PyTorch 2.11.0 CPU.

`tests/test_qwen27_kv_limit.py` (new, 16 tests) uses the `allocations` fixture of `tests/test_cuda_geometry.py` for its Triton stand-in. `prefill_chunk` is replaced by its cache writes (`_grow`, then the chunk's rows), since the kernels need a GPU. The chunking, `_grow`, `State`, `prefill`, `prefill_tp` and `commit` are the real ones.

- Fresh prompts of 29,815, 31,015 and 31,497 tokens through `prefill` and both ranks of `prefill_tp`. Without a limit they reach 59,624, 62,024 and 62,992 rows. With `limit=32768` they stay at 32,768, and every committed row is intact.
- The 31,015-token growth sequence, with and without the limit.
- A prompt resumed from a limited state keeps the bound (32,100 tokens from 16,000: 64,000 rows unlimited, 32,768 limited). A resumed state's own limit wins over the keyword.
- A 16,000-token prompt, then a reply committed through `commit` in 12-row windows up to 32,767 rows: 64,000 rows unlimited, 32,768 limited, every row intact.
- `Qwen27Engine` passes `limit=context_window` on one GPU (with and without drafts), on rank 0 and on rank 1 (`follow`).

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| New file on this branch | 16 passed, with and without an import-only Triton stand-in |
| New file on `main`'s sources | 16 failed: 15 raise `TypeError` on the new `limit` keyword; in the engine test the three call sites pass 0 |
| Whole host suite (`tests` without `tests/cuda`), `main` (34bae79) | 133 failed, 1,319 passed, 298 skipped, 4 xfailed, 18 errors |
| Same, this branch merged into `main` (34bae79) | 133 failed, 1,335 passed, 298 skipped, 4 xfailed, 18 errors |

The whole-suite runs had an import-only Triton stand-in. The same 151 ids fail or error on both, for host reasons: no `transformers` tokenizer, no Triton backends, MLX 0.31.1 where GLM-5.3-Flash needs 0.32.2, and two tests that read `tools/` and `CHANGELOG.md`, which the test tree used here did not include. `ruff check` on the three source files reports the same two findings as on `main` (an E731 and an F841 in `engine.py`).

`tests/cuda/test_qwen27_prefill.py::test_a_cache_limit_changes_no_bits` (new, GPU) uses the file's toy model in two cases: 9,000 rows with limit 9,100 (the third chunk grows to 9,100 rows, not 12,000), and 1,000 rows with limit 1,100 (the reply grows the buffer to 1,100 rows, not 2,048). It checks that:

- a limited `prefill_state` equals an unlimited one (state and last-row `normed`);
- `prefill(..., limit=)` gives the same first token;
- serial and drafted replies from the limited state equal the unlimited serial reply (90 tokens);
- the states after the reply are equal, and the limited one stays within its limit.

## GPU status

One DGX Spark (GB10, sm_121); container: Python 3.12.3, PyTorch 2.13.0a0 (NVIDIA 26.07), CUDA 13.3, Triton 3.7.1. `TORCH_CUDA_ARCH_LIST=12.1` was set: without it the 0.3.5 extensions do not build in this container (the failure #56 reports, fixed on `main` in 0.3.6.1). Branch head 8c4c98c.

| Run | Result |
|---|---|
| `tests/cuda/test_qwen27_prefill.py` | 14 passed, including `test_a_cache_limit_changes_no_bits` (2 cases) |
| `tests/cuda` | 290 passed, 7 skipped; `main` (beddbb7): 288 passed, the same 7 skipped |

Still pending:

2. The 27B on one GB10 at `--context 32768`, `main` against this branch, a fresh 31,015-token prompt: the reply's `token_sha` (equal expected), and `torch.cuda.memory_allocated` after the prefill.
3. Two ranks (two GB10s): the same reply hashes on both branches.

## Evidence

Surface: the engine's growth rule run on CPU tensors. No GPU, no model.

- **One prompt.** The real `chunks` and `_grow`, run over every fresh prompt length below 32,768, give the figures above. A fresh 31,015-token prompt leaves a 62,024-row K/V buffer per attention layer where admission assumes 32,768: 3.8 GiB against 2.0 GiB at 65,536 B a row.
- **Request sequences.** A replay of the one-stream engine's rules on buffer sizes: `_grow`, `commit`'s growth, the two-entry prompt-end cache and `_drop_extensions`. It matches the real `_grow` on single prompts. It ran 4,000 random sequences of one to four requests, each a fresh prompt or a continuation of the previous one, with prompt and reply lengths drawn within the window. Rows are counted as the estimate counts them: kept entries, the live state and one growth copy, the copy as a whole buffer set. For a fresh prompt the copy term is the estimate's accounting, not allocated memory, since a fresh state's old buffers are freed one layer at a time.

| `--context` | Estimate (4 buffers) | Peak, no limit | Peak, with the limit |
|---|---|---|---|
| 32,768 | 131,072 rows (8.0 GiB) | 216,136 rows (13.2 GiB), 1.65× | 131,012 rows, 1.00× |
| 262,144 | 1,048,576 rows (64.0 GiB) | 1,560,192 rows (95.2 GiB), 1.49× | 1,046,304 rows, 1.00× |

With the limit the peak was at most 1.00× at every window tried: 8,192, 32,768, 65,536, 100,000, 131,072 and 262,144.

- The worst sequence at 32,768 is three fresh prompts of 31,015, 29,815 and 31,497 tokens. At the third prompt's last chunk, the two kept entries hold 62,024 and 59,624 rows and the live state 62,992: 184,640 rows (11.3 GiB) before any growth copy, 1.41× the whole estimate.
- One long chat stays within the estimate. Each turn resumes the previous prompt end; at the 262,144 window the worst of 300 simulated chats peaked at 0.75×. The overshoot needs two or three distinct long prompts.
- Which window a DGX Spark admits by default was not checked.

## Overlaps

- The prompt-end cache change in #65 adds `keep_at=` on the same lines: 5 conflict blocks in `decode.py`, `decode_tp.py` and `engine.py`, on the `prefill` and `prefill_tp` signatures and their three call sites (`keep_at=` against `limit=`). Whichever lands second needs a rebase, which also gives each PR's host-test stand-ins (`prefill`, `prefill_tp`, `prefill_chunk`) the other's keyword; on a host merge with that done, both host files pass.
- The `ignore_eos` change in #63 also edits `engine.py`. Git merges the two cleanly.
- No other open upstream PR shares a file with this one.

Not in this change: the drafter's caches, which have their own bounded estimate (`draft_geometry(..., bounded=True)`), and the other families (`glm5_next`, `qwen4_exp`, `nemotron_h`), which were not checked.

---

items.title: glm5_next: long contexts on a latent MLA cache (256k on two Sparks)
items.body:
Fixes #53

## Problem

Past its 2,051-token dense window, GLM-5.3-Flash on 0.3.5.1 answers `!!!!...` on two DGX Sparks, and the per-head
KV cache admits at most ~40k tokens there (details in the issue).

## What this changes

- **Latent cache** (`glm5_next/cuda/latent.py`). The DSA layers are NoPE MLA: head h's key is `Wk_h c`, its value
  `Wv_h c`, with `c` the token's 512-wide normalized latent. The cache keeps `c` only (bf16, 1 KB a token and layer,
  shared by the heads and both ranks). The query absorbs `kv_b`'s key blocks (read as the checkpoint stores them,
  4-bit), attention runs over latents, and the attended latent is expanded once through the value blocks.
  `TF_GLM_LATENT=0` keeps the per-head path.
- **Sparse selection** (`sparse.py`). Token selection for all rows of a chunk at once over the pools the chunk can
  see, rounded up to a power of two (fixed sizes also stopped allocator growth at 128k), and the top 512 pools by
  one radix-select kernel: the same set as a stable descending sort, 45 → 6 ms a layer for a 2,048-row chunk at 128k.
- **CUDA graphs past the dense limit** (`graphs.py`), one per pool bucket.
- **Prompt-chunk kernels**: latent attention tiles of all 32 heads (16 in decode windows); the KDA chain of a prompt
  chunk as three kernels (state-independent work for all rows, then the delta rule alone). Both keep the bits of the
  kernels they replace, tested.
- **Admission** (`cuda/geometry.py`): `mla_geometry(latent=True)` sizes the latent cache and its scratch, so
  `--context 0` allocates 487,495 tokens on two Sparks.
- **Several conversations**: up to 8 conversations' prompts are kept; when another conversation takes the caches, a
  kept prompt's rows are saved, within `TF_GLM_CACHE_GIB` (default 3) for states and rows together. As in 0.3.5, only
  prompts are snapshotted.
- `TF_GLM_PROFILE=1` prints a prefill's time and memory by block.
- `docs/recipes/glm-5.3-flash.md` describes the latent cache and the measurements below.

Upstream's prefill matmuls and grouped CUDA experts are used unchanged.

## Exactness

Every kernel computes a row alone in an order fixed by its own position, so drafted replies equal serial ones and
prompt chunks give the same bits for any chunking. New tests: `tests/cuda/test_glm_latent.py` (latent attention
against a float64 definition of the expanded MLA attention, window rows against serial steps, 16- vs 32-head tiles),
`tests/cuda/test_glm_long_context.py` (drafted == serial past 2,051 tokens, sparse graphs == eager, resumed ==
fresh prefill, switching conversations, the memory budget), plus radix top-k and KDA three-kernel bit tests in
`test_glm_kernels.py`. One existing check in `test_prompt_chunks_leave_the_same_state` compares prefill and decode
cache rows within 3e-2 instead of 2e-2 for the latent rows (values up to ~4, a few bf16 steps).

`tests/cuda`: 336 passed, 7 skipped on a GB10.

## Measured

Two DGX Sparks (GB10, 128 GB each), `Vontra/GLM-5.3-Flash-MLX-4bit-MTP`, MTP drafts only, `--context 262144`, a cold
synthetic codebase with one hidden fact:

| Prompt | Prompt reading | First token | Decode at that depth | Hidden fact |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | :---: |
| 32,770 tokens | 1,155 tok/s | 28 s | 42.7 tok/s | found |
| 130,839 tokens | 1,110 tok/s | 118 s | 45.1 tok/s | found |
| 262,099 tokens | 1,033 tok/s | 254 s | 40.1 tok/s | found |
| 0.3.5.1, 32,770 tokens (`--context 36864`) | 626 tok/s | 52 s | – | `!!!!` |

At least 14 GB stayed free on each Spark through the 256k prompt. Short prompts (64 tokens, 5 seeds; code/chat,
sampled/greedy): 49.8 / 42.3 / 60.9 / 48.0 tok/s, against 51.0 / 42.7 / 55.9 / 47.8 for 0.3.5.1. Drafted == serial 9/9.

🤖 Generated with [Claude Code](https://claude.com/claude-code)

items.title: feat: a quantized KV cache for Flash Next on CUDA (--kv-dtype int8 or int4)
items.body:
TensorFold's Flash Next CUDA engine can now keep its KV cache in 8 or 4 bits instead of bf16, behind a flag. The command is `tensorfold serve MODEL --kv-dtype int8` (or `int4`). The default stays bf16, so nothing changes for an existing command, and the MLX path refuses anything but bf16 because this only exists on CUDA.

What you get is memory, not speed. On one DGX Spark the 8-bit cache is 1.68x smaller than bf16 and decodes at the same speed on short prompts, a few percent faster once the prompt is a few thousand tokens. The 4-bit cache is 3.17x smaller, costs about 12% decode speed at short context, and is roughly even by 4,000 tokens. Both change the output. I measured how much, and the numbers are below rather than summarized.

This is the same scheme ExLlamaV3 uses for `-cq 8` and `-cq 4` (the default grid, no companding): groups of 32 along the head dim, the group rotated by a 32-point Hadamard, one fp16 scale per group taken as the group's absmax, and a midpoint grid. 4-bit packs two codes per byte. The indexer keys and the pooled block keys stay bf16, so the saving applies to the K and V tensors only. The query is rotated on the way in and the merged attention output on the way out, which lets the stored keys and values stay in the rotated domain instead of being rotated back on every read.

## What changed

- `cd90ecc`, the 8-bit cache. `src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/cuda/kvcache.py` is new and holds the storage, the Hadamard, and the quantize and dequantize kernels, plus a pure-torch reference quantizer that the tests check against. `glue.py` quantizes keys and values as it writes the cache and rotates the query. `attention.py` dequantizes inside the attention kernel and rotates the merged output back. `forward.py`, `decode.py` and `engine.py` thread the dtype through, and the MTP drafter's own cache uses the same dtype as the main cache, so drafts and verification see the same representation. `cli.py` gains `--kv-dtype {bf16,int8,int4}`, CUDA only.
- `710ad04`, the 4-bit cache, on the same path. One `bits` parameter runs through the kernels rather than a second copy of them. The quantize and dequantize each had to be split into per-width kernels: Triton compiles every branch of a function, and a shared function returned a different shape at 4 bits (two codes per byte) than at 8, which broke compilation of the 8-bit path. `attention.py` loads the packed nibbles and unpacks before the dot.
- `09eb756`, `--mtp-confidence` on the CUDA serve path. The draft chain stops early once a draft's probability drops below this, and the default is 0.3. I added it because the speed numbers people quote for this model were measured at 0.6, and there was no way to ask for that. It is included here because the measurements below depend on it.
- `33a151e` and `05b49a8`, the tests. `tests/cuda/test_flashnext_kvquant.py` checks both widths: the kernels write the reference quantizer's bits exactly, the scales match ExLlamaV3's own quantizer, the cache round-trips inside the grid, attention output stays within a stated tolerance of bf16, a window of rows matches the same rows computed one at a time, chunked prefill matches one shot, drafted decoding matches serial by token-id SHA-256, and the end-to-end logits stay close to bf16. `tests/test_cuda_cli.py` covers the flag parsing, including the refusal on the MLX path.
- `139b0a4` and `1f4131e`, the docs. `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-flash-next.md` gains a section on the flag, the README's option list names it, and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` credits the scheme to ExLlamaV3 (MIT, Copyright (c) 2025 Turboderp).

13 files, +920 / -49, 8 commits, no merge commits, based on `bb4b4a3`.

## Measured on a GB10 (DGX Spark)

One DGX Spark (GB10, driver 580.178.04, CUDA 13.0, torch 2.11, 128 GB unified). Every timing arm ran in an exclusive session with the GPU otherwise idle. The model is `Vontra/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-MLX-4bit-MTP`, the MLX 4-bit affine checkpoint (group size 32) with MTP drafting. It is not an EXL3 checkpoint. This branch is cut from upstream `main`, and upstream cannot load EXL3 packs. That is what #42 adds, so the EXL3 numbers and these are not comparable and I have not mixed them.

### Memory

Bytes per token for one attention layer's K and V plus the fp16 scales, head dim 256, 2 KV heads. The scales are included. Leaving them out overstates the saving, and the whole-cache figure is the one that matters:

| cache | bytes/token/layer | vs bf16 |
| --- | ---: | ---: |
| bf16 | 2,048 | 1.00x |
| int8 | 1,088 | 1.88x |
| int4 | 576 | 3.56x |

Across the whole model the saving is smaller, because the indexer keys and the pooled block keys stay bf16 either way. For Flash Next that works out to 1.68x at int8 (30,784 bytes per token down to 18,304) and 3.17x at int4. At a 262,144-token context the K and V pool drops from 7.52 GiB to 4.47 GiB at int8.

### Speed

Drafted decode, greedy, 400 tokens, median of 3 reps, thinking off. Depth 6 with confidence 0.6 is the policy, and depth 7 at 0.75 is the single best point I measured. SM clock was 2502 to 2528 MHz of a 3003 max during decode, so these are not peak-clock numbers. The client is the same for every arm.

Short prompts, 8,192-token context, tok/s:

| cache | code | devops | prose |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| bf16 | 86.76 | 64.45 | 52.27 |
| int8 | 85.17 | 64.25 | 53.84 |
| int4 | 76.73 | 59.79 | 50.61 |

Depth 7 at confidence 0.75, code prompt only: bf16 88.16, int8 87.16, int4 77.88.

A 4,121-token prompt in a 32,768-token context, depth 6 at confidence 0.6. Here the reps are tight enough to trust the gap, so I list them:

| cache | median | the three reps | prefill, tok/s |
| --- | ---: | --- | ---: |
| bf16 | 75.44 | 74.18, 75.44, 75.60 | 158.3 |
| int8 | 79.72 | 78.14, 79.72, 79.78 | 158.0 |
| int4 | 76.14 | 74.74, 76.14, 76.22 | 158.4 |

Read together: at short context the dequantize costs more than the bandwidth saves, so int8 is a wash (about 98% of bf16) and int4 gives up about 12% on code. By 4,000 tokens of context int8 is 5.7% faster and its slowest rep beat bf16's fastest, while int4 is even with bf16, inside the noise. Prefill is identical across all three, which is what you would expect, since prefill is dominated by the weights and not the cache.

### Quality

Teacher-forced, 2,048 positions from the pack's own bench corpus, full vocabulary, the KL summed in fp32. The same weights in every arm, only the cache dtype changes. NLL is in bits per token.

| cache | NLL | top-1 | KL vs bf16, mean | KL p50 | KL p95 | KL max | top-1 agreement vs bf16 |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| bf16 | 2.7613 | 0.6680 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 0 | 1 |
| int8 | 2.8217 | 0.6665 | 0.2093 | 0.0119 | 1.133 | 11.31 | 0.8916 |
| int4 | 2.7198 | 0.6636 | 0.3911 | 0.0244 | 2.146 | 17.44 | 0.8662 |

The floor of this measurement is zero in the only sense I could test. I scored the bf16 cache, reloaded the model, and scored it again: same NLL to the digit, KL of 0. The engine is deterministic, so the KL above is the cache and not run-to-run noise. I had first tried to get a floor by varying the prefill chunk size, and that came back as zero too, but for a bad reason: the chunk size never reaches the forward pass, so the two arms were the same run. I am not using that zero.

Two things about this table that are easy to misread. The median KL is small (0.012 bits at int8, 0.024 at int4) while the mean is large, which means most positions barely move and a few move a lot. And int4's NLL is lower than bf16's. That is not int4 being more accurate. A quantized cache shifts the distribution, and a lower NLL on one corpus is a sign of that shift, not a quality win. Top-1 agreement is the cleaner summary: int8 keeps the bf16 top token on 89.2% of positions, int4 on 86.6%.

## Tests

```bash
PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest -q tests/cuda/test_flashnext_kvquant.py   # 30 collected
PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest -q tests/cuda/test_flashnext_forward.py   # 16 passed
PYTHONPATH=src python -m pytest -q tests/cuda/test_flashnext_kernels.py   # 35 passed
```

`test_flashnext_kvquant.py` holds 30 tests across the two widths. The checks that matter:

- the kernels write exactly the bits the reference quantizer does, at 8 and at 4 bits, and the scales match ExLlamaV3's own quantizer on the same groups;
- the cache round-trips inside the grid, and packing then unpacking 4-bit codes returns the same codes;
- attention over a quantized cache stays within a stated tolerance of attention over bf16;
- a window of rows matches the same rows computed one at a time (`torch.equal`), and chunked prefill matches one shot;
- drafted decoding matches serial decoding by token-id SHA-256, through `tensorfold serve`, at both widths;
- the end-to-end logits stay close to the bf16 cache.

The host suite, run with the same exclusions as upstream (`--ignore=tests/test_alternating_kv.py --ignore=tests/test_dflash_tree_search.py`), shows the same 4 failures and 130 passes as `upstream/main`. Those 4 are environmental (this box has no MLX) and are present on main.

## Overlap with open PRs

`git merge-tree` is clean against `upstream/main`. It is also clean against #42 (`pr/exl3`), even though the two branches both edit `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-flash-next.md`, `README.md`, `src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/cuda/forward.py`, `src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/__init__.py` and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`. The edits are in different regions and merge without help. I will rebase on #42 if it lands first.

#40 also touches `families/qwen4_exp/cuda/{attention,decode,engine,forward}.py`, and #29 touches `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-flash-next.md` and the MLX-side decode path. I have not merge-tested those two. Both are small overlaps and I will rebase on whichever lands first.

This also answers the request in #23, partly. That issue is a GLM model running out of memory at 64k on two Sparks and asks for an fp8 cache or a `--kv-dtype`. The flag is the one asked for, but the implementation covers Flash Next only. GLM, the 27B and MiMo are not included, and I do not have a GLM checkpoint here to test against.

## What is not claimed

- No long context past 4,121 tokens. I measured at short prompts and at one 4,121-token prompt. 24k, 128k and 262k are not measured. The memory math above says they fit, and the speed there is an extrapolation from the 4k result, not a measurement.
- No EXL3 checkpoint. Everything here is the MLX 4-bit pack. The EXL3 packs need #42, and the speeds in #42 and the speeds here are different models measured on different branches.
- No peak-clock numbers. The SM clock sat at 2502 to 2528 MHz of a 3003 max during these runs. A pinned clock would read higher, and I have not measured by how much.
- int4 is not faster. It is smaller. At short context it is slower than bf16 by about 12% on code, and at 4,000 tokens it is even. Its reason to exist is the 3.17x memory cut, and it costs 13.4 points of top-1 agreement to get there.
- The quality numbers are one corpus of 2,048 positions, teacher-forced. They say how far the distribution moves, not how that shows up in generated text. I did not run a side-by-side generation comparison.
- The indexer keys and pooled block keys are not quantized, so a model whose cache is dominated by those would see a smaller saving than the table suggests. Flash Next is not such a model, but GLM might be, and I have not checked.

items.title: fix: Qwen3.8 Flash Next and 27B on EXL3 checkpoints stop at the end of the chat turn
items.body:
On EXL3 checkpoints of Qwen3.8 Flash Next and Qwen3.8-27B, the CUDA engine does not stop a reply at the end of the chat turn. It reads its stop ids from config.json only: the top-level `eos_token_id`, else `text_config`'s. These packs have no top-level id, and `text_config` names only `<|endoftext|>` (248044). The turn's end, `<|im_end|>` (248046), is listed in `generation_config.json` alone.

So on 0.3.6.1, `Config.read` returns `(248044,)` for turboderp's Flash Next pack (3.05bpw_h5_ng5), for the SAGE Flash Next packs I serve (4.15 bpw, and CYBER-FROST-3.8 at 3.5 bpw), and for turboderp's 27B packs at 3.00 and 4.00 bpw. The MLX checkpoints are fine because they list both ids at the top level.

On one DGX Spark (GB10), CYBER-FROST-3.8-EXL3-SAGE-3.5bpw served on 0.3.6 with a ~16k-token prompt, thinking on and a `get_weather` tool request streamed `<|im_end|>\n<|im_start|>user...` as content, called the tool three times and leaked `<think>` into the answer.

## The change

Both families' `Config.read` now add `generation_config.json`'s `eos_token_id` after config.json's, in order and without duplicates. A checkpoint that names no stop id anywhere raises a `ValueError` instead of failing later.

- `families/qwen4_exp/cuda/weights.py`: a small `stop_ids()` helper, used by `Config.read`.
- `families/qwen3_5/cuda/weights.py`: the same logic inline in `Config.read`.
- `tests/test_flashnext_eos.py` and `tests/test_qwen27b_eos.py`: CPU tests with synthetic configs for the EXL3 layout, the MLX layout, no generation_config.json, scalar values, and no id at all.

`ple_eos` (the n-gram tables' end id) still comes from `text_config`, so the Flash Next n-gram path reads the same id as before.

## Checked

Against the real configs on disk, with this branch at 0.3.6.1, `Config.read` returns:

| Checkpoint | Before | After |
| --- | --- | --- |
| turboderp Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-exl3, 3.05bpw_h5_ng5 | (248044,) | (248044, 248046) |
| Flash Next SAGE 4.15 bpw EXL3 | (248044,) | (248044, 248046) |
| CYBER-FROST-3.8-EXL3-SAGE-3.5bpw | (248044,) | (248044, 248046) |
| turboderp Qwen3.8-27B-exl3, 3.00bpw | (248044,) | (248044, 248046) |
| turboderp Qwen3.8-27B-exl3, 4.00bpw | (248044,) | (248044, 248046) |
| Flash Next MLX 4-bit | (248046, 248044) | (248046, 248044) |
| Vontra Qwen3.8-27B-MLX-4bit | (248046, 248044) | (248046, 248044) |

The new tests pass along with `tests/test_cuda_cli.py` and `tests/test_cuda_build.py` (26 tests, CPU).

End to end on the Spark with the Flash Next change: CYBER-FROST served on 0.3.6 with the same ~16k-token thinking-on prompt and tool request now returns one `get_weather` call with `finish_reason: tool_calls`, and no leaked tags. Its token hash matches 0.3.6 serving a copy of the pack whose config.json lists both ids.

## Not claimed

- I did not serve a 27B EXL3 request end to end. The 27B change is checked by the config reads above and the CPU tests, and it is the same logic as the Flash Next change.
- GLM-5.3-Flash is not changed and not affected: its loader reads `text_config` first, and Mia-AiLab's EXL3 checkpoint lists its three stop ids there.
- Stop ids are the only change. Drafting and exactness are untouched. Drafted and serial replies were not re-checked on this exact branch, but the Flash Next change gave drafted equal to serial 3/3 on 0.3.6.

## Overlap

- #67 also edits `qwen4_exp/cuda/weights.py`. It merges cleanly with this branch.
- #47 (mine, the quantized KV cache) briefly carried the Flash Next half of this fix. I have moved it here and taken it back off that branch.

items.title: feat: read EXL3 checkpoints on CUDA (any codebook, 1 to 8 bits, mixed-K packs)
items.body:
TensorFold's CUDA engines can now read ExLlamaV3's trellis checkpoints (EXL3) in any linear, at whatever width the checkpoint keeps per tensor, with one kernel shared by every family. Two engines use it in this PR: Qwen3.8-27B (2 to 6 bits, `mul1`) and Qwen3.8 Flash Next, including mixed-K packs where one expert matrix sits at 2 bits and the next at 8.

The real checkpoints I have on this box are the 27B at `3.00bpw` and `4.00bpw`, Flash Next's mixed-K SAGE pack and turboderp's `3.05bpw`, and MiMo-V2.6-Flash's `2.50bpw`. `mcg` and `3inst` are verified bit-exact against ExLlamaV3's `reconstruct` on real converter output, 50 of 50 groups each, from partial packs. Their full-pack conversions were still running while I wrote this, so beyond that specific check the two codebooks rest on synthetic data, and I say so below rather than leaving it to be discovered.

Speeds on one DGX Spark, greedy, same client for both engines. The 27B `3.00bpw` pack with the DFlash2 drafter decodes at 63.2 / 45.7 tok/s (code / chat) against ExLlamaV3's 39.6 / 30.1 on the same pack and drafter. Flash Next's SAGE pack reads 47.3 / 67.3 against ExLlamaV3's serial path at 22.3 / 22.2. Drafted replies are identical to `"draft": false` replies by token-id SHA-256 on both families, 30 of 30 replies each. That is the check I ran the most times, because it is the one the engine's contract stands on.

Nothing here changes an existing path. GLM-5.3-Flash's own EXL3 kernel is untouched and the MLX 4-bit engines of both families are unchanged. The diff is 49 files, +5,673 / -37, 8 commits, no merge commits, based on `bb4b4a3`.

What is in it, commit by commit:

- `28ef5a4`, the format, for every codebook and width. `src/tensorfold/cuda/exl3/format.py` parses a checkpoint's tensor groups out of the safetensors headers alone (`trellis` int16 `[K/16, N/16, 16*bits]`, `suh`/`svh` or the packed `su`/`sv` signs, an optional `bias`, and the zero-size `mcg` / `mul1` marker), names the codebook and the width per tensor, and carries a NumPy float64 reference decoder for every codebook at 1 to 8 bits plus the half widths (`mul1`). `decode.cuh` holds the header-only device functions that decode a 16x16 tile straight into the B fragments of two `mma.m16n8k16`. `python -m tensorfold.cuda.exl3.inspect MODEL_DIR` prints what a checkpoint holds from its headers without loading it. A family that reads every codebook and width declares `EXL3_VARIANT = "any"`, and TensorFold then checks `config.json` before anything is downloaded (`src/tensorfold/families/__init__.py`). `pyproject.toml` gains the new `*.cu` / `*.cuh` package data. Tests: `tests/test_exl3_format.py` (a bit-by-bit decoder for all 27 codebook and width combinations, the group parsing, the inspector on a synthetic mixed checkpoint) and `tests/test_unsupported_checkpoints.py` (the refusals). Nothing in this commit imports torch.
- `2be548d`, a row-invariant EXL3 linear, 1 to 128 rows. `src/tensorfold/cuda/exl3/linear.{py,cu,cpp}`: `y = ((((x * suh) @ H_K) @ W_q) @ H_N) * svh + bias`, no cuBLAS, no split-K that depends on the row count, no reduction across rows. The K split and the warps a program uses are a function of `(K, N)` only, the splits are summed in split order, and `mma.m16n8k16` keeps rows independent, which is the CUDA recipe's verify contract. `tools/bench_exl3.py` times it against ExLlamaV3's `LinearEXL3.bc.run` on a checkpoint's own tensors, with CUDA graphs over enough copies to exceed L2. Tests: `tests/cuda/test_exl3_linear.py` (row invariance at 1, 2, 3, 16, 17, 64 and 128 rows, the device decoder against the reference bit for bit, a float64 reference, ExLlamaV3 when it is importable) and `tests/cuda/test_exl3_checkpoint.py` (a real checkpoint's every width against `reconstruct`).
- `b16f2db`, the low-bit loader. At 1 and 2 bits a lane's windows span two 32-bit words, so a warp now loads its k step's words as one coalesced run, takes each tile's two words from their owners by shuffle, and keeps the next k step in flight while the current one decodes. That holds up to 6 bits; at 7 and 8 bits it measured 1 to 2% slower, so those widths load per tile. Same arithmetic in the same order: 2472 outputs over every codebook, width, split and row count are `torch.equal` to the kernel before this commit.
- `1703060`, grouped routed experts, mixed widths inside a layer. `src/tensorfold/cuda/exl3/experts_{grouped.cuh,cu,cpp,cb0.cu,cb1.cu,cb2.cu}` and `experts.py`: one grouped trellis GEMV per projection runs a whole MoE layer in one launch, each expert matrix at its own width (1 to 8 bits in half-bit steps) in any codebook. The codebook is the compilation unit, the widths present in a layer are the instances built, the trellis stays where the checkpoint put it (an expert is a pointer), the grouping happens on the device, and there are no atomics or host synchronisations, so a CUDA graph can capture the pipeline. `tests/cuda/test_exl3_experts.py` runs the decode against a bit-by-bit decoder and against ExLlamaV3's `reconstruct`, rows alone against the same rows in windows of 1, 2, 3, 16, 17, 64 and 128, a float64 reference, graph replay against eager after allocator churn, and the fused down+combine against the two launches it replaces.
- `ad19d4a`, `"return_token_ids"` on the CUDA server (`src/tensorfold/cuda/server.py`, 6 lines). The reply's token ids ride in the response's `tensorfold` block, and in the final chunk with `stream_options.include_tensorfold` when streaming. That is how drafted == serial gets checked through the OpenAI path. Nothing changes for a request that does not ask for it.
- `4b95136`, Qwen3.8-27B on EXL3. `src/tensorfold/families/qwen3_5/cuda/exl3_load.py` fills the same `Config`/`Layer`/`Weights` dataclasses the MLX path fills. The pack's trellis groups run on the shared linear, tensors the pack leaves alone are read as stored, the packs' centred RMSNorm weights (`w - 1`) get their 1 back, and `exl3_load.PLANS` holds the measured `(K split, warps)` per projection shape at 3 and 4 bits, a function of shape and width alone, so a verify window keeps one reduction. `cuda/b16.{cu,cpp,py}` is the plain fp16/bf16 linear for the unquantized tensors (one warp per output, no cuBLAS). `cuda/dflash2.py` lets the DFlash2 drafter read the target's 6-bit head over its draft vocabulary by slicing the head's 128-column strips as stored, so the drafter's logits are the target head's bit for bit and nothing is decoded or requantized. `tests/cuda/test_qwen27_exl3.py` checks that every tuned split keeps a row's bits, a GDN verify window against serial steps on both weight paths, that drafted decoding keeps serial's tokens, and the sliced head against the target head.
- `f836a4b`, Qwen3.8 Flash Next on EXL3. `src/tensorfold/families/qwen4_exp/cuda/exl3.py` (718 lines) fills the same weight structures: dense groups (attention, DeltaNet, MTP, head) on the shared linear with same-input projections stacked side by side, routed experts and the shared expert (as expert 512 of the table) on the grouped kernel at their own widths, the packs' unquantized tensors on an fp16 Triton matmul whose tiles and K split depend on the shape only, and the `ple.ngram_embedding` shards through ExLlamaV3's n-gram row codec, where a row is an fp16 scale and 160 tail-biting `mul1` values, decoded bit for bit like `ngram_dequant`. MTP drafts decode the head's draft-vocabulary rows and requantize them to 4-bit groups for the draft head; verification uses the full EXL3 head. `tests/cuda/test_qwen4_exp_exl3.py` checks the fp16 matmul against fp64 and its row invariance, the n-gram rows bit-equal to the row codec, a real layer's experts against fp64, and the model cut to 4 layers: a window of 1 to 128 rows gives one-row steps' logits bit for bit, a kept prefix continues like serial, and MTP-drafted decoding (eager and in CUDA graphs, greedy and sampled) emits serial's tokens.
- `d409822`, docs and notices. `docs/recipes/exl3.md` (the format, what a family declares, the layer's arithmetic, the kernel table, the traps), `docs/recipes/exl3-universal-experts.md` (the grouped kernel and the measured comparison against ExLlamaV3's two dispatch paths), the EXL3 sections of `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-27b.md` and `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-flash-next.md`, `docs/recipes/cuda.md`, the two recipe lists, `README.md`, `src/tensorfold/families/README.md`, `src/tensorfold/families/qwen3_5/cuda/README.md` (its kernel table gains `b16.cu` and `exl3_load.py`), and `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md`, where the existing ExLlamaV3 entry (MIT, Copyright (c) 2025 Turboderp) now covers the shared module, the grouped expert kernel and the two families' EXL3 readers, and the checkpoints the families list are named with their licenses. The README's speed table and the hero image that mirrors it are unchanged: this PR adds two rows to its checkpoint table (both EXL3 packs, NVIDIA only) and keeps the speeds in the two recipes.

## Measured on a GB10 (DGX Spark)

One DGX Spark (GB10, driver 580.178.04, CUDA 13.0 through torch 2.11.0+cu130, 128 GB unified, SM clock 2405 to 2418 MHz of 3003 during the timing sessions). Every timing row comes from a `gpurun timing` session with the GPU otherwise idle and the page cache of each pack dropped before its server starts. The client is the same for every engine, `tools/bench_openai.py --tokens 64 --reps 5` (one warm-up, seeds 1234-1238, greedy as temperature 0), and the cell is the median of the five. Each column names the commit its numbers came from. "ExLlamaV3" always means the fork at commit `249f22a`, whose package reports `1.5.1.post1`; the commit and the version string name the same tree.

### The kernels, against ExLlamaV3's

Dense linear, `tools/bench_exl3.py`, medians of 9 CUDA-graph replays on an idle GB10, the checkpoint's own tensors, the ExLlamaV3 fork at `249f22a` on the same tensors (`4c37180`; `docs/recipes/exl3.md` carries the same table):

| tensor | bits | bytes | rows | TensorFold | ExLlamaV3 | GB/s ratio |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| MiMo `layers.0.self_attn.q_proj` | 2 | 12.6 MB | 1 | 57.0 us (221 GB/s) | 59.0 us (213 GB/s) | 1.04 |
| MiMo `layers.0.self_attn.q_proj` | 2 | 12.6 MB | 16 | 60.0 us (210 GB/s) | 65.9 us (191 GB/s) | 1.10 |
| MiMo `layers.2.self_attn.o_proj` | 3 | 12.6 MB | 1 | 72.9 us (173 GB/s) | 73.0 us (172 GB/s) | 1.01 |
| MiMo `layers.2.self_attn.o_proj` | 3 | 12.6 MB | 16 | 68.4 us (184 GB/s) | 63.5 us (198 GB/s) | 0.93 |
| MiMo `layers.41.self_attn.o_proj` | 6 | 25.2 MB | 1 | 114.0 us (221 GB/s) | 113.5 us (222 GB/s) | 1.00 |
| MiMo `layers.41.self_attn.o_proj` | 6 | 25.2 MB | 16 | 123.7 us (203 GB/s) | 116.0 us (217 GB/s) | 0.94 |
| MiMo `lm_head` | 6 | 468.7 MB | 1 | 2074.5 us (226 GB/s) | 2071.8 us (226 GB/s) | 1.00 |
| MiMo `lm_head` | 6 | 468.7 MB | 16 | 2113.0 us (222 GB/s) | 2045.8 us (229 GB/s) | 0.97 |

The loader commit (`b16f2db`) measured against the commit before it, same harness, two exclusive slots, GB/s at 1 row: MiMo 2-bit `q_proj` 157 -> 220, 2-bit `o_proj` 76 -> 186, 2-bit `down_proj` 79 -> 193, 3-bit `q_proj` 158 -> 192, 5-bit `q_proj` 188 -> 218, 6-bit `lm_head` 227 -> 232; 27B `3.00bpw` 3-bit `down_proj` 163 -> 194 (160 -> 187 at 8 rows, 153 -> 180 at 16), `4.00bpw` 4-bit `in_proj_qkv` 196 -> 216. Nothing measured got slower, and the 6-bit head cells are within 1.5%. ExLlamaV3's own linear reads 176 to 233 GB/s on the same tensors in the same runs, and the 237 GB/s streaming ceiling of this box is the rest of the gap.

Grouped routed experts, MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL-EXL3 `2.50bpw` real layers (`mul1`, per-expert 2 to 5 bits), `tools/mimo_exl3_bench.py`, medians of 5 reps x 30 iters x 2 sets, GB/s over the trellis bytes actually read (`4c37180`/`f836a4b` parents; `docs/recipes/exl3-universal-experts.md` has the same table with the intermediate row counts):

| layer (expert widths) | rows | TensorFold | TF + CUDA graph | ExLlamaV3 `exl3_moe_mixedk` | ExLlamaV3 `exl3_moe_coop` |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| L3 (2-bit everywhere) | 1 | 179.6 GB/s | 195.6 | 49.9 (3.6x slower) | 177.8 |
| | 8 | 219.6 | 222.0 | 77.8 (2.8x) | 220.2 |
| L30 (2-3 bit) | 1 | 209.7 | 217.2 | 70.5 (3.0x) | not dispatched |
| | 8 | 224.7 | 226.3 | 115.9 (1.9x) | |
| L47 (2-4 bit) | 1 | 204.2 | 209.2 | 86.7 (2.4x) | not dispatched |
| | 8 | 210.3 | 213.5 | 140.0 (1.5x) | |

The part that matters for reading that table: MiMo's layers are mixed-K, so what ExLlamaV3 actually dispatches there is its per-expert `exl3_moe_mixedk` path, and this kernel is 1.5x to 3.6x faster per layer. Where a layer is uniform, ExLlamaV3 dispatches its `coop` kernel instead, and `coop` is still the faster of the two on this box. On the uniform L3 layer the two are within 2% (179.6 against 177.8 at 1 row, 219.6 against 220.2 at 8), and on the GLM-5.3-shaped synthetic 4-bit `mcg` layer `coop` reads 219 to 232 GB/s against 208 to 220 here. This work does not beat `coop` on uniform layers. It removes the mixed-K penalty and lands at `coop`'s level rather than above it. The dense table says the same thing: ExLlamaV3 is ahead on the small-N 3-bit shapes at 16 rows (184 against 198 GB/s) and on the 6-bit 16-row cells (203 against 217, 222 against 229).

### Qwen3.8-27B, EXL3 packs and the MLX 4-bit checkpoint

`tensorfold serve`, or ExLlamaV3's `Generator` behind a minimal OpenAI shim (`-cs 8192`), DFlash2 at its default 7 drafts. Dynamic draft length was slower on every column. Cells are code / chat, as the project's README table has them. Every number in this table comes from `4c37180` on `wip/exl3-engines`, measured before this branch existed, so treat it as this code's numbers rather than this branch's; a re-run on `pr/exl3` is in flight and I will paste it in a comment. The 27B rows use `turboderp/Qwen3.8-27B-exl3` revision `6fe61ad6` (`3.00bpw`) and `113cf7ab` (`4.00bpw`), drafted with `z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2`.

| | GB/token | Code, greedy | Chat, greedy | ExLlamaV3 code / chat, greedy | ratio (ours / theirs) |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| TensorFold, EXL3 3.00bpw + DFlash2 | 10.14 | **63.2** | **45.7** | 39.6 / 30.1 | 1.60 / 1.52 |
| TensorFold, EXL3 4.00bpw + DFlash2 | 13.18 | 52.1 | 45.3 | 35.8 / 25.7 | 1.46 / 1.76 |
| TensorFold, MLX 4-bit + DFlash2 | 14.42 | 48.2 | 44.9 | ExLlamaV3 does not serve it | |
| TensorFold, EXL3 3.00bpw, serial | 10.14 | 16.7 | 16.6 | 16.5 / 16.5 | 1.01 / 1.01 |
| TensorFold, EXL3 4.00bpw, serial | 13.18 | 14.5 | 14.4 | 15.8 / 15.8 | 0.92 / 0.91 |
| TensorFold, MLX 4-bit, serial | 14.42 | 12.8 | 12.8 | ExLlamaV3 does not serve it | |
| BF16 (reference, for the bandwidth floor) | 51.25 | n/a | n/a | n/a | n/a |

`GB/token` is the weight bytes one serial decode step reads (every linear, the head, one embedding row, the norms) at the bits per weight the engine actually holds. The bandwidth floor at the measured 237 GB/s streaming ceiling of this box is 23.4 tok/s at `3.00bpw` and 18.0 at `4.00bpw`, and the measured serial step is 16.7 and 14.5, so a step is 59.4 ms of wall time against a 42.8 ms floor. On the GPU that step is 57.8 ms, of which the EXL3 projections are 51.9 ms for 10.1 GB (194 GB/s) and the 6-bit head alone 238 GB/s. What is left is drafting: the tree verifies several rows a round, and the recipe's step profile plus the `--no-drafts` rows above is the bookkeeping behind it. Sampled columns are in `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-27b.md`; 3.00bpw code sampled is 82.1 (ours) against 45.0 (ExLlamaV3).

Quality, same eval set and engine, teacher-forced (`~/tfwork/results/qwen27b-quality.md`; wikitext-2 test, 16 x 1024-token windows, 16,368 scored positions, full 248,320-token vocabulary, fp64 sums):

| checkpoint | bits/weight body / head | GB/token | NLL | dNLL vs BF16 | top-1 vs BF16 | mean KLD |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| BF16 (reference) | 16 / 16 | 51.25 | 2.0328 | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| EXL3 2.50bpw | 2.517 / 6.00 | 8.62 | 2.0775 | +0.0447 | 0.8759 | 0.0854 |
| EXL3 3.00bpw | 3.017 / 6.00 | 10.14 | 2.0430 | +0.0102 | 0.9126 | 0.0431 |
| EXL3 4.00bpw | 4.016 / 6.00 | 13.18 | 2.0400 | +0.0072 | 0.9534 | 0.0122 |
| MLX 4-bit | 4.501 / 4.50 | 14.42 | 2.0640 | +0.0312 | 0.8975 | 0.0480 |
| EXL3 5.00bpw | 5.015 / 6.00 | 16.22 | 2.0361 | +0.0033 | 0.9693 | 0.0042 |

The 3.00bpw pack beats the MLX 4-bit checkpoint on every measure here and is cheaper to read (KLD 0.0431 against 0.0480, 10.14 against 14.42 GB/token) even though the MLX pack is nominally wider. The arithmetic floor of this measurement is KLD 2.11e-04, because the engine returns bf16 logits. Brackets and the row-level caveats are in the file the table comes from.

### Qwen3.8 Flash Next, both EXL3 packs

Cells are code / chat, greedy and sampled, median of seeds 1234-1238. Every number here comes from `5e76c85` on `wip/flashnext-exl3`, measured before this branch existed. ExLlamaV3 (`249f22a`) has no draft support for this model, so its column is its serial path.

| pack | engine | Code, sampled | Chat, sampled | Code, greedy | Chat, greedy |
| --- | --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| mixed-K SAGE 4.15bpw (2-8 bits) | TensorFold, MTP drafts | **58.2** | 52.0 | 47.3 | **67.3** |
| | TensorFold, serial | 34.3 | 34.0 | 34.5 | 33.5 |
| | ExLlamaV3, serial | 22.3 | 22.2 | 22.3 | 22.2 |
| turboderp 3.05bpw | TensorFold, MTP drafts | **79.1** | 56.3 | **79.0** | 62.4 |
| | TensorFold, serial | 34.9 | 34.9 | 35.1 | 35.0 |
| | ExLlamaV3, serial | 37.0 | 36.9 | 37.1 | 36.9 |
| MLX 4-bit (the existing path) | TensorFold, MTP drafts | 66.8 | 59.4 | 71.8 | 58.6 |
| | TensorFold, serial | 36.8 | 36.7 | 37.0 | 36.8 |

Two things about that table. The SAGE pack's code prompt emits a real `<think>` block where the other packs and the chat prompt do not, so SAGE's drafted row is a much longer reply than its neighbours: the numbers are real, the comparison across packs is not, though SAGE's own serial against drafted pair is. And SAGE is a mixed-K pack of ours, so it is the one row here with no ExLlamaV3 counterpart for drafting at all.

Serially, on the mixed-K pack TensorFold is 1.51x to 1.55x ExLlamaV3's serial path, and on the uniform 3.05bpw pack it is 5 to 6% behind it (34.9 against 37.0). That pack is one ExLlamaV3 has tuned for, and it is the one place in this PR where ExLlamaV3's serial decode wins. Both EXL3 packs are also 5 to 9% behind TensorFold's own MLX 4-bit path in serial. With drafts, both packs beat ExLlamaV3's serial speed by 1.5x to 2.1x.

On the same packs, teacher-forced over 2,048 positions, the two engines' mean NLLs agree within 0.0005 (SAGE 1.0640 against 1.0642; 3.05bpw 0.8510 against 0.8506) and their top-1 accuracies within half a point (0.718 against 0.720; 0.774 against 0.779). The per-position NLL difference has a mean absolute value of about 0.10 and a median of 0.018 / 0.011, which sounds large next to the agreement figures, so here is the context: ExLlamaV3 reproduces its own top-1 on only 96.4% (SAGE) and 97.2% (3.05bpw) of positions when the same text is split differently, meaning the first 1,025 tokens on their own instead of as part of all 2,049. Where its top two logits are at least 0.5 apart the two engines agree on 98.8% / 99.1% of positions, and 99.7% at a gap of 1.0. Two engines that keep near-ties differently look like this.

Measured after this branch was frozen, and belonging to the follow-up PR rather than this one: the same `3.05bpw` pack with TensorFold's newer default drafting policy (depth 6, confidence 0.6) reads 91.6 / 71.8 / 55.3 tok/s (code / devops / prose, 400 tokens, min-median-max of 3) against TabbyAPI on this box at 87.2 / 63.9 / 54.9, with serial at 36.0 to 36.1 and the best policy measured at 94.5 (depth 7, confidence 0.75). At 128 tokens it is 77.1 / 59.4 / 54.1 against 76.2 / 56.7 / 55.1, at 64 tokens 82.4 / 56.7 / 56.6 against 83.6 / 57.6 / 61.2, so prose is behind at very short replies. Time to first token is 0.14 to 0.18 s against 0.51 to 0.77 s. TabbyAPI runs the recipe's 8-bit KV where ours is bf16. Nothing on this box reached 100 tok/s in any arm: the best single request was 94.46 (TensorFold, code, 400 tokens), then exllamav3's 89.52 and the recipe's own `chat.py` at 80.04. Greedy replies diverge between the two engines inside the first 10% of the reply (first differing token: code 7 of 400, devops 48, prose 26). TensorFold's replies are identical across repeats, TabbyAPI's are not. Those numbers, the policy sweep and the changes behind them live in `~/tfwork/results/flashnext-recipe.md`.

## Tests

Host suite, no GPU, the same command and `--ignore` set on every tree:

```bash
PYTHONPATH=<tree>/src python -m pytest tests -q -p no:cacheprovider -rf \
  --ignore=tests/test_alternating_kv.py --ignore=tests/test_dflash_tree_search.py
```

- `upstream/main` `bb4b4a3`: 4 failed, 130 passed, 27 skipped in a venv with no torch (`~/tfwork/venv-notorch`: numpy, tokenizers, jinja2, safetensors, huggingface_hub, pytest), and 4 failed, 130 passed, 27 skipped with torch present (`~/tensorfold/venv`, `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=`).
- Every commit of this branch, `28ef5a4` through `d409822`, same command on the no-torch venv: 4 failed, 167 passed, 28 skipped, the same counts on all eight commits. `d409822` on the torch venv: 4 failed, 168 passed, 27 skipped. The 27 against 28 skip difference between those two rows is the venv, where one MLX-only test skips rather than passes when torch is present, not the branch.
- The same four failures appear on all three trees, all present on `upstream/main`, none of them ours: this box has no MLX (`test_nucleus_without_top_k_matches_the_whole_vocabulary_draw` imports `mlx.core`), the CLI refuses a model with no CUDA engine before the context check (`test_context_override_cannot_exceed_model_window`), and the other two import a family's MLX kernel package (`test_every_family_names_an_importable_kernel_version`, `test_serve_finishes_a_config_only_cache_before_loading`).
- The two files that carry the new format's tests on the tip: `tests/test_exl3_format.py` 36 passed, 1 skipped (no-torch venv), and `tests/test_unsupported_checkpoints.py` 9 passed, against 8 on `upstream/main`.
- Logs: `~/tfwork/scratch/p/host/summary.txt` and `~/tfwork/scratch/p/host/notorch_<rev>.log`.

CUDA tests, run from the installed wheel built at the tip with nothing on `sys.path` but the wheel. The tests are copied out of `git archive d409822` with `--rootdir` outside the source tree, so a stale source tree cannot be what ran. One file per invocation, so each count stands on its own, with `ninja` on `PATH` and a fresh `TORCH_EXTENSIONS_DIR`:

```bash
TENSORFOLD_EXL3_MODEL=<MiMo-V2.6-Flash-RL-EXL3 2.50bpw> \
  python -m pytest -q tests/cuda/test_exl3_linear.py        # 56 passed
  python -m pytest -q tests/cuda/test_exl3_checkpoint.py    #  9 passed
  python -m pytest -q tests/cuda/test_exl3_experts.py       # 85 passed, 18 skipped
  python -m pytest -q tests/test_exl3_format.py             # 37 passed  (host, no GPU)
TENSORFOLD_QWEN27_EXL3=<qwen27b-exl3-3.00bpw> TENSORFOLD_QWEN27_DRAFTER=<z-lab/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2> \
  python -m pytest -q tests/cuda/test_qwen27_exl3.py        # 14 passed
TENSORFOLD_EXL3_FLASHNEXT=<flashnext-exl3-sage-4.15bpw> \
  python -m pytest -q tests/cuda/test_qwen4_exp_exl3.py     # 16 passed
```

The 18 skips in the expert file are the ExLlamaV3 comparison cells this ExLlamaV3 fork cannot instantiate: the half-integer widths only exist with `mul1`, and its `reconstruct` stops at 3.5. After the run the extension cache held six `.so` files for six extension directories, so every kernel this branch ships got built from this source inside the run.

One thing worth knowing about that first attempt: it failed with 187 errors, and the cause was environmental, not this branch. The JIT builds died because `ninja` was not on `PATH`, which left empty extension directories behind, and the next import of each of those found a directory with no `.so`. Those runs are not in the numbers above. If you build these tests yourself, put `ninja` on `PATH` and clear `TORCH_EXTENSIONS_DIR` first.

Per-commit evidence. Each commit checked out detached in its own worktree (`~/tfwork/wt/p-commits`) with its own `TORCH_EXTENSIONS_DIR`, because the two linear commits share the extension name `tensorfold_exl3_linear_v2` and no commit should be served another's `.so`. Real packs named by the same environment variables.

| commit | what it is | its own tests |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `28ef5a4` | the format and the refusals | 46 passed (`tests/test_exl3_format.py` + `tests/test_unsupported_checkpoints.py`) |
| `2be548d` | the row-invariant linear | 65 passed (`tests/cuda/test_exl3_linear.py` + `test_exl3_checkpoint.py`) |
| `b16f2db` | the low-bit loader | 65 passed (the same two files, on the changed kernel) |
| `1703060` | the grouped experts | 85 passed, 18 skipped (`tests/cuda/test_exl3_experts.py`) |
| `4b95136` | Qwen3.8-27B | on the tip: 14 passed (`tests/cuda/test_qwen27_exl3.py`, 66 s). The per-commit run got 8 passed and then hung in `test_window_rows_equal_serial_steps`, ten minutes asleep with the GPU idle, so it was killed and is not counted. Re-run afterwards at this commit with its own `TORCH_EXTENSIONS_DIR`: 35 s, passed. The hang was a build lock in the extension directory that eight commits shared |
| `f836a4b` | Flash Next | 16 passed (`tests/cuda/test_qwen4_exp_exl3.py`) |
| `ad19d4a` | `return_token_ids` | server imports and starts clean (9 skipped in that run; no GPU) |
| `d409822` | docs only | 11 changed markdown files listed, package imports clean |

Row invariance and exactness, as the recipe book asks (`torch.equal`, never `allclose`):

- the dense linear at 1, 2, 3, 16, 17, 64 and 128 rows, every codebook and width, against the 1-row result (`tests/cuda/test_exl3_linear.py`);
- the grouped experts at the same row counts and widths, plus a real MiMo layer's rows alone against an 8-row window (`tests/cuda/test_exl3_experts.py`);
- both the linear and the expert kernels equal ExLlamaV3's `reconstruct` bit for bit;
- the grouped pipeline is `torch.equal` to GLM-5.3-Flash's own `exl3_mm.routed` on 4-bit `mcg` data, GLM's arithmetic in the same order, and within 2e-4 relative of a float64 `reconstruct`-based reference;
- on the 27B, a GDN verify window equals serial steps and the drafter's sliced head equals the target head bit for bit; on Flash Next, a 1-to-128-row window gives one-row steps' logits bit for bit.

Drafted == serial through `tensorfold serve`, comparing the token-id SHA-256 of every reply between `"draft": false` and drafts on (two prompts, the raw prompt as chat, two 256-token chats, greedy and seeds 1234-1238):

- Flash Next 3.05bpw + MTP: 30 of 30 replies equal (4,224 tokens, 1,337 rounds, 3.16 tokens a round) on `5e76c85`, and the same 30 of 30 with the same aggregates on `pr/exl3` at `d409822`, from the installed wheel through `tensorfold serve` (`~/tfwork/results/p/sha_fn-3.05.json`).
- Qwen3.8-27B 3.00bpw + DFlash2: 30 of 30 replies equal (4,224 token ids, 926 rounds) on `pr/exl3` at `d409822` (`~/tfwork/results/p/sha_q27-3.00.json`). The 27B server does not report draft tallies the way Flash Next's does. The same harness on `wip/exl3-engines` at `4c37180` gave 12 of 12 replies on `3.00bpw` and 12 of 12 on `4.00bpw`, greedy and five seeds.
- Flash Next's SAGE pack: 30 of 30 replies equal on `5e76c85` (4,224 tokens, 1,444 rounds, 2.93 tokens a round).

Style and hygiene. LF in the index, `git diff --check` clean, `git ls-files --eol` i/lf for every file I touched. No version bump. Torch is imported only inside engine modules, since the CLI imports every family on the Mac too. New `*.cu`/`*.cuh` package data in `pyproject.toml`. Versioned extension names (`tensorfold_exl3_linear_v2`, `tensorfold_exl3_experts_v1`). `ruff check --select E4,E7,E9,F,E501,W --line-length 120` over the 27 changed `.py` files reports 17 findings; the same command on the 13 of those files that exist on `upstream/main` reports 10, all of them still present (5 E501, 4 E741, 1 F401). The 7 new ones are all E741, using `I` as the expert width in `cuda/exl3/experts.py` and its test, a rule the tree already carries 50 of. I can fold a rename in if you would rather have those files clean.

## Overlap with other open PRs

Checked with `git merge-tree --write-tree` against each open external PR's head as I wrote this, and by intersecting changed-file lists:

| PR | files we both touch | `git merge-tree` vs `pr/exl3` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| #9 | `README.md`, `docs/recipes/README.md`, `src/tensorfold/families/README.md`, `THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md` | conflicts: `README.md`, `docs/recipes/README.md` (both merge cleanly with `upstream/main`) |
| #10 | `README.md`, `docs/recipes/README.md` | conflict: `README.md` (clean with `upstream/main`) |
| #28 | `README.md` | clean |
| #29 | `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-flash-next.md`, `docs/recipes/README.md`, `README.md`, `src/tensorfold/families/__init__.py` | clean |
| #34 | `docs/recipes/qwen3.8-27b.md`, `README.md`, `src/tensorfold/families/qwen3_5/__init__.py` | clean |
| #35 | `src/tensorfold/cuda/server.py` | clean |
| #37 | `README.md` | clean |

I will rebase on whichever of those lands first. The only real overlap is a table row and a list line in `README.md` and `docs/recipes/README.md`, so it is a small conflict either way.

## What is not claimed

- GLM-5.3-Flash on a real EXL3 checkpoint was not run here. Its own path (`families/glm5_next/cuda/exl3.py`, 4-bit `mcg`, routed experts only) is untouched by this PR, and there was no GLM EXL3 checkpoint on this box. What I checked is parity on GLM-5.3-shaped synthetic 4-bit `mcg` data against GLM's own `exl3_mm.routed`, `torch.equal`, not on a real GLM pack.
- Codebooks on real checkpoints. `mul1` is verified on real packs: every quantized tensor of `turboderp/Qwen3.8-27B-exl3` `4.00bpw` decodes bit for bit like ExLlamaV3's `reconstruct`, 409 of 409 groups, and the same holds for the MiMo pack and the Flash Next packs through their family tests. `mcg` and `3inst` have real partial packs here, 50 of 50 groups each and bit-exact, including the `mcg` marker values and the absence of markers in `3inst`. The full-pack conversions for `mcg`, `3inst` and a mixed per-tensor recipe were still running, so I have not measured agreement, NLL or speed on those packs. Everything else about those two codebooks, and the half-bit widths, rests on synthetic data plus the NumPy reference and the bit-by-bit decoder, plus the 4-bit `mcg` parity above.
- Where ExLlamaV3 is still faster. Its uniform `exl3_moe_coop` path reads 219 to 232 GB/s on uniform layers against 208 to 220 here, up to about 5%. Its `LinearEXL3` wins several 16-row cells of the dense table (3-bit small-N: 198 against 184 GB/s; 6-bit: 217 against 203 and 229 against 222). On the 27B's `4.00bpw` pack its serial decode is 10% ahead (15.8 against 14.5 tok/s), and on Flash Next's uniform 3.05bpw pack 5 to 6% ahead (37.0 against 34.9).
- Quantization quality is measured for the 27B only, and only against a BF16 reference. The Flash Next agreement table is against ExLlamaV3, not against a BF16 forward. Row invariance says nothing about whether serial output is right.
- No 8-bit KV cache for these families. TensorFold has none for `qwen3_5` or `qwen4_exp`, so every long-context number here is a bf16 KV cache against the recipe's `-cq 8,8`. The engine's context capacity is fixed at start and one stream decodes at a time, both documented in the two recipes' Limits sections.
- Prefill is not tuned. It runs 64-row chunks through the decode kernels, so prompt processing is slower than a dedicated prefill kernel would be.

## Not in this PR

MiMo-V2.6-Flash's engine is a follow-up: the grouped expert kernel this PR adds is what it needs, but its reader, its bench and its numbers are not here. The Flash Next serving improvements measured while this branch was frozen are also a follow-up, covering per-shape K splits, the graph-captured draft pick, 128-row prefill chunks instead of 64, and the depth-6 / confidence-0.6 default drafting policy that takes the `3.05bpw` pack to 91.6 / 71.8 / 55.3 tok/s at 400 tokens against TabbyAPI's 87.2 / 63.9 / 54.9 on the same box. Their numbers, tables and method are in `~/tfwork/results/flashnext-recipe.md`, and none of it is in any commit of this branch. One line to be plain about where that stands: cold 24k prefill is 481 tok/s against TabbyAPI's 642 on this box and the recipe's published 1,129, so prefill is the known weak spot rather than decoding. Both follow-ups are separate PRs, offered once this one is in and rebased on it.

If you would rather review this in two pieces, the kernel infrastructure (`cuda/exl3/*` plus the server's `return_token_ids`) and then the two families that use it, say so and I will split it at that boundary. That is exactly where the branch's commits already fall.

items.title: feat: GLM-5.3-Flash on Apple Silicon (glm5_next MLX family) — rebased on 0.3.4
items.body:
Rebased onto 0.3.4.1 (bb4b4a3) and grown a little since the last push: GLM-5.3-Flash rides the lane engine's family rounds on a Mac, prefills on the 2,048-token grid like every other family, reads mixed-bit (5/6/8-bit override) checkpoints through the same row-exact path, and carries kingjamez's M5 Ultra fixes. Thank you both for testing — the two comments below shaped most of what changed.

**What is in the branch now (13 commits on bb4b4a3)**

- **0.3.4 / 0.3.4.1.** `glm5_next` says `LANES = True`; `runtime.GLMFlash` speaks `engine/lane_family.py`'s contract (`exact_width` and `window_costs` measured on the real weights at load, `speculate` / `settle` / `unspeculate` for the MTP head, `gpu_tokens` so the serial reference runs one step ahead, `engine_settings` for the row cap). The engine's cost-based depth rule replaces the old `depth_for`. Prompts go through `_family_feed` on the engine's grid, so `tests/test_family_prefill_grid.py` and the resume-from-a-grid-point behaviour apply to this family unchanged; the serial-engine commit is gone with the engine.
- **kingjamez's M5 Ultra findings (folded from the comment; co-authored in the commit).** `MLX_ENABLE_TF32=0` set in `tensorfold/__init__.py` before mlx loads (an explicit value wins) — the row kernels repeat MLX's fp32 order, so prefill and decode only agree bit for bit in fp32. GLM-5.3's template ignores `enable_thinking`; a trailing bare `<think>` is now closed as `<think></think>` when thinking is off, with his unit test. `TF_GLM5_SPLIT_SHARED` override. The MTP head reads the final-normed row by default (`TF_GLM_MTP_INPUT=normed`, `raw` restores the streams' mean): +1.0 point of first-draft acceptance and 86.9 → 87.9 tok/s on his M5, 61–76 → 66–78% and +0.5 tok/s on our M3 Ultra; drafts only, so exactness is unchanged. Not folded: `VERIFY_MS_M5` / `depth_for`, because 0.3.4 measures each window's cost on the machine at load and picks the depth from that — his M5 timings are now read off the GPU itself.
- **Mixed-bit checkpoints (YJesus's question).** `families/glm5_next/layouts.py` maps the mlx-lm / oMLX converted layout onto the loader's names (fused `conv1d` [3C,T,1], `forget_gate.*`, the absorbed `embed_q` / `unembed_out` pair in place of `kv_b_proj`, `mtp.0.*` with a bf16 `eh_proj`, a vision tower to skip, per-tensor `quantization` overrides). A stack whose parts differ in bits stays separate parts (`QSplit`); `project` runs each at its own width. The kernels grew 8-, 6- and 5-bit `qmv_rows` / `expert_qmv` / `qmv_quad_rows` variants from MLX 0.32.2's one-row `qmv_fast` / `qmv_quad` loops (`fast_shape` = MLX's own rule), and the fused MoE takes an 8-bit shared expert beside 4-bit routed experts, so a mixed-bit checkpoint decodes through the fused, row-invariant path rather than one MLX call per row. Validated on grant-ai's abliterated mixed-bit conversion (554 per-tensor overrides — the same count Vontra's `GLM-5.3-Flash-MLX-oQ4-MTP` card lists): load-time `rows_match_serial` passes on the full model, drafted == `"draft": false`, 36.8 → 46.3 tok/s once the 8-bit tensors took the fused path. We have not loaded Vontra's oQ4 checkpoint itself — more on that in the reply below.

**Measured, this branch, drafted replies byte-identical to `"draft": false` (content, reasoning, assembled tool calls)**

| machine | checkpoint | decode tok/s (greedy, drafted) | serial | exact |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| M3 Ultra 60-core, 256 GB (S4), MLX 0.32.2, `--context 1048576 --mtp-drafts 1` | Vontra 4-bit MTP | 58.9 (glm_exact harness) / 57.6 (200-token mark, 2 passes) | 48.8 | 15/15 (6 greedy, 6 seeded T 0.6–1.0 top-p/top-k, tool call + result leg, 32K context) |
| M3 Ultra 80-core, 512 GB (S2), production 0.3.0-based build, same kernels | Vontra 4-bit MTP | 62.9 | — | kit G3 5/5 |
| M3 Ultra 60-core, 256 GB (S5), 0.3.0-based build + these kernels | grant-ai abliterated mixed-bit | 46.3 (from 36.8 before the 8-bit kernels) | — | kit G3 5/5, load-time rows_match_serial |
| M5 Ultra, 256 GB — **kingjamez's numbers**, an earlier head of this PR | Vontra 4-bit MTP | 87.6 (88.2 sampled; 127.1 on a 1,040-token edit at `--mtp-drafts 4`) | 68.8 | 12/12 |

- Load-time check on S4 today: every window up to 16 rows gives each row its one-row bits; forward ms by width 1: 20.5, 2: 27.8, 3: 36.3, 4: 45.6, 8: 84.7.
- Prefill on this branch is the reference path (317 tok/s at 8K, 263 at 32K on S4, cold, sliding with context); the flat absorbed-latent prefill is a separate PR stacked on this one (PR #39) so it can be judged on its own.
- Full suite on the Mac (`pytest tests`, S4): **392 passed, 71 skipped** (CUDA + real-weights).
- Against the 0.3.0 serial engine the family rounds still cost this family a little on the M3 Ultra (59.5 vs ~57 tok/s at one draft, measured last night, 4 passes each); noting it rather than hiding it. The rounds are GPU-bound; at ~9 GB of weights a token the floor on this GPU is near 14.5 ms, so 100 tok/s on an M3 Ultra needs fewer bytes a token, not more fusion. kingjamez's serial step on the M5 Ultra is 14.5 ms with a floor near 10.

Thanks to Ash for the recipe book (the strategy-C method is how every one of these numbers was found), to the mlx-vlm authors (#2105 KDA kernel, #2245 indexed sparse attention, ported with notices), to oMLX for the reference runtime, and to kingjamez and YJesus for testing and asking. All numbers are logged runs, same prompts each time.

— Chad

items.title: perf: Flash Next prefill path on the grid, 1.4-2.5x faster prompts, still exact
items.body:
0.3.4.1 prefills Flash Next prompts through MLX's forward on the 2,048-token grid. It's exact across resumes, but
MLX's forward attends over every key, so prompts slow down as the context grows, and so do follow-up turns. A
follow-up turn prefills again from the last grid point. This PR adds a prefill path for prompt chunks of more than
16 rows. It runs on the same grid with the same exactness, and `TF_FLASH_PREFILL=0` goes back to MLX's forward.

Measured on an M3 Ultra (256 GB, MLX 0.32.2) with the 4-bit MTP conversion, through the server at
`--context 153600 --prompt-cache-gib 24`. The follow-up is a turn of about 440 new tokens on the cached prefix,
which prefills 1.8k–2.2k tokens again from the grid point.

| Prompt | 0.3.4.1 cold TTFT | This PR cold TTFT | 0.3.4.1 follow-up | This PR follow-up |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 30k | 43.9 s (684 tok/s) | **31.7 s** (948) | 3.08 s | **1.95 s** |
| 100k | 215.1 s (465) | **105.8 s** (945) | 7.97 s | **3.17 s** |
| 145k | 386.7 s (375) | **157.3 s** (922) | 10.39 s | **3.32 s** |

Peak memory stays near the weights and caches, as 0.3.4.1 intends. In process at 32k and 100k, the prefill path
peaks at 113 / 115 GiB, against 110 / 113 GiB for MLX's forward.

## What changed

- **Sparse attention in prompt chunks** (`SparseAttention._sparse_rows`). A chunk past the indexer's budget uses
  the decode's own block selection (`index_select`: fp32 scores, radix top 512, ties to the lower block). A new
  grouped-query kernel, `prefill.attention_rows_gqa`, reads only each row's selected blocks and tail:
  - one threadgroup per KV head, row and quarter of the row's keys;
  - the 12 query heads of a KV head share each 16-key tile in threadgroup memory;
  - the quarters merge in order, as in the decode kernel.
- **Hyper-connections through the fused decode's kernels** (`prefill_hc.py`), with MLX's matmuls between them. The
  n-gram rows come from the decode's lookup tables, bit-identical.
- **MLX's own 4-bit kernels with prefill tiles** (`prefill_mm.py`, compiled at runtime from the headers MLX ships),
  bit-identical to MLX where they run:
  - `qmm_t_impl` with 64×64 or 64×32 tiles;
  - `affine_gather_qmm_rhs` with its alignment as template arguments (2–7% faster).

  They step aside, leaving the matmul to MLX:
  - where MLX splits K;
  - on GPUs with the M5's tensor units;
  - if they fail a once-per-process check against MLX's bits.
- **DeltaNet's four in-projections** go through the fused decode's stacked matrix as one matmul.
- **The MoE** sorts its rows by expert and sums the sorted outputs without unsorting them.
- **Slices of 2 layers are queued ahead of the GPU** (`prefill_hc.QUEUE_LAYERS`). This mirrors 0.3.4.1's queue
  for MLX's forward, and the bits are the same however the graph is sliced (checked on the real model: hidden
  states and all 121 cache arrays).
- **Prefix-snapshot keys** name the forward that prefilled them (`FlashNext.prefill_key`, via a `prefill_key` hook in
  `families.kernel_version`), so a snapshot from the other forward is never resumed.
- **Docs:**
  - a Prefill section in the Flash Next recipe;
  - the recipe book's "A known limit" rewritten as "Resumed prompts" (since 0.3.4.1, resumed prompts are exact);
  - the README's link to it.

## Exactness

**Resumed equals fresh.** I sent three two-turn conversations: 9k, 30k and 61k tokens of code, thinking on,
seeded sampling, 900-token replies. Each turn 2 resumed from turn 1's cache was compared with the same turn 2 sent
to a restarted server with nothing cached, including no saved session snapshots.

| | Result |
| --- | --- |
| This PR's prefill path on the grid | **3 of 3** byte-identical |
| The same path prefilled anywhere (control) | 0 of 3 |

**Quality.** The prefill path rounds differently from MLX's forward. Attention sums keys in another order, and
the hyper-connections use the fused decode's arithmetic. So the check is quality against MLX's own rounding
noise (its 1,024-token chunks instead of 2,048). The measure is teacher-forced NLL and top-1 accuracy on the next
1,024 tokens of real text:

| Context | MLX's forward | Its 1,024-token chunks (noise) | Prefill path |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| 8k | 1.8653 / 53.6% | 1.8660 / 54.6% | 1.8713 / 54.3% |
| 32k | 0.7838 / 78.2% | 0.7839 / 78.0% | 0.7817 / 78.5% |
| 100k | 0.5513 / 86.1% | 0.5499 / 86.1% | 0.5453 / 85.8% |

**Decoding is unchanged.** Drafted replies were byte-identical to `"draft": false` at 40k, both greedy and seeded.
Without drafts, prose and code decode at 89.1 / 88.8 tok/s, against 89.0 / 88.7 on 0.3.4.1.

## Validation

- `tests/test_qwen4_exp_prefill.py` has 19 GPU tests:
  - each kernel against MLX (bit for bit) or the reference module;
  - the index selection against the reference's fp32 scores;
  - the fall-back paths (M5 tensor units, a failed self-check, a kernel that doesn't build);
  - snapshot keys;
  - a 4-layer model end to end: the prefill path and the bf16 reference must land equally close to an fp32
    forward. It is mutation-checked: dropping the PLE term, or offsetting the indexer's RoPE, fails it.
- Full suite: 322 passed, 69 skipped (CUDA), on MLX 0.32.2 and on 0.31.2 (the oldest allowed).
- Server checks with the prefill path:
  - a passphrase found at 50% of a 100k prompt and at 20% and 80% of 145k ones;
  - a valid `edit_file` tool call on a 25k-token prompt;
  - a 5k-character file rewritten byte for byte after 31k and 61k tokens of other code.

## Not measured, and possible next steps

- Only the M3 Ultra was measured. On an M5, the matmuls stay MLX's, while the attention and hyper-connection
  kernels still apply; it's worth a run on the M5 Max.
- A 4,096-token grid for Flash Next would be a little faster. On 0.3.4 with 4,096-token chunks, this path ran
  1,040–1,073 tok/s cold, and follow-ups at 100k–145k took 2.4–2.6 s. The 2,048 grid is kept here to match the
  engine.
- The CUDA engine is untouched.
